$comment: Content for Change Makers (node g34, ages 15-18, Chapter 5): NEW v2 build to GDD 34 (mechanic-embodying),
the campaign / collective-change node (Thread E · Gender & Respect). Scales Lead the Way (g33) into organised,
collective change: pick a cause you care about (gender equality, GBV, or any community issue), make a plan,
build a movement, measure impact, and take a real, safe first step. 84 researched, India-grounded scenarios
across find-your-cause → make-the-plan → build-the-movement → the-law-as-a-tool → make-it-stick → launch-it,
each encoded as one of the shared v2 play actions (branch / reflect / sort / strike-rewrite / match / role-play
/ spot): no binary "tap the right card". Lead: branch (your move), sort, strike-rewrite. Change is possible
AND practical; start small and real; almost nothing meaningful is achieved alone; activism must be SAFE,
LAWFUL, NON-VIOLENT, ETHICAL, SUSTAINABLE and, for sensitive causes, backed by trusted adults or institutions.
The law is a tool: India has real laws against GBV and for equality (Domestic Violence Act 2005, POSH Act 2013,
Dowry Prohibition Act, BNS 2023) plus helplines (181, 1098, 112) a campaign can use and point people to.
India: student councils, panchayats, NGOs, Beti Bachao Beti Padhao; India's own young changemakers. Builds on
g26 & g33; pairs g35 (Justice League) for rights & redress. gameId "change-makers".
title: Change Makers
greet: Hey, I’m Lensy. ✊ Change is possible and practical. Pick a cause, make a plan, build a movement, and take a real first step: not alone, safe and lawful.

badge.title: Change Makers ✊
badge.blurb: You can find a cause, make a real plan, build a movement, use the law as a tool, and take a safe, lawful, ethical first step that lasts. 🌱

helpLine: Keep it safe, with trusted adults. The law is on your side (Domestic Violence Act 2005, POSH Act 2013, BNS 2023), plus helplines: 181, Childline 1098, 112.
reassure: You don’t have to do this alone or take risks. Keep it safe and lawful; for sensitive causes work with trusted adults. If anyone’s in danger: 181, 1098, 112. ✊

scenarios.hook: "You're too young and small to change anything."

myth.un: You're too young and small to change anything.
myth.re: Young people have driven major change throughout history; you don't have to be older or in charge.
myth.why: Most movements started with ordinary young people.

scenarios.relearn: You're not too young to make change; young people always have.

scenarios.hook: "Real change has to be loud, huge and radical."

myth.un: Change has to be loud, huge and radical.
myth.re: The most durable change usually starts small, specific and collaborative.
myth.why: Big change is built from small, concrete steps.

scenarios.relearn: Durable change usually starts small, specific and together, not loud.

scenarios.hook: You care about many issues, from gender fairness to hostel safety, and don't know where to start.

steps.prompt: Your friend asks which one you'll work on. What do you do?

options.text: Take on all of them at once in one big plan
options.then: The list keeps growing. By week's end, nothing has moved.

options.text: Pick whichever is trending online this week
options.then: It gets attention, but you're not sure you care about it.

options.text: Pick one you care about and can act on locally
options.then: You choose fairer chores in your hostel. It feels real and doable.

options.text: Wait until the perfect cause finds you
options.then: Weeks pass. Your notebook of causes grows, and you start none.

steps.why: One cause you care about and can act on gives a real starting point.

steps.prompt: A classmate asks what makes a cause worth your effort. What do you say?

options.text: Because it's popular and everyone is talking about it
options.then: She shrugs. "Popular things fade."

options.text: Because someone has to, and I'm the only one
options.then: She looks concerned. "You don't have to do it alone."

options.text: I haven't decided yet and might change it next week
options.then: She nods. "Then I can't really help you yet."

options.text: It matters to me, and I can act on it here
options.then: She nods. "That's a real reason."

steps.why: A real, local, personal reason gives your cause staying power.

steps.prompt: A teacher suggests testing your cause with one small action this month. What do you do?

options.text: Plan a big event to show you're serious
options.then: The plan grows heavy. It stalls before it begins.

options.text: Read everything about it before you start
options.then: You read for weeks. The month ends with no action.

options.text: Say yes and do it later when you have time
options.then: The month ends. Nothing has been tested yet.

options.text: Pick one action, set a date and invite an ally
options.then: You plan a notice-board survey for Friday. A friend signs on.

steps.why: A small, dated action with an ally tests your cause in real life.

steps.prompt: Soon, a second cause tempts you as well. What do you do?

options.text: Start the second cause too, since both matter
options.then: Both slow down. You're tired within a fortnight.

options.text: Drop the first for the new one
options.then: The new one is exciting. The first is left unfinished.

options.text: Pick the second only if it gets more attention
options.then: You compare numbers and lose track of what you care about.

options.text: Finish this one first, then choose the next
options.then: The first step wraps up. You pick your next with more clarity.

steps.why: Finishing one cause before starting another keeps your effort real.

scenarios.debrief: One genuine, local, doable cause is the place to start.
scenarios.relearn: Start with one cause you care about and can actually act on.

scenarios.hook: Your cause is "end inequality", and it feels too big to grip.

steps.prompt: Your teacher asks what exactly you'll work on. What do you say?

options.text: Keep it big and vague so nobody can argue
options.then: She smiles politely. She can't picture what you'll do.

options.text: Say you'll fix inequality across the whole country this year
options.then: She raises an eyebrow. "Where would you start?" You don't know.

options.text: Ask her to choose the problem for you
options.then: She suggests one, but it doesn't feel like yours.

options.text: Narrow it to something concrete, like fairer hostel chores
options.then: She nods. "That's something you can see change," she says.

steps.why: A concrete, local version of a big cause is something you can actually move.

steps.prompt: A friend asks if something small, like hostel chores, can really matter. What do you say?

options.text: You're right, so let's aim for the whole city
options.then: She grins. A week later nobody knows where to start, so you come back to the hostel.

options.text: It is small, so let's not bother with a plan
options.then: She shrugs. The work drifts with no direction.

options.text: Maybe you're right and we should find a bigger one
options.then: She nods. You're back at the start, with the hostel chores still waiting.

options.text: Small and real beats big and vague. It can grow later
options.then: She thinks. "I'd rather see something real change."

steps.why: A small, real goal can grow, while a vague big one stays out of reach.

steps.prompt: The team asks for a goal you can measure. What do you pick?

options.text: Better behaviour from everyone in the hostel
options.then: Nobody agrees on what counts. Progress is hard to see.

options.text: Make everyone feel equal
options.then: It sounds fine, but nothing can be counted or checked.

options.text: Win an award for the campaign
options.then: The award is exciting, but it doesn't measure change.

options.text: A chore rota everyone follows by the end of term
options.then: You can check it weekly. The team can see progress.

steps.why: A measurable, time-bound goal shows when you've moved the cause.

steps.prompt: Later, a small trial goes well in one hostel wing. Someone suggests the whole school next. What do you do?

options.text: Go for the whole school at once
options.then: The plan balloons. The first wing's trial slips.

options.text: Leave it as it is, since it worked once
options.then: The trial stays in one wing. Others never hear about it.

options.text: Wait for permission from every teacher first
options.then: Weeks pass waiting. The idea cools.

options.text: Try one more wing first and note what you learn
options.then: A second wing adopts it. You adjust two rules.

steps.why: Growing one step at a time lets a small win spread without losing it.

scenarios.debrief: A concrete, narrowed cause is what you can actually move.
scenarios.relearn: Narrow a big cause to something concrete and local.

scenarios.hook: You want to do something about gender-based violence in your area.

steps.prompt: You have a free weekend and a lot of energy. What is your first move?

options.text: Plan to confront the people causing harm
options.then: Your friends go quiet. One asks what happens if it turns ugly.

options.text: Pick a safe angle, like awareness and helplines
options.then: You list ideas that put nobody at risk. It feels smaller, but doable.

options.text: Plan a poster drive on your own, without asking anyone
options.then: The posters look good. You start wondering who will let you put them up.

options.text: Wait until you feel ready for something big
options.then: A week passes. The idea sits in your notebook and keeps nagging you.

steps.why: A safe angle lets you act now without putting anyone at risk.

steps.prompt: A week later, a teacher overhears you and a friend talking about it. What do you do?

options.text: Tell her it's only a chat so she won't interfere
options.then: She smiles and leaves. You still have no one with experience backing you.

options.text: Ask her to back it and point you to a counsellor
options.then: She says yes and offers to introduce you to the school counsellor.

options.text: Tell her once the plan is fully finished
options.then: She nods, though she could have caught gaps earlier.

options.text: Keep adults out so nobody takes it over
options.then: The group feels free. Nobody knows how to handle it if someone opens up.

steps.why: Adults with experience keep the project safe and help it last.

steps.prompt: Your first session is planned. What goes on the handout?

options.text: Names of people who have been harassing girls
options.then: A teacher stops you. Naming people could put you and others at risk.

options.text: Accurate helplines and where to get support
options.then: A teacher checks the numbers. People can take the handout home.

options.text: Only a strong message telling people to be brave
options.then: It reads well. Readers still have nowhere to turn for help.

options.text: Stories classmates shared with you privately
options.then: Someone sees her story on the page and is upset. She didn't agree to this.

steps.why: Accurate helplines give people a safe next step. Names and private stories put people at risk.

steps.prompt: Weeks later, more students want to join. What do you do?

options.text: Keep it to close friends so nothing goes wrong
options.then: The group stays small. Others who care are left out.

options.text: Let new members run their own confrontations
options.then: One tries it. A teacher steps in, and everyone is shaken.

options.text: Welcome them and keep an adult backing the group
options.then: Eight join. A teacher helps explain the safe rules.

options.text: Hand all the decisions to the newest members
options.then: They're keen, but they don't know the rules yet.

steps.why: More hands help, and adult backing keeps the work safe.

scenarios.debrief: On sensitive causes like GBV, pick a safe angle and get adult backing.
scenarios.relearn: For GBV, act on a safe angle (awareness, helplines) with adult support.

items.text: "More girls finishing school in my block"
"One helpline drive in our hostel this term"

scenarios.relearn: Specific, local causes are actionable; 'fix everything' is too vague to start.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: thinking to a cause's root, not just its symptom, helps you target it. See why?
scenarios.affirm: Tackling a root cause, not just a symptom, is how change actually lasts.
scenarios.relearn: Think to a cause's root, not just its symptom, to target it well.

scenarios.hook: "If I can't solve it completely, there's no point starting."

myth.un: If I can't solve it completely, there's no point.
myth.re: Partial, real progress matters and builds; you don't need to finish it alone.
myth.why: Movements are relays, not solo sprints.

scenarios.relearn: Partial real progress matters; you don't have to finish it alone.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: caring deeply about something is the fuel, but it needs a plan. Ready to turn caring into a plan?
scenarios.affirm: Your care is the fuel; a plan is the engine, next, you build one.
scenarios.relearn: Caring is the fuel; turning it into a plan is the next step.

scenarios.hook: You care about a cause, but your friends say it isn't a big deal.

steps.prompt: At lunch, they laugh it off again. What do you do?

options.text: Laugh along and say it was only a thought
options.then: The table moves on. You feel a bit smaller.

options.text: Say it matters and you're starting anyway
options.then: They go quiet. One friend asks, "Okay, what are you actually doing?"

options.text: Argue until they admit it really matters
options.then: The talk gets heated. Nobody changes their mind.

options.text: Ask which cause would impress them instead
options.then: They name a few trendy ones. None of them is yours.

steps.why: Your reasons are enough to begin. You don't need applause first.

steps.prompt: A few days on, you're still thinking about the cause. What do you do next?

options.text: Ask the group to vote on whether it's worth it
options.then: Opinions split, and the vote says nothing about what you care about.

options.text: Wait for a teacher to say it's important
options.then: No one says anything. The idea stays on hold.

options.text: Start big so nobody can call it small
options.then: The plan swells. You're not sure where to begin.

options.text: Pick one small step you can do this month
options.then: You write it down: a short poster in the corridor. It feels doable.

steps.why: A small real step gets you moving without anyone's permission.

steps.prompt: A senior says it's a nice hobby, not real change. How do you answer?

options.text: Agree it may be a hobby and shrink it down
options.then: She nods. You feel less sure than before.

options.text: Ask what she has changed lately
options.then: She looks stung. The talk ends and no one is convinced.

options.text: Say it's small on purpose, with a first step
options.then: She hears your first step and nods. "Fair enough. That's real."

options.text: Say you'll prove it once you're famous enough
options.then: She laughs. Waiting for fame means waiting a long time.

steps.why: Starting small and showing a real step speaks louder than a debate.

scenarios.debrief: You don't need others to rate your cause big enough to begin.
scenarios.relearn: A cause you care about is worth starting, with or without applause.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two causes too vague to be a real starting point.

scene.text: "Get a bin and signage for our lane this term"
"A safe-walk route mapped for our campus"

scenarios.why: 'End all pollution forever' and 'fix the whole environment' have no concrete first step; the others are local and time-bound.
scenarios.relearn: Well-framed causes are concrete, local and time-bound.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a cause within reach, or beyond a first project?

items.text: A safety map for your campus
A helpline-poster drive in your hostel

scenarios.relearn: Campus and school-scale projects are within reach; rewriting law alone isn't a first project.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: which kind of cause pulls at you most?
scenarios.affirm: Whatever pulls at you, that genuine care is exactly where to begin.
scenarios.relearn: Start from the cause that genuinely pulls at you.

scenarios.hook: "Changemaking is only for special, extraordinary people."

myth.un: Changemaking is only for special, extraordinary people.
myth.re: Ordinary people, working together, drive most real change.
myth.why: You don't need to be exceptional, just willing to start.

scenarios.relearn: Changemaking is for ordinary people working together, not just the extraordinary.

scenarios.hook: You want fairer chores in your hostel, but you have no plan yet.

steps.prompt: Your friends are keen to start. What is your first planning move?

options.text: Set one clear goal you could reach this term
options.then: The group agrees on a rota goal for next month. Everyone has a target now.

options.text: Start posting about it every day to build interest
options.then: The posts get a few likes. Nobody knows what you want to change.

options.text: Write a full plan before telling anyone about it
options.then: Weeks go by. Your friends lose interest while you write.

options.text: Wait for a teacher to hand you a plan
options.then: Nothing arrives, and the group's energy fades.

steps.why: One clear, realistic goal gives your effort direction and a finish line.

steps.prompt: A friend wants the plan perfect before anything starts. What do you do?

options.text: Write a light plan, begin, and fix it as you go
options.then: The plan fits on one page. You start the next day.

options.text: Spend a month polishing the plan first
options.then: The plan looks great. The month passes without any action.

options.text: Skip planning and see what happens
options.then: The first week is lively. Nobody knows who is doing what.

options.text: Copy another group's plan exactly as it is
options.then: It fits their hostel. It doesn't fit yours.

steps.why: A lightweight plan you begin beats a perfect one that never launches.

steps.prompt: Your goal needs a who and a how. What do you add?

options.text: Allies who'll help, and tactics that fit the goal
options.then: The wardens, the mess committee, and three friends are on the list.

options.text: A catchy hashtag and a logo
options.then: The logo is lovely. The rota is still unchanged.

options.text: A list of rules for everyone else to follow
options.then: People bristle at being told what to do.

options.text: Nothing more. The goal says it all
options.then: Nobody knows who should do what next.

steps.why: Allies and fitting tactics turn a goal into a plan others can join.

steps.prompt: A month in, it's time to check the plan. What do you do?

options.text: Review the plan and adjust what isn't working
options.then: Two tasks change. The rota begins to run smoothly.

options.text: Keep everything exactly as written
options.then: Some tasks don't fit, and nobody says so.

options.text: Throw the plan away and start over
options.then: You lose a month of progress and your allies' trust.

options.text: Hide the parts that didn't work
options.then: The report looks great. The same problems return.

steps.why: Checking and adjusting is how a lightweight plan becomes a good one.

scenarios.debrief: A clear, realistic goal turns a cause into a project.
scenarios.relearn: Set one clear, realistic goal to turn a cause into a plan.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a strong project goal, or a weak one?
scenarios.relearn: Strong goals are specific and measurable; 'raise awareness somehow' is too vague.

scenarios.hook: Match the stakeholder type to who they are.
scenarios.relearn: Map your allies, those affected, the decision-makers, partners and bystanders.

scenarios.hook: Your goal is a girls' study corner in the school library.

steps.prompt: Many tactics are possible. Which do you choose first?

options.text: Ask the librarian with a short written proposal
options.then: She reads it and says she'll think it over. It's a start.

options.text: Run a big online trend, since it's exciting
options.then: The trend gets attention. The librarian hasn't heard of it.

options.text: Hold a march through the school corridor
options.then: Staff tell you to stop. The library hears nothing about the idea.

options.text: Hand out flyers about why reading matters
options.then: People read the flyers. Nobody asks about a study corner.

steps.why: A tactic that fits your goal reaches the person who can decide.

steps.prompt: A teacher says the librarian will want proof that students would use it. What do you do?

options.text: Run a quick sign-up with classmates
options.then: Thirty names appear on the sheet in two days.

options.text: Show her the likes on your posts
options.then: She nods, and still wants to know who would use it.

options.text: Say it's obvious that students want it
options.then: She nods politely. She needs something she can show.

options.text: Bring ten friends to demand the corner
options.then: The librarian is startled and asks you to leave.

steps.why: Real names from classmates show the need and support your ask.

steps.prompt: A friend says awareness posters alone are enough. What do you say?

options.text: Posters help, but the direct ask does the work
options.then: She nods. "Okay. Posters for awareness, plus the ask."

options.text: You're right. Posters are all we need for this
options.then: Posters go up and look great. The librarian hasn't heard from anyone.

options.text: No, skip posters and only email the adults in charge
options.then: No posters go up. Classmates do not know the project exists.

options.text: Let's make the biggest posters in the whole school
options.then: You spend a week on posters. The ask to the librarian waits.

steps.why: Different tactics have different jobs, and the goal decides which come first.

scenarios.debrief: Tactics should be chosen to fit the goal, not the other way round.
scenarios.relearn: Pick tactics (awareness, advocacy, service, organising) that fit your goal.

scenarios.hook: Sort the goal to the tactic that fits.
scenarios.relearn: Rule-change and helping now suit advocacy/service; shifting attitudes and building suit awareness/organising.

scenarios.hook: Your plan has a goal but no timeline.

steps.prompt: Your teacher asks when the plan will show results. What do you say?

options.text: I'll add a timeline with a few milestones
options.then: She nods. "Good. Bring it to me by Friday."

options.text: Soon. We'll know it when we see it
options.then: She looks puzzled. "How will you know?"

options.text: Whenever the team has time for it
options.then: She raises an eyebrow. "Teams are busy. Then?"

options.text: By the end of the year, whatever happens
options.then: She says that's a long way off to plan from.

steps.why: A timeline with milestones turns a wish into a plan.

steps.prompt: Your teacher asks you to set a first milestone two weeks out. What goes under it?

options.text: One small, specific task with a name
options.then: The task is clear. A teammate puts her name beside it.

options.text: A big task with no owner
options.then: Everyone assumes someone else will do it.

options.text: Everything we hope to do this term
options.then: The list is long. Nobody can say where to begin.

options.text: Just the word 'start'
options.then: The word sits on the page. Nobody knows what to do first.

steps.why: A small task with an owner makes a milestone easy to meet.

steps.prompt: The first milestone slips by a week. What do you do?

options.text: Look at why it slipped, then adjust the dates
options.then: A teammate was ill. You shift two dates and carry on.

options.text: Pretend it didn't slip and keep the old dates
options.then: The next milestone arrives with the work not yet done.

options.text: Drop the timeline, since it clearly doesn't work
options.then: The plan goes back to drifting.

options.text: Blame the slowest person on the team
options.then: She goes quiet. The team starts hiding delays.

steps.why: A timeline helps you spot slips early and adjust calmly.

scenarios.debrief: A timeline and milestones turn a wish into a workable plan.
scenarios.relearn: Add a sensible timeline and milestones to your plan.

scenarios.relearn: Goal, allies, tactics, timeline and a measure are the backbone of a plan.

myth.re: A lightweight plan you actually begin beats a perfect one that never launches.
myth.why: You learn and refine by doing, not by planning forever.

scenarios.relearn: A lightweight plan you start beats a perfect plan you never launch.

scenarios.hook: Sort: belongs in a project plan, or not yet?
scenarios.relearn: Goal and allies come first; logos and virality aren't the priority.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: a plan turns 'I wish' into 'here's how'. Feel the difference?

scenarios.hook: You're mapping who could help with your equality project.

steps.prompt: Your list of helpers is short. What do you do?

options.text: List teachers, clubs, NGOs and peers who share the goal
options.then: The list grows to fifteen names in an afternoon.

options.text: Assume you're on your own
options.then: The list stays short, and the work feels heavy.

options.text: List only your closest friends
options.then: They're kind, but they don't know a teacher or an NGO.

options.text: List only people who agree with everything you say
options.then: The list is neat and small. Others who could help are left out.

steps.why: Mapping widely shows you more support than you thought.

steps.prompt: A teacher you've never spoken to might help. What do you do?

options.text: Ask for ten minutes and share a short plan
options.then: She listens, asks a question, and offers a room.

options.text: Skip her, since she hasn't offered
options.then: She learns of your project from someone else, weeks later.

options.text: Wait for her to ask first
options.then: Nothing happens, and the idea sits idle.

options.text: Ask her to take over the whole project
options.then: She says she's too busy, and the idea is no longer yours.

steps.why: A short, clear ask makes it easy for a busy teacher to say yes.

steps.prompt: A local NGO's youth worker is open to meeting. What do you do?

options.text: Meet with a clear ask, and bring a teacher
options.then: The youth worker shares two contacts and a free workshop.

options.text: Say you can do it all yourselves
options.then: She smiles politely. The offer fades.

options.text: Let them run your project for you
options.then: They run it well. It's no longer your team's project.

options.text: Skip it, because they're older than you
options.then: The contacts and experience go unused.

steps.why: Partners bring experience and weight to your plan.

steps.prompt: Your list has grown long. How do you use it?

options.text: Sort it into allies, those affected, and decision-makers
options.then: Three columns appear. You see who to talk to first.

options.text: Message everyone at the same time
options.then: Replies come in at once. Nobody knows who is doing what.

options.text: Choose only the most famous names
options.then: The famous names don't reply. The others are never asked.

options.text: Keep it private so nobody feels left out
options.then: The list is never used, and the team doesn't know it exists.

steps.why: Sorting your map shows who can help and who can decide.

scenarios.debrief: Mapping allies reveals support you didn't know you had.
scenarios.relearn: Map allies: teachers, clubs, NGOs and peers who share your goal.

scenarios.hook: Match the tactic to an example.
scenarios.relearn: Awareness, advocacy, service, organising and partnering each have concrete forms.

scenarios.hook: Sort: realistic for a student project, or over-reach?
scenarios.relearn: Class and school-scale tactics are realistic; national campaigns and protests aren't a first project.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: a good plan is honest about what you can do now. Agree?
scenarios.affirm: An honest, right-sized plan is the one that actually gets done.
scenarios.relearn: A good plan is honest about what you can do now.

scenarios.hook: Your plan for a safer walk to school is ready, and you want to run it alone.

steps.prompt: Your classmate Farah asks what you're working on. What do you do?

options.text: Say it's nearly done and you'll show her later
options.then: Farah nods and walks off. You keep going alone, a little more tired.

options.text: Post it in the class group and wait for volunteers
options.then: Two thumbs-up come in. Nobody offers to do anything.

options.text: Tell her the goal and ask her to take one part
options.then: Farah says she can map the dark stretches on her way home.

options.text: Say she can help once everything is perfect
options.then: She shrugs. The plan stays in your notebook, still being polished.

steps.why: A clear, specific ask turns interest into a first ally.

steps.prompt: A week later, mapping the route is taking far longer than planned. What do you do?

options.text: Work late every night to catch up yourself
options.then: You finish the map but fall asleep in class the next day.

options.text: Name three small tasks and ask people to pick one
options.then: Classmates choose tasks. The work splits up and moves faster.

options.text: Shrink the project until you can finish it alone
options.then: The plan fits in your bag now, but it no longer reaches the main road.

options.text: Ask a friend to "help out" without saying how
options.then: He says sure. A week on, neither of you knows what he was meant to do.

steps.why: Splitting clear tasks lets the work grow beyond one person's hours.

steps.prompt: Your teacher asks who is on your team. What do you say?

options.text: It's all my work so far, and I'd like to keep it that way
options.then: She is impressed but worried, and asks who will carry it if you fall ill. A few classmates offer to pitch in.

options.text: A big group of students is behind it
options.then: She asks to meet them all. You admit it's only a few so far, and she says to bring them along.

options.text: Tell her honestly where things stand and ask for her advice
options.then: She notes it down and offers to book a room. A few classmates join your next meeting.

options.text: I don't need a team, only your approval
options.then: She says approval helps but the work needs hands. Soon after, a few classmates step in to help.

steps.why: Being honest about where the team stands and asking for advice builds a team.

steps.prompt: The first month ends, and the classmates who pitched in ask what happens next. What do you do?

options.text: Post one thank-you to the whole class and move on
options.then: People feel noticed in a general way, and a few drift away.

options.text: Quietly finish the report yourself so it's neat
options.then: The report looks tidy. The helpers never see the result.

options.text: Say it was mostly your work, since you led it
options.then: The helpers glance at each other. Next time, fewer offer.

options.text: Thank each helper by name and ask what to try next
options.then: Each person smiles. Two suggest new ideas for next month.

steps.why: Naming each helper and planning next steps keeps the team together.

scenarios.debrief: Almost nothing meaningful is achieved alone. A few allies make it real and lasting.
scenarios.relearn: Recruit allies; meaningful change is collective, not solo.

scenarios.hook: You want to recruit your friend Ishaan to a campaign for safer cycling paths.
scenarios.setup: You find him alone in the canteen.

steps.prompt: Ishaan looks up and asks: "You wanted to ask me something?"

options.text: "You have to join, or I'll feel really let down."
options.then: He shifts in his seat. "That's a lot of pressure."

options.text: "Everyone else is joining, so you should too."
options.then: He frowns. "Then you don't really need me."

options.text: "If you can't, I'll understand. Never mind."
options.then: He shrugs. "Okay. I'm curious, though. What is it about?"

options.text: "I'm starting something. Your skills would really help. Want in?"
options.then: He grins. "What kind of skills? Tell me more."

steps.why: A warm, specific invitation tells him why you want him there.

steps.prompt: The next day, Ishaan asks: "What exactly would I do for your cycling campaign?"

options.text: "Whatever you like. We'll figure it all out later on."
options.then: He frowns. "That doesn't tell me much."

options.text: "We need people who do everything."
options.then: He laughs nervously. "Everything? I don't have the time."

options.text: "You could run the sign-up table for an hour on Friday."
options.then: He nods. "An hour I can do."

options.text: "Just be there. Your name on the list is enough."
options.then: He nods slowly. "So I'd just be a name."

steps.why: A small, specific job makes it easy to say yes.

steps.prompt: Ishaan says: "My parents might not like me joining campaigns."

options.text: "Don't tell them. It's your life."
options.then: He bites his lip. "I don't like hiding things."

options.text: "They're too old-fashioned to understand."
options.then: He stiffens. "They're not like that."

options.text: "Then forget it. I'll find someone else."
options.then: He looks down. "Okay. Sorry. Can I at least ask them first?"

options.text: "Fair. Shall I show them the plan with you?"
options.then: He relaxes. "Yes. They'd like to see it first."

steps.why: Respecting his family's concern and sharing the plan builds trust.

steps.prompt: A week later, Ishaan says: "I talked to my parents. I'll do it. Will you check in on me?"

options.text: "No, you're on your own. That's how you learn."
options.then: He frowns. "I thought we were a team."

options.text: "I will. Just don't ask me too often."
options.then: His smile fades. "I'll try not to."

options.text: "Sure. Everyone in the team will check in on you."
options.then: He looks nervous. "Everyone? That's a lot."

options.text: "Yes. Friday at lunch, and tell me if it's too much."
options.then: He smiles. "Thanks. That makes it easier."

steps.why: Offering a clear check-in shows you'll support him, not drop him.

scenarios.relearn: Invite allies warmly and specifically; don't pressure them.

scenarios.hook: You want your teacher's backing for a student campaign to start a school recycling drive.
scenarios.setup: You catch Mr. Rao after class, just before he leaves.

steps.prompt: Mr. Rao says: "You wanted a word? I have ten minutes."

options.text: "Can you just sort it out for us?"
options.then: He raises an eyebrow. "Sort what out? What are you asking me for?"

options.text: "Everyone in class wants this, so you should say yes."
options.then: He sighs. "I'm not sure that's how it works."

options.text: "I'll explain later. Can you just sign here?"
options.then: He pulls his pen back. "Sign what, exactly?"

options.text: "Here's our goal and plan. Could you mentor us?"
options.then: He takes the page. "This is clear. Tell me about your team."

steps.why: A clear goal and plan make it easy for him to back you.

steps.prompt: Mr. Rao says: "Tell me about the drive itself. Who is on your team, and what's your timeline?"

options.text: "It's just me for now, but I work really fast."
options.then: He nods slowly. "Movements take more than one person."

options.text: "The whole class, and the timeline is flexible."
options.then: He frowns. "That sounds like no plan at all."

options.text: "A few classmates, and a first drive before term ends."
options.then: "Good. That's realistic for a first project."

options.text: "I'll figure that out once you say yes to helping."
options.then: He sighs. "A team matters, but let me see what you have so far."

steps.why: Naming a team and a realistic timeline shows you've thought it through.

steps.prompt: Mr. Rao says: "I can help, but you'll need the principal's permission."

options.text: "Then I'll skip it and run the drive quietly."
options.then: He shakes his head. "That could land you in trouble."

options.text: "Could you help us write the request?"
options.then: "Yes. Draft it, and I'll read it tonight."

options.text: "Can you ask her for us? I'm nervous."
options.then: He smiles kindly. "I'll support you, but you should speak too."

options.text: "Never mind. It's too complicated."
options.then: He looks at you. "It's one step, not a mountain."

steps.why: Asking for his help with the request keeps it adult-backed and in your hands.

steps.prompt: Mr. Rao says: "Come back next week with the draft request."

options.text: "Can you write it for us instead?"
options.then: He chuckles. "I'll guide it. You write it."

options.text: "We'll try, but we might need more time."
options.then: He nods. "Then tell me early."

options.text: "Maybe. We'll see how it goes."
options.then: He looks doubtful. "I'd like a date."

options.text: "Yes. We'll bring the draft on Thursday."
options.then: He smiles. "Good. I'll keep that slot free."

steps.why: Naming a date makes your commitment real and easy for him to plan around.

scenarios.relearn: A clear goal-and-plan ask earns adult backing and partnership.

scenarios.hook: Five classmates have joined your campaign for a fairer canteen queue.

steps.prompt: At the first meeting, everyone looks to you for what happens next. What do you do?

options.text: Keep every task and promise to send updates
options.then: They nod politely. By the next meeting, two have stopped replying.

options.text: Give the fun jobs to your closest friends
options.then: Your friends enjoy it. The others quietly notice who was picked.

options.text: Let everyone do whatever they feel like
options.then: Three people make posters. Nobody books the room.

options.text: Ask what each person is good at and match roles
options.then: Aman likes numbers and Priya draws well. Roles take shape before you finish.

steps.why: Roles that fit people's strengths give everyone a real part.

steps.prompt: Two weeks on, one member has barely spoken in meetings. What do you do?

options.text: Call on her in every meeting to get her talking
options.then: She goes red and mumbles. She starts to dread the next meeting.

options.text: Leave her be until she's ready to speak
options.then: She keeps listening. Nobody asks her view, and she stops coming.

options.text: Let the louder members decide to keep things fast
options.then: Decisions come quickly. The quieter ones stop offering ideas.

options.text: Ask her privately what she'd like to take on
options.then: She says she'd rather write the notice than speak up. You hand it to her.

steps.why: Asking privately what fits lets quieter members join in on their own terms.

steps.prompt: The team splits four to two on how to run the survey. What do you do?

options.text: Go with the four and move on quickly
options.then: The work moves. The two feel their view was never heard.

options.text: Decide it yourself as the person who started it
options.then: Nobody argues, and nobody feels the plan is theirs.

options.text: Wait until everyone agrees completely
options.then: A week passes without a decision, and the energy drops.

options.text: Hear both sides, then let the team vote openly
options.then: The vote is clear, and the two who lost still agree to help.

steps.why: Hearing everyone and deciding openly keeps all members included.

scenarios.debrief: A team runs on shared, suited roles and real inclusion, so people stay.
scenarios.relearn: Share roles by strength and keep everyone included.

scenarios.hook: Your idea for a student-run study group needs more classmates to join.

steps.prompt: You're writing the first notice for the class group. What goes in it?

options.text: A big claim that every student is failing without this
options.then: People react. Then a teacher asks where the claim comes from. You have no answer.

options.text: The goal, what you need, and one clear next step
options.then: Classmates reply with questions, and two sign up the same day.

options.text: A long message covering every detail of the plan
options.then: Most people skim the first lines and scroll on.

options.text: A funny meme with just the group's name
options.then: It gets laughs. Nobody knows what to do next.

steps.why: A clear goal and one next step let people understand and join.

steps.prompt: A classmate says this doesn't affect her. What do you say?

options.text: Everyone who cares will join, so it's your call
options.then: She shrugs. Nothing in that gave her a reason.

options.text: You're being selfish if you stay out of it
options.then: She stiffens and walks off, and word of it gets around.

options.text: Tell her what you both want from it, plainly
options.then: She pauses. "Okay, I do struggle with that too," she says.

options.text: It will change the whole school this term
options.then: She raises an eyebrow. The promise sounds bigger than your team.

steps.why: Naming a shared reason works better than pressure or big promises.

steps.prompt: Your message works on some people and not others. What do you do?

options.text: Send the same message again, louder
options.then: You post it twice more. People mute the group.

options.text: Add stronger claims so it stands out
options.then: Interest spikes for a day. Then people ask for proof.

options.text: Ask a few people which part was unclear, then fix it
options.then: Three say the same line confused them. You rewrite it, and sign-ups pick up.

options.text: Decide the others just don't care
options.then: You stop trying. A few curious classmates never hear from you again.

steps.why: Asking what was unclear improves the message and keeps it honest.

scenarios.debrief: Clear, honest messaging about the shared goal brings people in.
scenarios.relearn: Communicate clearly and honestly about the shared goal.

scenarios.hook: A local NGO offers to partner on your campaign for brighter street lights near school.

steps.prompt: Their coordinator, Mr. Nair, sends you a friendly message. What do you do?

options.text: Say yes quickly before they change their mind
options.then: He is pleased. You haven't yet asked what they expect from you.

options.text: Say thanks, but you'd rather keep all the credit
options.then: He wishes you luck and says the door stays open. He sends a draft plan anyway.

options.text: Ask for funds first and decide the rest later
options.then: He is taken aback. The talk becomes about money, not your goal.

options.text: Meet him with a teacher and ask what they can offer
options.then: He explains their experience with ward officials and offers an introduction.

steps.why: Meeting with a trusted adult and asking what they offer is safe and clear.

steps.prompt: A few days later, the NGO shares a draft plan with some changes, just in case. What do you do?

options.text: Accept every change so they stay happy
options.then: The plan looks polished. It no longer feels like yours.

options.text: Reject every change to protect your original
options.then: They stay on, but the plan gets less of their experience.

options.text: Take the plan without showing your team
options.then: Your team finds out later and feels nobody asked them.

options.text: Compare it with your goal and agree on shared decisions
options.then: You keep your goal, borrow their timeline, and agree to decide together.

steps.why: Sharing decisions keeps the goal yours and uses their experience.

steps.prompt: Their name could go on your first event poster. What do you decide?

options.text: Leave it off so it looks fully student-led
options.then: The poster looks tidy. The NGO feels quietly sidelined.

options.text: Put only their name on it, since they're known
options.then: More people stop at the stall. Your team feels invisible.

options.text: Skip the poster and rely on word of mouth
options.then: Few people turn up. The question of credit never gets settled.

options.text: Put both names on it and tell the full story
options.then: People see a student team with an experienced partner, and trust it more.

steps.why: Sharing credit keeps trust and lets the partner's weight help the cause.

steps.prompt: After the event, the NGO suggests a follow-up project. What do you do?

options.text: Say yes to everything they suggest right away
options.then: The plan becomes huge. Your team starts to feel stretched.

options.text: Say no thanks, since one event is enough for now
options.then: They respect it. A good partnership fades after one event.

options.text: Wait for them to plan it and just show up
options.then: Their plan arrives. It's good, and it isn't yours.

options.text: Review what worked together, then agree the next project
options.then: You list the lessons and pick a shorter, clearer second project.

steps.why: Reviewing together and choosing a project that fits keeps a partnership strong.

scenarios.debrief: Partnerships multiply a small project's reach and staying power.
scenarios.relearn: Partner with clubs, NGOs and community to multiply impact.

scenarios.hook: Only a handful of people come to your first meeting, far fewer than you hoped.

steps.prompt: Walking home, you feel flat about it. What do you do first?

options.text: Decide the cause isn't wanted and stop
options.then: You put the notebook away, until a friend asks about it a few days later.

options.text: Blame the people who didn't turn up
options.then: You vent in a message, and a friend who was only busy feels hurt.

options.text: Ask those who came what would help
options.then: They say lunch break would work better, since after school clashes with tuition.

options.text: Hold off and try again much later
options.then: Time passes. Interest cools, and those who came wonder what happened.

steps.why: Asking the people who came shows you what to change.

steps.prompt: A few days on, someone asks when the next meeting is. What do you say?

options.text: Say there isn't a meeting planned yet, so check back later
options.then: She shrugs. The chance passes without a date.

options.text: Say it will be much bigger this time
options.then: She comes and finds a small group again. She feels let down.

options.text: Give her the new time and ask her to bring one friend
options.then: She says yes. The next meeting has a few new faces.

options.text: Say you're thinking of dropping the whole thing
options.then: She says that's a pity. Nobody suggests how to save it.

steps.why: A fresh date and a small ask keep momentum without hype.

steps.prompt: The second meeting is a little bigger but still small. How do you see it?

options.text: As proof it was never going to work
options.then: The mood in the room drops, and two people go quiet.

options.text: As too slow, so you compare it to famous campaigns
options.then: Everything you read makes your team look tiny, and your energy slips.

options.text: As a sign you need one huge event to prove it
options.then: You start planning something big. The team worries about the time.

options.text: As progress, and plan one small next step together
options.then: The team lists two small goals for the month and feels a lift.

steps.why: Small growth is real progress, and it points to the next adjustment.

steps.prompt: A month on, your team is steadier. What do you do to keep it that way?

options.text: Trust your memory, since you were there for it all
options.then: Details blur. The same mistake happens again.

options.text: Plan a big event to celebrate and prove the team works
options.then: The event takes weeks. People tire before it happens.

options.text: Stop reviewing, since it's working now
options.then: A new clash comes up. Nobody notices until people stop coming.

options.text: Keep a simple log of what worked and what didn't
options.then: The log shows lunch slots work best. The next meeting is easier to plan.

steps.why: A simple log turns each setback into a lesson the team keeps.

scenarios.debrief: Setbacks are part of the process to adapt to, never a verdict.
scenarios.relearn: Treat setbacks as iteration: learn, adjust, keep going.

scenarios.hook: Sort: builds a movement, or stalls it?
scenarios.relearn: Including allies, clear messaging and shared roles build a movement; solo work, pressure and credit-hoarding stall it.

scenarios.hook: In a team meeting, Samar suggests a plan that is better than yours.
scenarios.setup: Everyone is watching to see how you react.

steps.prompt: Samar says: "What if we run a survey first, then pick the events?"

options.text: "Mine is more ready, so let's stick with it."
options.then: Samar sits back. "Sure. Fine."

options.text: "That's better than mine. Let's go with yours."
options.then: Samar looks relieved. "Thanks. Could you help me set it up?"

options.text: "Interesting. We can try yours after mine."
options.then: Samar nods slowly. "Sure, if there's time."

options.text: "Who made you the expert on this?"
options.then: The room goes silent. Samar looks at the floor.

steps.why: Saying openly that a better idea is better helps the team and builds trust.

steps.prompt: Later, Samar says: "I'd still like to write a survey on this. Could you help with the questions?"

options.text: "Your idea, your job. I'll check it at the end."
options.then: Samar nods stiffly. "Okay."

options.text: "I'll take it over. I know how to do these."
options.then: Samar looks deflated. "Oh. Okay."

options.text: "Ask someone else. I'm busy."
options.then: Samar blinks. "Right. Sorry I asked."

options.text: "Happy to. Let's draft them together tomorrow."
options.then: Samar smiles. "Great. Bring your questions too."

steps.why: Helping make the better idea happen shows you really back it.

steps.prompt: Another teammate asks: "This is your project. Where does Samar's idea fit in?"

options.text: "Samar's plan was a bit better, I guess."
options.then: Samar looks down. "A bit?"

options.text: "You're right. Let's vote on whose plan wins."
options.then: Samar goes quiet. The room tenses.

options.text: "I'm just trying it out. We'll see."
options.then: She nods, unsure. Samar frowns.

options.text: "It's our project. We use whichever idea works best."
options.then: She shrugs. "Fair. I just wondered."

steps.why: Putting the team's goal ahead of whose idea it was keeps trust intact.

scenarios.relearn: Backing the best idea, not your own ego, strengthens the team.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: watching support grow as people join, that's the heart of a movement. Feel it?
scenarios.affirm: Momentum from people joining is exactly what makes change feel possible.
scenarios.relearn: A movement is the momentum of people joining a shared goal.

scenarios.hook: Two teammates disagree with your approach, though all of you want fairer sports time for girls.

steps.prompt: Rohan says your assembly talk is too soft to work. What do you do?

options.text: Tell him he can leave if he doesn't like it
options.then: Rohan shrugs and goes quiet. He keeps coming to meetings but sits at the back.

options.text: Switch to his idea entirely to keep him happy
options.then: He's pleased. The others feel their input vanished overnight.

options.text: Ask what worries him and find what you agree on
options.then: He says the principal ignores talks. You both want results, and that's a start.

options.text: Ignore him and keep planning
options.then: He raises it louder each time, and tension builds.

steps.why: Asking why finds the shared goal behind a disagreement.

steps.prompt: Another teammate says Rohan's way is too aggressive and he shouldn't help. What do you do?

options.text: Agree privately that Rohan is a problem
options.then: She smiles, and a small group forms behind your back.

options.text: Ask Rohan to apologise in front of everyone
options.then: He does, stiffly. The room goes quiet and uneasy.

options.text: Point to the shared goal and ask how each idea serves it
options.then: People look at the goal on the board, and the argument softens.

options.text: Say you'll decide and nobody should argue
options.then: People stop talking. The disagreements move to the corridor.

steps.why: A shared goal holds a group together better than agreement on every tactic.

steps.prompt: Weeks later, Rohan says he still disagrees but wants to help. What do you do?

options.text: Say he can join once he fully agrees with the plan
options.then: He backs off. The team loses a keen worker.

options.text: Welcome him but keep him away from decisions
options.then: He senses it. His help turns half-hearted from then on.

options.text: Welcome him and give him a role that uses his energy
options.then: He takes the petition drive. The group now has both approaches.

options.text: Ask him to prove he's committed first
options.then: He bristles. A simple offer turns into a test.

steps.why: A role for someone who shares the goal grows the movement without a purity test.

scenarios.debrief: Movements grow by bringing people along, not by purity tests.
scenarios.relearn: Bring people along with respect; shared goals beat total agreement.

scenarios.hook: Ways to grow support. Spot the two that repel people, not draw them.
scenarios.why: Shaming and guilt-tripping repel people; warm invites and small, specific roles draw them in.
scenarios.relearn: Catch shame and guilt in 'recruiting'; warmth and specific roles grow real support.

scenarios.hook: Your team has worked for weeks on a clean-water campaign, and spirits are low.
scenarios.setup: You stand up to speak before the meeting.

steps.prompt: Tanvi says quietly: "Honestly, I'm not sure we've achieved much."

options.text: "We're failing. This is hopeless, honestly."
options.then: Tanvi's face falls. "Then why are we here?"

options.text: "We're amazing! We'll definitely win everything!"
options.then: Tanvi gives a small laugh. "Come on. Be real."

options.text: "Don't be so negative. It brings the team down."
options.then: Tanvi falls silent and looks at her notes.

options.text: "We've come further than last week. Let's keep going."
options.then: Tanvi nods slowly. "Okay. When you put it that way, yes."

steps.why: Naming real progress honestly lifts people without false hype.

steps.prompt: Yash says: "We keep adding tasks, but nothing seems to finish."

options.text: "We just need to push harder. Everyone stays late."
options.then: Yash sighs. "Stay late on a school night?"

options.text: "Maybe you're right. Maybe this was too big."
options.then: Yash looks uneasy. "I didn't mean we should quit."

options.text: "Let's finish two tasks this week and park the rest."
options.then: Yash sits up. "That I can work with."

options.text: "It's fine. Tasks always pile up."
options.then: Yash shrugs. "Okay." The pile doesn't shrink.

steps.why: A few finishable tasks turn effort into visible progress.

steps.prompt: Tanvi asks: "What do I tell my mum when she asks if this is worth my time?"

options.text: "Tell her it will change the whole school soon."
options.then: Tanvi hesitates. "I can't promise that."

options.text: "Tell her it's just a small hobby for now."
options.then: Tanvi looks hurt. "It doesn't feel like a hobby."

options.text: "Say it's your call, not your mum's."
options.then: Tanvi frowns. "I'd like her to understand it."

options.text: "Tell her what we've done so far and what's next."
options.then: Tanvi smiles. "That's easy. I can show her the list."

steps.why: Honest, concrete answers help families see the value without overpromising.

scenarios.relearn: Honest encouragement about real progress keeps a team going.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a good partner for a student campaign, or risky?
scenarios.relearn: Teachers, clubs, known NGOs and counsellors are good partners; strangers, fame-promisers and control-grabbers are risky.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: bringing people along with respect, not pressure, is the kind of movement that lasts. Agree?
scenarios.affirm: Movements built on respect, not pressure, are the ones that endure.
scenarios.relearn: Bringing people along with respect builds a movement that lasts.

scenarios.hook: Your campaign for a safer school gate has real momentum, and everyone is keen.

steps.prompt: You see a chance to run extra events this month. What do you do?

options.text: Schedule them all and expect the team to fit them in
options.then: People agree out loud and quietly feel stretched.

options.text: Run the extra events yourself so nobody is bothered
options.then: You manage, but you're tired, and the team feels left out.

options.text: Skip the extra events so nobody gets tired
options.then: The team stays comfortable. The momentum cools a little.

options.text: Ask the team what they can take on, then plan together
options.then: They suggest one extra event, and two members offer to run it.

steps.why: Asking what people can handle keeps the pace fair and growing.

steps.prompt: One member says exams are close and she feels guilty about missing tasks. What do you say?

options.text: Everyone is busy and you'll manage
options.then: She stays, but her work gets rushed and she stops joining the chat.

options.text: A good campaign can't wait for exams
options.then: She nods and goes silent. Two others wonder if they're next.

options.text: Her exams matter too, so you'll trim her tasks
options.then: She looks relieved and says she'll come back strong after exams.

options.text: It's fine, and you quietly take her tasks without telling anyone
options.then: The work gets done. You pile up the extra with no help.

steps.why: Real life matters to the team, and a flexible plan lets people stay.

steps.prompt: A month in, the team meets daily and it's all anyone talks about. What do you do?

options.text: Keep going at full speed while the energy lasts
options.then: The pace holds for a week, then people start missing meetings.

options.text: Drop to one meeting a month to be safe
options.then: People rest, but the project loses its thread.

options.text: Ask the most dedicated to do more so others can rest
options.then: A few carry the load. They're tired within a fortnight.

options.text: Set a weekly rhythm with a rest day and shared tasks
options.then: Meetings get shorter. People joke again, and the work continues.

steps.why: A steady rhythm with rest and shared tasks keeps a team going for the long haul.

scenarios.debrief: A sustainable pace keeps a movement alive past the first burst.
scenarios.relearn: Keep a humane pace so your team doesn't burn out.

scenarios.hook: "There's no law to back a cause like gender-based violence."

myth.un: There's no law on your side for something like GBV.
myth.re: India has real laws against GBV, the Domestic Violence Act, POSH Act, Dowry Prohibition Act and the BNS.
myth.why: The law can be a tool a campaign uses and points people to.

scenarios.relearn: Real laws against GBV exist; the law can be a campaign tool.

scenarios.hook: Match the issue to a law that addresses it (India).
scenarios.relearn: India has specific laws: DV Act, POSH Act and the Dowry Prohibition Act.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a real legal protection / right (India), or not?

scenarios.hook: Your campaign wants people to know where to turn for help with gender-based violence.

scenarios.debrief: A real first step is what turns a plan into change.
scenarios.relearn: Take one concrete, safe first step this week.

scenarios.hook: Your planned first step is a college-wide awareness week.

steps.prompt: It needs a dozen volunteers and a month to organise. What do you do?

options.text: Keep it huge and wait until you can do it
options.then: Weeks pass. Gathering a dozen people isn't getting easier.

options.text: Try to do all of it in a rush this week
options.then: You're up past midnight, and the poster is half done.

options.text: Pass it to someone more experienced
options.then: A senior says she has no time. It lands back with you.

options.text: Shrink it to one session you can run this week
options.then: You cut it to a twenty-minute talk in one class. It fits your week.

steps.why: A first step you can truly do this week beats a grand one that never starts.

steps.prompt: A week later, a friend asks what your first step is. What do you tell her?

options.text: A college-wide week, once we have more volunteers
options.then: She nods. "When, though?" You don't know.

options.text: I'm still working out the full plan
options.then: She waits. "Let me know when it's ready."

options.text: A twenty-minute talk in one class this week
options.then: She grins. "That I can come to."

options.text: Something small, but I'll skip it until it's ready
options.then: She shrugs. Weeks later, it's still not ready.

steps.why: A small, specific step gives people something to join.

steps.prompt: Someone offers to help. What do you ask for?

options.text: Help with the whole awareness week
options.then: He laughs nervously. "That sounds huge."

options.text: A promise to join every month
options.then: He winces. "I can't promise that."

options.text: One small job on Friday
options.then: He nods. "Okay. I can handle that."

options.text: Whatever they feel like doing
options.then: He shrugs. Nothing specific gets done.

steps.why: A small, specific job is easy to say yes to.

scenarios.debrief: A genuinely doable first step beats a heroic one that never happens.
scenarios.relearn: Make the first step small enough to actually do this week.

scenarios.hook: You want a friend to take a first step with you.
scenarios.setup: You catch her at the end of class.

steps.prompt: Your friend asks: "What's this thing you keep talking about?"

options.text: "Will you commit your whole year to this?"
options.then: She leans back. "My whole year? I don't know."

options.text: "It's huge. I need everyone on board for months."
options.then: She laughs nervously. "That sounds exhausting."

options.text: "It's one small thing this week. Will you try it?"
options.then: She smiles. "One small thing? Okay. Tell me more."

options.text: "I need an answer today. Are you in or out?"
options.then: She frowns. "Don't push me."

steps.why: A small, specific ask is easy to say yes to.

steps.prompt: She says: "Fine. Tell me what I'd actually do."

options.text: "Whatever you like. I'll figure it out as we go."
options.then: She shrugs. "That doesn't help me say yes."

options.text: "Lead the whole campaign while I plan the rest."
options.then: She stares. "Me? I only just heard of it."

options.text: "Help me put up two posters on Friday."
options.then: She nods. "I can do that. What time?"

options.text: "I'll tell you later, once I've worked it out."
options.then: She taps her pen. "I need something clearer than that. Just give me one small thing."

steps.why: A clear, small task is easier to agree to.

steps.prompt: She adds: "Whatever it is, I might get busy. What if I can't?"

options.text: "Then you'll have let the whole team down."
options.then: She winces. "Now I'm not sure I want to."

options.text: "Don't say yes if you're not sure."
options.then: She nods slowly. She says maybe next time.

options.text: "That's fine. Tell me early and we'll adjust."
options.then: She relaxes. "Okay. I'll tell you by Thursday."

options.text: "Then I'll just find someone more reliable than you."
options.then: She looks hurt. "Wow. Okay."

steps.why: Room for real life keeps the ask easy and the friendship intact.

scenarios.relearn: A small, specific ask makes it easy for someone to start with you.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a real first step, or still just planning?

items.text: Booking a room for one workshop
Sending one email to a teacher
Inviting two friends to help on Saturday
Re-reading your plan for the tenth time

scenarios.relearn: Booking a room, emailing a teacher, inviting friends are real steps; thinking and polishing aren't yet.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: 'pick one real thing, bring a few people, take one safe step', that's how it always starts. Ready?
scenarios.affirm: One real thing, a few people, one safe step, that's the whole secret, and you have it.
scenarios.relearn: Pick one real thing, bring a few people, take one safe step.

scenarios.hook: "Don't act until you can do it perfectly."

myth.un: Don't act until you can do it perfectly.
myth.re: An imperfect real step teaches you more than a perfect imagined one; you learn by doing.
myth.why: Perfect inaction changes nothing.

scenarios.relearn: Take the imperfect first step; you learn by doing.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: what's the one small step you could actually take this week?
scenarios.affirm: Whichever you pick, doing it this week is how your change begins.
scenarios.relearn: A single concrete step this week is how change begins.

scenarios.hook: You finished your first step and now wonder whether to keep going.

steps.prompt: A friend asks if you're planning more. What do you say?

options.text: That was enough. Let's stop here
options.then: She nods. Weeks later, you wonder if you stopped too soon.

options.text: One more small step next week
options.then: She smiles. "Count me in for that."

options.text: Maybe a huge event next, to top it
options.then: She raises an eyebrow. "Huge? When?" You don't know.

options.text: Let's wait and see if anyone asks
options.then: Nobody asks. The idea sits, and you think about it anyway.

steps.why: Change builds from one small step to the next.

steps.prompt: A week later, you are tired, and any next step feels like a chore. What do you do?

options.text: Skip it, since you've done enough
options.then: The week passes. Starting again feels harder.

options.text: Shrink it and share the job
options.then: You ask a friend to take half. It feels lighter.

options.text: Do it all yourself and say nothing
options.then: You get it done and feel drained.

options.text: Postpone it until you feel motivated
options.then: The motivation doesn't arrive. The step waits.

steps.why: A smaller, shared step keeps you going without burning out.

steps.prompt: A month on, a teacher asks what has changed. What do you tell her?

options.text: That it has changed everything
options.then: She smiles politely. She asks for an example.

options.text: That nothing has changed yet, so it failed
options.then: She frowns. "Slow isn't failing."

options.text: That you'll tell her when it's big
options.then: She nods. You miss a chance to get her backing.

options.text: The small steps so far, and what's next
options.then: She reads your list. "That's real progress. I'll help."

steps.why: Honest, small progress earns support and keeps the work going.

scenarios.debrief: Change is a series of next small steps, not one leap.
scenarios.relearn: After the first step, keep taking the next small one.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two launch moves that aren't safe or real.

scene.text: A small workshop with a teacher's backing
A risky solo stunt to grab attention
Publicly naming and shaming someone online
Putting up posters the club agreed to

scenarios.why: The risky stunt and the public shaming aren't safe or lawful; the backed workshop, the verified helpline and the agreed posters are.
scenarios.relearn: Launch with safe, backed, real moves, not risky stunts or shaming.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: you now have the craft, cause, plan, movement, impact, safety, and a first step. Feel like a changemaker?
scenarios.affirm: You have the whole toolkit now, you're genuinely equipped to make real change.
scenarios.relearn: With cause, plan, movement, impact, safety and a first step, you're a changemaker.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: biggest take-away from Change Makers?
scenarios.affirm: Any of those, acted on, turns you from someone who cares into someone who changes things.
scenarios.relearn: Start small and real, bring people, stay safe and lasting, take one step.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: a generation of young changemakers, taking real, safe steps, worth being part of?
scenarios.affirm: Every young person who takes one real step helps build a fairer, safer world, starting now.
scenarios.relearn: Young changemakers taking real, safe steps build a fairer world.

scenarios.hook: Three classmates tell you they care about your cause.

steps.prompt: They look at you, waiting. What do you do first?

options.text: Say you'll call when you need them
options.then: They nod. Days pass with no word from you, and the three start to drift to other things.

options.text: Add them to a chat and see who helps
options.then: The chat fills with hellos, then goes quiet. Nobody picks up a task.

options.text: Give each a small job that fits their strength
options.then: Nisha takes the posters, Imran the sign-up list, Gauri the teacher meeting.

options.text: Ask them all to pick whatever they find most useful
options.then: Two make the same poster. One waits to be told what to do.

steps.why: Clear roles that fit people turn interest into work.

steps.prompt: A few days later, another classmate, Meera, hears about the cause and asks how she can really help. What do you say?

options.text: Say any help is welcome and she'll figure it out
options.then: She nods, then waits for someone to tell her what to do.

options.text: Say it's not urgent and she can join later
options.then: She shrugs. The offer never comes back around.

options.text: Name one task that fits her and how it helps the goal
options.then: She takes the notice-board updates and sees it's how you reach everyone.

options.text: Praise her loudly in the chat and leave it at that
options.then: She grins, and still doesn't know what to do.

steps.why: A task that fits her and a reason it matters turn willingness into work.

steps.prompt: The team needs a regular meeting time. What do you do?

options.text: Go with the first time someone suggests in the chat
options.then: Whoever replied first is happy. Two others see it too late and miss it.

options.text: Pick a time you like and expect them to adjust
options.then: Two come, a little resentful. One quietly stops.

options.text: Skip meetings and assign jobs by message
options.then: Jobs get done, but nobody feels like a team.

options.text: Ask for everyone's free slots and pick the overlap
options.then: Friday lunch works for all. Everyone shows up.

steps.why: Asking for everyone's availability shows respect and keeps the team together.

scenarios.debrief: A team forms when each person gets one clear, fitting role.
scenarios.relearn: Turn willing classmates into a team by giving fitting roles early.

scenarios.hook: A loud volunteer keeps talking over the quieter girls on your team.

steps.prompt: In today's meeting, Karan cuts off Anjali mid-sentence again. What do you do?

options.text: Let Karan run things, since he gets decisions made fast
options.then: The meeting ends in ten minutes. Anjali doesn't speak again.

options.text: Message Anjali later to say you noticed
options.then: She says thanks. At the next meeting it happens again in front of everyone.

options.text: Tell Karan off in front of the whole team
options.then: Karan sulks and the room tenses. Nobody speaks freely.

options.text: Pause the talk and ask Anjali to finish her point
options.then: Anjali finishes. Her idea for a help-desk changes the plan.

steps.why: Naming the interruption in the moment protects her turn without a fight.

steps.prompt: At the next meeting, Karan says quieter people can just message him their ideas to save time. What do you say?

options.text: Agree that speed matters most
options.then: Meetings get quicker. The quieter ones start skipping them.

options.text: Say he's the problem and ask the team to vote him out
options.then: The team hesitates. A fight about Karan replaces the agenda.

options.text: Suggest trying a turn rule for two weeks
options.then: Karan shrugs and agrees to try it. The next meeting still runs on time.

options.text: Drop it to avoid an argument
options.then: Karan carries on. The quieter girls trade glances.

steps.why: A simple, tested norm protects voices without blaming anyone.

steps.prompt: Anjali says speaking up still feels hard. What do you do?

options.text: Tell her to just be more confident
options.then: She nods and says nothing more. Meetings feel the same.

options.text: Speak on her behalf from now on
options.then: Your points are clear, but Anjali's voice is gone from the room.

options.text: Ask what would make it easier and try her ideas
options.then: She asks for the agenda a day ahead so she can prepare. The team does it.

options.text: Say it's fine and she'll get used to it
options.then: She stays silent and slowly attends less.

steps.why: Asking what would help turns a rule into real inclusion.

scenarios.debrief: Inclusion isn't automatic. Norms make every voice heard.
scenarios.relearn: Set norms so quieter teammates are included, not talked over.

scenarios.hook: Your hostel-chores campaign needs real backing before it can start.

steps.prompt: You want an adult on your side. Who do you approach first?

options.text: Nobody yet. You'll finish the whole plan first
options.then: You work for weeks. When you finally ask, the term is nearly over.

options.text: A popular senior, to gain support quickly
options.then: He likes the idea but says the warden won't care. He has no say in it.

options.text: Post a complaint about the warden online
options.then: People comment. The warden hears about it from others and is upset.

options.text: The warden, with a clear goal and a short plan
options.then: Ms. Das reads it and says she'll bring it to the hostel meeting.

steps.why: A clear goal and short plan make it easy for the right adult to back you.

steps.prompt: The warden asks what exactly you want changed. What do you say?

options.text: Everything about hostel life that feels unfair
options.then: She sighs. Without a specific ask there's nothing she can approve.

options.text: Whatever she thinks is best
options.then: She gives a vague answer and says she'll think it over.

options.text: A weekly chore rota everyone shares, from this term
options.then: She nods, says specific is easier, and asks for a draft rota.

options.text: That the other wing be punished for skipping chores
options.then: Her face hardens. The talk turns into who is to blame.

steps.why: A specific, doable ask is easy for an adult to approve.

steps.prompt: A few days later, the warden has thought it over. She says a two-week trial of a shared chore rota could work if hostel mates are on board. What do you do?

options.text: Announce the rota on the notice board and leave it at that
options.then: Some follow it. Others ignore it, saying nobody asked them.

options.text: Run the trial quietly with your close friends
options.then: Your corridor sticks to it. Other floors hear of it, and some skip chores, saying nobody asked them.

options.text: Ask the warden to enforce it herself
options.then: She says she'll remind people, but the rota isn't really anyone's.

options.text: Ask each floor for one rep and share the rota with them
options.then: Reps from each floor join. The trial starts with people who feel it's theirs.

steps.why: Reps from each floor make the trial a shared effort.

steps.prompt: Halfway through the trial, some floors skip their chores. What do you do?

options.text: Report the floors to the warden for breaking the new rota
options.then: The warden notes it. The floors feel blamed, not asked.

options.text: Do their chores yourself so the trial looks good
options.then: The hostel looks neat. The rota becomes yours, not theirs.

options.text: Stop the trial, since people won't follow it
options.then: The trial ends early. Nobody learns what could have worked.

options.text: Ask the floors what's blocking them and adjust the rota
options.then: They say exam weeks clash. You swap duties on those days.

steps.why: Asking what's blocking people helps you fix the rota instead of blaming.

steps.prompt: Later, the warden asks what should happen to the rota from here. What do you say?

options.text: Keep it, but only if you stay in charge of the whole rota
options.then: She agrees. It all depends on you, and you can't run it forever.

options.text: Drop it, since the trial showed it can't work
options.then: She nods. The rota ends with no lesson drawn.

options.text: Say it's up to her and leave it there
options.then: She decides. The hostel mates feel left out of it.

options.text: Keep it with changes, and a plan for others to take it over
options.then: The warden agrees. Volunteers from each floor will run it from next month.

steps.why: A plan for others to take over helps a change last beyond you.

scenarios.debrief: A clear goal-and-plan ask earns an adult's real backing.
scenarios.relearn: Win backing by bringing the right adult a clear, concrete ask.

scenarios.hook: Half your team wants posters and half wants a help-desk, and the meeting is stuck.

steps.prompt: Voices are rising. What do you do?

options.text: Pick your favourite and overrule the rest
options.then: You choose posters. The help-desk group goes silent.

options.text: Split into two rival teams working apart
options.then: Both start well. Soon they argue over who gets the notice board.

options.text: Ask the teacher to decide for you
options.then: Mr. Iyer decides quickly. Nobody feels the choice belongs to the team.

options.text: Ask what each side is hoping to achieve
options.then: Both say they want students to know where to get help. The room settles.

steps.why: Asking what each side wants finds the goal you share.

steps.prompt: A new teammate asks what the campaign is really for. What do you say?

options.text: Whatever the group happens to decide each week
options.then: She looks lost. Each week it seems to be something else.

options.text: One line on the shared goal that both ideas serve
options.then: She says that makes sense. Posters bring people in, and the desk helps them.

options.text: Posters matter most, and the desk can wait
options.then: She nods. Half the team hears that again and bristles.

options.text: We haven't agreed yet, so pick a side
options.then: She picks one to be polite. The split grows a little wider.

steps.why: A one-line shared goal lets both tactics serve the same purpose.

steps.prompt: Next week's room is booked for only one activity. What do you do?

options.text: Give it to whichever group argues the loudest
options.then: The louder group celebrates. The other feels it was a contest.

options.text: Toss a coin and let the winner take the room
options.then: The coin settles it. The loser takes it badly.

options.text: Cancel both until everyone agrees
options.then: The week passes without activity, and the stuck mood returns.

options.text: Run one stall: posters outside, help-desk beside
options.then: Both groups set up together. People stop at the posters, then ask the desk.

steps.why: A combined plan lets both tactics serve the goal without a winner.

scenarios.debrief: Disagreement on tactics is fine if you anchor on the shared goal.
scenarios.relearn: Settle tactic disputes by returning to the goal you all share.

scenarios.hook: A senior with a big following offers to take over and make your campaign famous.

steps.prompt: He's friendly and quick about it. What do you say?

options.text: Yes, followers matter more than who runs it
options.then: He's delighted. The team learns about it from his post.

options.text: No thanks, you'd rather do it on your own
options.then: He shrugs and walks off, saying he may still share it. Your posts reach the same few people.

options.text: Welcome the help, but the team keeps the goal
options.then: He agrees and asks what exactly you need from him.

options.text: You'll think about it, then never reply
options.then: He waits, then says he'll share it his own way. The team wonders what happened.

steps.why: You can welcome help and still keep the goal and team in your hands.

steps.prompt: A week later, the senior posts about your campaign with his own logo on it. What do you do?
