options.text: Let it go because the reach is too good to risk
options.then: The post spreads. Fewer people know the team behind it.

options.text: Reply publicly and call him out
options.then: Followers pile in. The argument becomes the story.

options.text: Delete your own posts so only his remains
options.then: The feed looks neat, and the team's work is invisible.

options.text: Ask him to credit the team and use your goal line
options.then: He edits the post. The team name appears, and so does your goal.

steps.why: Asking for credit and the right message keeps the work yours.

steps.prompt: His post brings many new followers who want to join. What do you do?

options.text: Add everyone to the team chat right away
options.then: The chat floods. The first tasks get lost in the noise.

options.text: Let the senior handle them since he has the reach
options.then: He sends them a link. The team never meets them.

options.text: Count the followers as the campaign's success
options.then: The number looks big. It doesn't say what changed.

options.text: Invite them to a meeting to share goal and roles
options.then: Some come. A few take real tasks, and the team grows.

steps.why: Real members with roles matter more than a follower count.

scenarios.debrief: Accept reach that serves the goal. Don't trade the cause for fame.
scenarios.relearn: Take help that grows the cause, but keep the goal and team yours.

scenarios.hook: Two weeks in, fewer people turn up to your campaign meetings each time.

steps.prompt: Only a few chairs are filled today. What do you do?

options.text: Decide the cause has run its course and stop meetings
options.then: No meeting is called. A few members keep checking the chat for news.

options.text: Message those who skipped, saying they promised to come
options.then: Two reply with excuses. Nobody says what's really in the way.

options.text: Ask the team what's getting in the way of coming
options.then: They say meetings run long and clash with tuition. It's fixable.

options.text: Make meetings livelier with snacks and games
options.then: The first one is fun. People still skip when tuition clashes.

steps.why: A dip is feedback, so ask what is getting in the way.

steps.prompt: A member says shorter lunch-time meetings might suit people better. What do you do?

options.text: Keep the old time, since everyone agreed to it earlier
options.then: Same small crowd for now. The suggestion goes nowhere, though a few drift back after exams.

options.text: Switch the time without telling members who are absent
options.then: The lunch crowd grows, and the earlier regulars find out late.

options.text: Try a short lunch slot for two weeks and compare turnout
options.then: Fifteen minutes at lunch brings more people. You note who came.

options.text: Say it's only an excuse and they should just come
options.then: The member goes quiet. Others hold back their ideas.

steps.why: Trying a small change and checking the result is how teams adjust.

steps.prompt: A month later, turnout has crept up but isn't full. What do you do?

options.text: Treat it as fixed and stop asking
options.then: Things hold for a while, until new problems go unspoken.

options.text: Push for full attendance now that it has improved
options.then: People feel pressure. A few stop coming again.

options.text: Keep asking for feedback and adjust as needed
options.then: The team adds a short agenda and a rota for who leads.

options.text: Compare your numbers with a bigger club's
options.then: The comparison stings. Your team feels small and unsure.

steps.why: Asking regularly keeps the team improving.

steps.prompt: A new member joins and asks how decisions get made here. What do you say?

options.text: I decide, since I started it
options.then: She nods but wonders if her ideas count.

options.text: We vote on everything, even small things
options.then: Meetings stretch, and she watches the clock.

options.text: There's no real system. We see what happens
options.then: She looks puzzled and unsure where she fits.

options.text: We ask each other what's working and adjust together
options.then: She smiles. "That's easier than I expected," she says.

steps.why: A habit of asking and adjusting is what makes a team want to stay.

steps.prompt: A month later, attendance dips again. What do you do?

options.text: Treat it as proof the earlier fix didn't work
options.then: The team drops its latest change. Turnout falls further.

options.text: Say it always happens and ignore it
options.then: A few more skip. The group shrinks quietly.

options.text: Switch to a completely new format right away
options.then: People are confused. Nobody knows what the plan is now.

options.text: Ask the team, change one thing and check again
options.then: Members say they're tired. You shorten meetings, and turnout recovers.

steps.why: A repeatable habit of asking and adjusting beats a one-off fix.

scenarios.debrief: A drop is data. Ask, learn and adjust.
scenarios.relearn: When momentum dips, treat it as feedback and adjust. Don't quit.

scenarios.hook: A boy who once mocked your cause now asks to join, and he seems sincere.

steps.prompt: Dev waits for your answer while a teammate frowns. What do you do?

options.text: Say no because of what he said earlier
options.then: He nods and walks off. He tells his friends you never forgive anyone.

options.text: Let him join but keep him out of every discussion
options.then: He sits in meetings and says nothing. He senses it and keeps his distance.

options.text: Ask the team to vote on whether he's allowed in
options.then: The vote splits. He waits outside, feeling judged.

options.text: Talk to him and give him a small first task
options.then: Dev says he laughed to look cool. He wants to make up for it.

steps.why: A small first task lets him show he means it, and the team sees it too.

steps.prompt: A teammate says the group is split about Dev. What do you do?

options.text: Say it's settled and nobody should bring it up
options.then: The topic goes underground and the whispering continues.

options.text: Ask Dev to prove himself to everyone
options.then: Dev tries hard. The team starts watching him like an exam.

options.text: Hold a short talk and agree what you expect from everyone
options.then: People voice worries and hopes. The group agrees on shared rules for all.

options.text: Back the louder group to keep things calm
options.then: The louder group is pleased. The rest feel unheard.

steps.why: Shared expectations for everyone beat a case-by-case trial.

steps.prompt: Later, Dev asks what he could do next. What do you say?

options.text: The team is full for now
options.then: He nods, hiding his disappointment. The door feels shut.

options.text: You can have a bigger role once everyone fully trusts you
options.then: He shrugs. A team that wanted more hands has fewer.

options.text: Take the hardest task to prove you're serious
options.then: He struggles with it and feels like he failed a test.

options.text: Ask what he'd like to own, and give him a bigger task
options.then: He picks the sign-up table. By Friday it's the busiest corner.

steps.why: Growing trust through fitting tasks helps people change.

scenarios.debrief: Movements grow by letting people change. Shared goals beat grudges.
scenarios.relearn: Let people who've grown join; don't run purity tests.

scenarios.hook: You've been doing every campaign task yourself, and you're worn out.

steps.prompt: A teammate asks how it's going. What do you tell her?

options.text: That it's fine and you can handle it
options.then: She believes you. Another week goes by with everything on you.

options.text: That it's tiring, but you don't want to bother her
options.then: She says take care and doesn't offer. You carry on.

options.text: That you're doing too much and need to hand some over
options.then: She nods. "I thought you liked doing it all," she says.

options.text: Nothing, and quietly let a few tasks slip
options.then: Tasks slip. She notices something is wrong, but not what.

steps.why: Saying it out loud is how the load gets shared.

steps.prompt: Later that week, three tasks are due. What do you do?

options.text: Do all three, but start earlier
options.then: You finish, tired, with no time left to revise for your exam.

options.text: Hand them out, then redo them yourself afterwards
options.then: You end up doing twice the work. They notice you redid it.

options.text: Drop all three and hope nobody notices
options.then: Two are missed. The team notices and doesn't know why.

options.text: Hand over tasks and agree who checks in
options.then: Three people take one each. You sleep properly that night.

steps.why: Handing over clear tasks with a check-in shares the load and keeps work moving.

steps.prompt: Campaign messages keep buzzing on your phone late at night. What do you do?

options.text: Reply to all of them, since someone should
options.then: You answer till midnight. Your energy the next day is gone.

options.text: Mute the chat without saying anything
options.then: You rest, but the team wonders why you've gone silent.

options.text: Ask people to message you less at night
options.then: They try. The late messages still come to you, so nothing is shared.

options.text: Set quiet hours and tell the team when you'll reply
options.then: People respect it. Two others copy you.

steps.why: Clear rest hours protect you and show others they can protect theirs.

scenarios.debrief: Sharing the load keeps both you and the movement going.
scenarios.relearn: Delegate and rest; carrying it all alone burns the movement out.

scenarios.hook: At a team meeting, Zoya sharply disagrees with your plan in front of everyone.

steps.prompt: The room goes quiet. What do you do?

options.text: Shut it down and say the plan stands
options.then: Zoya sits back. The room stays silent after that.

options.text: Agree straight away to end the tension
options.then: The tension eases. Nobody knows whether you weighed her point.

options.text: Say you'll talk after the meeting and move on
options.then: The meeting continues. Her point hangs unanswered in the room.

options.text: Ask her to explain her concern and hear it out
options.then: Zoya says the plan misses younger students. The team listens.

steps.why: Hearing her out shows the team that disagreement is safe.

steps.prompt: Later, the team is divided over the plan. What do you do?

options.text: Decide it yourself since you made the plan
options.then: The plan stays as it was. Zoya's frown deepens.

options.text: Put it off until everyone agrees
options.then: The team waits a week. Agreement doesn't arrive.

options.text: Say what each side has right, then decide together
options.then: People nod. The team picks a mixed plan, and the vote goes smoothly.

options.text: Ask the loudest member to speak for the group
options.then: He does. The quieter members stay out of it.

steps.why: Weighing both views and deciding together builds ownership.

steps.prompt: At the next meeting, another teammate has a doubt. What do you do?

options.text: Remind her that Zoya already raised concerns
options.then: The teammate takes the hint and keeps quiet.

options.text: Ask her to share the doubt privately with you
options.then: She sends it later. The rest of the team never hears the point.

options.text: Welcome the doubt and ask the team to weigh in
options.then: More hands go up. Two small fixes appear before the end.

options.text: Joke it off to keep things light
options.then: People laugh. The doubt stays unsaid and shows up later.

steps.why: Making doubt welcome lets problems surface early.

scenarios.debrief: Safe disagreement makes a team stronger, not weaker.
scenarios.relearn: Welcome dissent, weigh it, and decide together. Don't crush it.

scenarios.hook: An online stranger messages you, offering funds and fame fast for your cause.

steps.prompt: The message is friendly and urgent. What do you do?

options.text: Send your team's names and details to get the money
options.then: He asks for your school's name too, and tells you to hurry.

options.text: Ask him for proof by replying with more questions
options.then: He sends a link and a vague promise. The pressure to hurry grows.

options.text: Trust him, since he says he wants to back a good cause
options.then: You reply warmly. He asks when you're free for a private call.

options.text: Decline, and tell a teacher or parent about it
options.then: Your teacher thanks you and says offers like this need checking.

steps.why: A fast-fame offer from a stranger is risky, and a trusted adult can help check it.

steps.prompt: A few days later, he writes again, saying a big sponsor is ready to back you. What do you do?

options.text: Reply once to tell him to stop
options.then: He answers fast in a friendlier tone. The messages keep coming.

options.text: Put it to a team vote on whether to take his offer
options.then: Half want the money and the vote is close. Nobody has checked who he is.

options.text: Agree to meet him alone to hear the offer in full
options.then: He picks a place you don't know and asks you to come alone. It feels off.

options.text: Don't reply, and save the messages to show an adult
options.then: You keep the screenshots. Your teacher helps you report the account.

steps.why: Saving messages and telling an adult is how you get safe, real help.

steps.prompt: A local shopkeeper offers to sponsor your poster printing. What do you do?

options.text: Accept right away and keep it from the school
options.then: He gives the money. Your teacher is surprised when she hears of it later.

options.text: Turn him down, since any offer might be risky
options.then: He's disappointed. You print posters yourself, slowly.

options.text: Take the money and put his shop name on everything
options.then: The posters go up. Parents ask if your campaign is selling something.

options.text: Ask your teacher to meet him and confirm the offer
options.then: He's well known in the area, and your teacher helps you thank him.

steps.why: Known local partners with adult backing are the safe, credible kind.

steps.prompt: Weeks later, a classmate says she got a similar message and feels uneasy. What do you do?

options.text: Tell her to ignore it, since nothing has happened
options.then: She nods slowly. She still feels uneasy.

options.text: Reply to the sender yourself to scare him off
options.then: He answers with new messages. The pressure keeps going.

options.text: Warn the whole class group and share her message
options.then: Her message goes to everyone. She feels exposed.

options.text: Believe her and go to a teacher together
options.then: She's relieved. Your teacher listens and helps her report it.

steps.why: Believing her and going to a trusted adult together keeps her safe, and it's never her fault.

scenarios.debrief: Good partners are known and local. Fast-fame strangers are risky, and it is never your fault if one pushes.
scenarios.relearn: Refuse fast-fame strangers; partner with people you can verify.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Mehak's idea for the launch event is clearly stronger than yours.

steps.prompt: Mehak pitches her idea to the team. What do you do?

options.text: Push your own idea so you stay the founder
options.then: The team goes quiet. Mehak looks down, and her idea is lost.

options.text: Take her idea and present it as your own later
options.then: It goes down well. When Mehak finds out, she's hurt.

options.text: Say both are fine and let the team pick without comment
options.then: The team picks yours as it's more familiar. Mehak's idea fades.

options.text: Say hers is stronger and offer to help build it
options.then: Mehak lights up. The team picks her idea.

steps.why: Backing the best idea openly helps the cause more than your pride.

steps.prompt: The team asks who should lead the launch. What do you say?

options.text: You should, since the cause started with you
options.then: The team hesitates. A small chill spreads.

options.text: Lead it together so credit stays shared with you
options.then: It sounds fair but gets confusing. Each of you waits for the other to decide.

options.text: Suggest Mehak leads, and ask where you can help
options.then: She accepts and gives you the sign-ups and printing.

options.text: You'd rather not be involved right now
options.then: You step back, sulky. The team wonders what happened.

steps.why: Letting the person with the best plan lead makes the team stronger.

steps.prompt: On launch day, a teacher praises the event and looks at you. What do you say?

options.text: Nothing, just accept the praise
options.then: It feels nice for a moment. Mehak notices and says nothing.

options.text: That it was a team effort, without naming anyone
options.then: The teacher nods. Mehak, who worked on it too, goes uncredited.

options.text: That you'd planned most of it from the start
options.then: The teacher is impressed. Mehak hears, and her face falls.

options.text: Thank her and say Mehak's work helped make it happen
options.then: Mehak hears it from across the room and grins.

steps.why: Naming who made it work builds trust and keeps the team strong.

scenarios.debrief: Backing the best idea over your ego is what real leaders do.
scenarios.relearn: Champion the strongest idea, even when it isn't yours.

scenarios.hook: A local NGO offers to co-run your awareness drive, but wants joint decisions.

steps.prompt: Their coordinator, Ms. Kapoor, waits for your answer. What do you say?

options.text: Say yes only if you keep sole control of the drive
options.then: She says that's your choice, and turns friendly but distant.

options.text: Yes, then use their name while skipping their advice
options.then: Their name draws crowds. She notices her advice is being ignored.

options.text: Anything, so long as they stay on board
options.then: She smiles. You haven't asked what "anything" means.

options.text: Yes, and ask how you'd share decisions in practice
options.then: She suggests a weekly check-in where each side has an equal say.

steps.why: Agreeing to share decisions, with the details clear, builds a real partnership.

steps.prompt: Teammates worry the NGO will take over. What do you do?

options.text: Tell them it's decided and they should accept it
options.then: They go along, and the team feels sidelined.

options.text: Side with them and push back on the NGO about everything
options.then: Ms. Kapoor finds you hard to work with. The relationship strains.

options.text: Keep their worries from the NGO
options.then: The worries grow in private and burst out at a bad moment.

options.text: Explain what the NGO brings and what stays with the team
options.then: Teammates relax once they see which choices are theirs.

steps.why: Naming who decides what builds trust inside and outside the team.

steps.prompt: The NGO suggests moving your event date. What do you do?

options.text: Say no, since the date is yours to set
options.then: Ms. Kapoor shrugs, and the next check-in feels cooler.

options.text: Accept it without asking anyone on the team
options.then: Half the team learns of it from the NGO's poster.

options.text: Say you'll think about it, then let it drift
options.then: Weeks pass. The date clashes with an NGO camp.

options.text: Weigh it together, then decide jointly with the team
options.then: You move the date by a week. Both sides feel heard.

steps.why: Joint decisions need joint talks, not a yes or no from one side.

scenarios.debrief: Partnering with shared decisions multiplies a small drive's reach and experience.
scenarios.relearn: Partner with known NGOs and share decisions to multiply impact.

scenarios.hook: Two teammates, Isha and Rahul, fall out after Rahul misses a poster deadline, and the group is splitting.

steps.prompt: Everyone is choosing sides in the chat. What do you do?

options.text: Take Isha's side publicly since she's your friend
options.then: Isha feels backed. Rahul and his friends go quiet.

options.text: Ignore it and hope it fixes itself
options.then: The chat gets sharper. A few people mute it.

options.text: Ask the teacher to sort it out for them
options.then: She talks to them. They feel the team doesn't trust them to handle it.

options.text: Talk to each privately, then refocus on the goal
options.then: Both say it isn't about the cause, but neither is ready to forgive the missed deadline.

steps.why: Cooling things privately and refocusing keeps the team together.

steps.prompt: A week later, Isha says she'll quit if Rahul is at the next event. What do you do?

options.text: Tell her she's being dramatic
options.then: She leaves the chat and the team goes tense. A few days later she rejoins.

options.text: Ask Rahul to skip the event to keep the peace
options.then: He agrees, hurt. He doesn't feel welcome after that.

options.text: Say you can't help with personal matters
options.then: She feels alone. The tension stays.

options.text: Hear her out and ask what would make it workable
options.then: She says she needs a clear role separate from Rahul's.

steps.why: Understanding what each person needs lets them keep working for the goal.

steps.prompt: Days later, Isha and Rahul are working together again, but others are wary. What do you do?

options.text: Say the matter is closed and no one should mention it
options.then: People stay quiet. The wariness goes underground.

options.text: Plan a team outing to fix the mood
options.then: It's fun, but the issue stays unspoken.

options.text: Put them in separate groups for good
options.then: The two rarely meet. The team loses its shared mood.

options.text: Remind everyone why you started and agree on team rules
options.then: People recall the goal. The team agrees to raise problems early and privately.

steps.why: Shared rules and a shared purpose help the team move on.

steps.prompt: Weeks later, two other members start a quarrel. What do you do?

options.text: Ask Isha and Rahul to settle it for them
options.then: They try, and the two members feel judged by their peers.

options.text: Make a rule that personal disputes aren't allowed
options.then: Nobody brings anything up. The quarrels go underground.

options.text: Let it play out, since it's their business
options.then: The quarrel spreads through the chat before you notice.

options.text: Talk to each privately, then refocus on the goal
options.then: Both calm down and the team keeps moving.

steps.why: A steady, private approach to conflict keeps the team calm every time.

scenarios.debrief: A leader cools conflict privately and points the team back to why.
scenarios.relearn: Defuse team conflict privately and refocus everyone on the shared goal.

scenarios.hook: Your homework-help project has helped a few classmates, and a bigger number would look impressive.

steps.prompt: The school newsletter editor asks how many classmates you've helped. What do you say?

options.text: A big round number, since it sounds more impressive
options.then: She prints it. A teacher later asks to see the list.

options.text: Lots of students, and leave it there
options.then: She prints "lots". Readers can't tell what changed.

options.text: The real number, and what you hope to reach next
options.then: She writes it down. It's small, and she says that sounds honest.

options.text: Count everyone who ever walked past your table
options.then: The number sounds big, but people wonder where the help is.

steps.why: Honest numbers let people trust what you say.

steps.prompt: A sponsor wants to see your results before helping. What do you do?

options.text: Round the figures up a little
options.then: She notices a mismatch and asks to see the register.

options.text: Show only the best week's results
options.then: She's impressed until she asks about the other weeks.

options.text: Say the records are private and ask her to trust you
options.then: She hesitates. With nothing to check, she holds back.

options.text: Share real counts with no names, plus what you've learned
options.then: She sees modest results and a clear plan, and offers to print your handouts.

steps.why: Real counts without names show honesty and respect for privacy.

steps.prompt: This month's count is lower than last month's. What do you do?

options.text: Leave this month out of the report
options.then: The report looks smooth. A member sees the gap and wonders.

options.text: Add last term's students to cover the gap
options.then: The total looks fine, but nobody can match it to this month.

options.text: Blame exams and say little else
options.then: Your report sounds reasonable but doesn't show what to improve.

options.text: Report the dip and what you'll change
options.then: People appreciate it. Two helpers offer extra evenings.

steps.why: An honest dip shows what to fix, and trust grows when you share it.

scenarios.debrief: Honest, specific numbers build the trust a movement runs on.
scenarios.relearn: Report real numbers; exaggeration eventually breaks a movement's trust.

scenarios.hook: Nisha rarely speaks in meetings, but her sketches in the margins are clearly strong.

steps.prompt: Your posters look dull and the deadline is close. What do you do?

options.text: Leave Nisha alone since she's shy
options.then: The posters stay dull. Nisha keeps sketching in her notebook.

options.text: Give her the most public role to bring her out of her shell
options.then: She's stiff and tense up front. She skips the next meeting.

options.text: Ask the whole group who wants to do the design
options.then: Two loud voices volunteer. Nisha stays quiet.

options.text: Ask what she'd like to own and offer the design work
options.then: Nisha's eyes light up. "I'd love to do the posters," she says.

steps.why: Asking what fits her draws out her strengths without pressure.

steps.prompt: Nisha says she doesn't think her ideas matter. What do you say?

options.text: Tell her not to be silly and to speak up more
options.then: She nods and says nothing. She speaks up less.

options.text: Say everyone's ideas matter, then move on
options.then: She thanks you, though it didn't touch the doubt.

options.text: Point to one specific thing she did that helped
options.then: You mention her sketch on the notice board. She smiles, a little surprised.

options.text: Offer to speak for her at meetings from now on
options.then: She relaxes, but her ideas now always reach the team through you.

steps.why: Specific praise shows her she matters more than a general reassurance.

steps.prompt: Some of Nisha's sketches ended up on the posters, and the team wants someone to present them at assembly. What do you do?

options.text: Present them yourself so she's spared
options.then: It goes smoothly, and Nisha's work gets less credit than it deserves.

options.text: Insist Nisha presents, to build her confidence
options.then: She goes pale and stumbles. She avoids the next meeting.

options.text: Let the group pick whoever is loudest
options.then: Dhruv presents and doesn't mention who designed them.

options.text: Ask Nisha how she'd like to share them and back her choice
options.then: She picks a short note with photos. It lands well.

steps.why: Letting her pick how to share makes her work visible on her own terms.

scenarios.debrief: Good teams draw out quiet strengths instead of overlooking them.
scenarios.relearn: Invite quieter members into roles that fit their real strengths.

scenarios.hook: Your campaign message makes sense to you, but classmates look confused.

steps.prompt: A friend says she read your notice twice and still isn't sure what it means. What do you do?

options.text: Add more serious words so it sounds important
options.then: The new notice sounds official. Fewer people read to the end.

options.text: Tell her to read it more carefully
options.then: She shrugs. Others in the group say nothing.

options.text: Explain it to her aloud and hope that's enough
options.then: She gets it. Everyone else is still stuck on the notice.

options.text: Ask which part lost her, then cut it to one line
options.then: She points at the third sentence. You rewrite it, and the line fits.

steps.why: Asking what confused her shows how to simplify.

steps.prompt: Your teacher says the notice should say who it's for and what to do. What do you do?

options.text: Add a paragraph explaining the background
options.then: The notice is long again, and the action is buried.

options.text: Add a catchy slogan and an exclamation mark
options.then: It sounds lively, but nobody knows what to do.

options.text: Keep it vague so more people feel included
options.then: It reaches everyone and moves no one.

options.text: Name the audience and one action in a single line
options.then: "Hostel students: join Friday's short meeting." People reply with questions about timing.

steps.why: Naming who it's for and one action makes a message easy to answer.

steps.prompt: A few classmates still don't get it. What do you do?

options.text: Blame them for not paying attention
options.then: Word spreads that you think people are slow.

options.text: Add jargon to sound more serious
options.then: Even your friends ask for a glossary.

options.text: Send the same message again from more accounts
options.then: The same unclear message arrives in more places.

options.text: Ask them what they heard, then adjust the line
options.then: They repeat it differently. You fix one word, and it clicks.

steps.why: Hearing what people understood shows what to change.

scenarios.debrief: A clear, honest one-liner about the goal is what brings people in.
scenarios.relearn: Make your message one honest, simple line so people can join.

scenarios.hook: After your teacher turns down your plan, a teammate suggests a protest outside her home.

steps.prompt: The team is angry and wants to go there on Sunday. What do you do?

options.text: Go along so you look bold and committed
options.then: Some cheer. A neighbour sees the group and calls the teacher.

options.text: Let the loudest few go ahead without you this time
options.then: They go. The teacher is shaken, and the school hears of your campaign for the wrong reason.

options.text: Message the teacher privately to warn her
options.then: She thanks you for the warning. The team still plans to go, and nobody has talked it through with them.

options.text: Say not at her home, and ask the school to meet
options.then: Some grumble. Others agree to write to the principal.

steps.why: A protest at someone's home is unsafe and unlawful, so choose a school-backed route.

steps.prompt: The principal says the team can bring a written request. What do you do?

options.text: Write an angry letter listing every complaint
options.then: It feels good to write. The principal reads it and feels attacked.

options.text: Post the complaint online and tag the school
options.then: Comments pour in. The principal feels cornered, not asked.

options.text: Let one person handle the whole thing alone
options.then: He tries, but he isn't sure of the details.

options.text: Write the goal and ask, with a teacher's advice
options.then: A teacher reads it and sharpens the ask. It's ready by Thursday.

steps.why: A clear request with adult advice is the safe, credible way to be heard.

steps.prompt: A parent warns that protests can get risky. What do you do?

options.text: Say you'll be extra careful at the next protest
options.then: She nods but stays worried. Careful isn't the same as safe.

options.text: Ignore it, since adults always say that
options.then: The team plans a sit-in without asking anyone.

options.text: Cancel everything so nobody gets into trouble
options.then: The team feels deflated, and the problem remains.

options.text: Ask which safe, lawful options exist, with a teacher
options.then: She suggests a signature drive and a meeting between students and staff.

steps.why: Safe, lawful, adult-backed action protects the team and the cause.

steps.prompt: Weeks later, the team gets a chance to meet the principal. How do you prepare?

options.text: Bring the angriest members to show how strongly you feel
options.then: The principal senses hostility and closes the topic.

options.text: Go ready to refuse anything less than your full demand
options.then: She hears an ultimatum. The talk stalls.

options.text: Skip preparing, since honesty is enough
options.then: You ramble. The ask gets lost.

options.text: Agree who speaks and bring the facts, with a teacher present
options.then: The meeting stays calm, and the principal agrees to a trial.

steps.why: Preparing facts and speakers, with a teacher present, makes the meeting count.

scenarios.debrief: Movement tactics stay non-violent, lawful and adult-backed.
scenarios.relearn: Redirect risky confrontations toward safe, lawful, backed action.

scenarios.hook: Twenty students have signed your team's pledge, your first small win.

steps.prompt: The team is buzzing, but someone says twenty is too few to matter. What do you do?

options.text: Agree it's too few and skip marking it
options.then: The buzz drops. The team gets back to work, a little flat.

options.text: Demand a much bigger number by next week
options.then: People groan. Two quietly start missing tasks.

options.text: Post about it online and wait for praise
options.then: Some likes arrive. The team never talks about what's next.

options.text: Celebrate it together before moving on
options.then: The team shares chai and reads the names. Energy comes back.

steps.why: Marking a small win keeps a team's energy up.

steps.prompt: Someone asks what comes next. What do you say?

options.text: Aim for the whole school by the end of the month
options.then: The goal feels exciting, then impossible, and the team slips.

options.text: Take a break until someone has a great idea
options.then: Days pass. The momentum cools.

options.text: Pick one goal the team can reach in a few weeks
options.then: The team agrees on more sign-ups and one clean-up day.

options.text: Leave it for the next meeting to decide
options.then: The next meeting starts without a plan.

steps.why: A next goal within the team's reach keeps it moving.

steps.prompt: A member says the pledge hasn't changed anything yet. What do you say?

options.text: A few signatures should be enough to change things
options.then: She doesn't believe it. Her doubt grows.

options.text: You're wrong and shouldn't be so negative
options.then: She goes quiet and stops sharing doubts.

options.text: Show what's real so far and what comes next
options.then: You list the signatures, the next goal and a date. She nods.

options.text: Agree it's pointless and suggest quitting
options.then: The mood sinks. The team wonders if they've failed.

steps.why: Real progress, honestly stated, answers doubt without hype.

steps.prompt: A month on, the pledge drive has slowed. What do you do?

options.text: Start a brand-new project to feel fresh
options.then: The new project excites people, and the pledge is forgotten.

options.text: Raise the target and demand more effort
options.then: People feel pushed and start to drift.

options.text: Wait for a bigger win before you celebrate again
options.then: Weeks pass without a celebration, and morale slips.

options.text: Review what worked, set one small goal and celebrate it
options.then: The team picks a clean-up day, and the energy returns.

steps.why: Small goals and small celebrations keep a volunteer team moving.

scenarios.debrief: Marking small wins keeps a volunteer team energised for the long term.
scenarios.relearn: Celebrate small wins together, then aim at the next reachable goal.

scenarios.hook: A classmate wants to help your clean-air campaign but can give only one hour a week.

steps.prompt: She asks if that's even worth it. What do you say?

options.text: That it's all-in or nothing, so she should wait
options.then: She nods, disappointed. A few days later she asks again if there's anything for one hour.

options.text: That one hour is fine, and you'll expect more later
options.then: She says yes. You add that more will be needed later, and she looks unsure.

options.text: That one hour counts, and you'll design a role for it
options.then: She's relieved. "I can do Thursday lunch," she says.

options.text: Ask her to drop another activity so she can do more
options.then: She looks unsure. She says she'll think it over.

steps.why: A flexible role that fits her time shows that one hour counts.

steps.prompt: Her role needs to be clear. What do you give her?

options.text: A long list so she can pick when she has time
options.then: She feels overwhelmed and does none of it.

options.text: A vague promise to find something later
options.then: She waits for weeks, then drifts away.

options.text: One repeatable task, like updating the sign-up sheet
options.then: She can do it in an hour, and others start relying on it.

options.text: The tasks nobody else wants
options.then: She does them dutifully and quietly resents it.

steps.why: A small, repeatable task fits an hour and keeps her useful.

steps.prompt: Others say it isn't fair that she does less. What do you say?

options.text: Agree, and ask her to do more
options.then: She stays, but the new load is too heavy. She leaves after a week.

options.text: It's her choice and none of their business to question
options.then: The team feels dismissed, and the grumbling goes on.

options.text: They can reduce their hours too
options.then: Some cut back. The work slows.

options.text: Everyone gives what they can, and her hour counts
options.then: People nod. Two others ask for lighter roles too.

steps.why: Honest roles for different capacities keep more people involved.

scenarios.debrief: Flexible, honest roles let more people genuinely contribute.
scenarios.relearn: Fit roles to what people can give; one honest hour still counts.

scenarios.hook: Your team has two minutes at the school assembly to share your campaign.

steps.prompt: You need one person to speak. How do you choose?

options.text: You speak, since it's your cause
options.then: The talk is fine, but the team sees you at the mic yet again.

options.text: Pick the most popular student
options.then: He gets cheers, then forgets the key points halfway.

options.text: Ask the teacher to pick someone
options.then: Ms. Roy picks a favourite who doesn't know the plan.

options.text: Pick whoever explains it most clearly
options.then: Fatima practises in front of the team and nails it.

steps.why: The clearest speaker carries the message best.

steps.prompt: A teammate asks what the assembly talk should include. What do you say?

options.text: Everything the team has done, in order
options.then: Two minutes pass before the main point arrives.

options.text: Your best jokes to win the crowd
options.then: People laugh. The ask gets lost.

options.text: Whatever feels right on the day
options.then: The talk wanders, and the ask goes missing.

options.text: The goal, one real result and one way to join
options.then: The talk keeps to it, and people ask where to sign.

steps.why: A short talk with one result and one way to join makes people act.

steps.prompt: After the assembly, a newcomer asks who really runs the campaign. What do you say?

options.text: You do, but others help
options.then: She nods. Few newcomers feel the cause is theirs.

options.text: The person who spoke, since they're the face of it
options.then: The speaker becomes the whole campaign, and the rest feel hidden.

options.text: Whoever has the most followers
options.then: She looks puzzled. It sounds like fame, not teamwork.

options.text: The whole team, and someone else speaks next time
options.then: She smiles. "I could try next time," she says.

steps.why: Sharing the stage and credit keeps the movement collective.

scenarios.debrief: Represent the team well and share credit so the work stays collective.
scenarios.relearn: Choose the clearest voice to speak, and credit the whole team.

scenarios.hook: Exams are near, and your team's energy is fading fast.

steps.prompt: Half the team hasn't replied in days. What do you do?

options.text: Push everyone to keep going through exams
options.then: People push for a week. Then marks and moods start to dip.

options.text: Let it quietly fall apart
options.then: No one says anything. The group chat goes silent.

options.text: Ask the active ones to do extra to cover
options.then: They try and feel worn down as exams approach.

options.text: Propose a pause and ask when to restart
options.then: People reply with relief. They suggest the Monday after exams.

steps.why: A planned pause with a restart date protects people and the project.

steps.prompt: A teammate worries the campaign will be forgotten. What do you say?

options.text: Tell her it will be fine and nobody will forget
options.then: She isn't sure, and worries more.

options.text: Ask her to keep it going alone for now
options.then: She tries and feels alone, with exams close.

options.text: Say that if it fades, it wasn't meant to be
options.then: She looks crushed. "We tried so hard," she says.

options.text: Pick a restart date and put it and a first task on the board
options.then: She smiles. A note says what happens after exams.

steps.why: A visible restart plan keeps the work alive during the pause.

steps.prompt: Meanwhile, someone shares a great idea for the campaign. What do you do?

options.text: Call a meeting now to start on it
options.then: Everyone shows up out of guilt, and revision waits.

options.text: Tell them it's too late to add ideas this term
options.then: They stop suggesting things.

options.text: Start working on it yourself right away
options.then: You make progress, but your own revision slips.

options.text: Thank them and save it for after the exams
options.then: Their idea goes on the list. They can study with it in mind.

steps.why: Saving ideas for the restart protects everyone's studies and the team's energy.

scenarios.debrief: A planned pause protects people and the movement's future.
scenarios.relearn: When life peaks, pause with a restart date instead of burning out.

scenarios.hook: Kabir keeps missing the tasks he promised, and the others are getting frustrated.

steps.prompt: Kabir has missed another deadline. What do you do?

options.text: Call him out in the group chat
options.then: Others pile on. Kabir stops replying.

options.text: Take his tasks on yourself without saying anything
options.then: The work gets done. You grow tired and a little resentful.

options.text: Wait and see if he notices himself
options.then: He doesn't. The others' frustration builds.

options.text: Ask him privately what's going on
options.then: Kabir says exams and a family event clash with his tasks.

steps.why: A private, curious question finds out what's wrong without shaming him.

steps.prompt: Later, Kabir says he can't keep up with his tasks. What do you say?

options.text: Everyone has exams, so he should manage
options.then: He nods and doesn't commit to anything.

options.text: It's fine, and his tasks are dropped completely
options.then: He's relieved, but he feels less a part of the team.

options.text: He can make up the missed work this weekend
options.then: He agrees tiredly. Two tasks are late again.

options.text: Re-scope his tasks to something he can finish
options.then: He takes the sign-up sheet. "That I can do," he says.

steps.why: Resizing a task to fit someone's real time keeps them in the team.

steps.prompt: A teammate asks how the team is handling Kabir's tasks while everyone else has exams too. What do you say?

options.text: He's a friend of mine, so this is an exception
options.then: She frowns. It sounds like favouritism.

options.text: It isn't fair, so you'll cut his role altogether
options.then: Kabir is hurt, and the team shrinks.

options.text: Mind your own business and focus on your tasks
options.then: She goes quiet, and the grumble moves elsewhere.

options.text: Everyone's role fits their time, and we review together
options.then: She nods. The team agrees to review roles every month.

steps.why: A shared review of roles keeps the team fair and honest about time.

scenarios.debrief: Kind, private accountability keeps both the person and the work.
scenarios.relearn: Handle a flaking teammate privately and re-scope, don't shame or absorb.

scenarios.hook: A classmate, Roshni, often says she cares about your cause but has never joined.
scenarios.setup: You catch her at the bus stop after school.

steps.prompt: Roshni says: "I keep meaning to join. I just don't know where I'd fit."

options.text: "You should really do more for this cause, you know."
options.then: Roshni shrinks. "I'm trying. It's not that simple."

options.text: "We need all the help we can get. Just come."
options.then: Roshni hesitates. "Maybe. I just don't want to be in the way."

options.text: "Think about it. No pressure at all."
options.then: Roshni smiles. "Okay. I will." Nothing changes.

options.text: "Could you run the sign-up table for an hour on Friday?"
options.then: Roshni brightens. "Oh. Just that? Yes, I can do that."

steps.why: A small, specific ask is easy to say yes to.

steps.prompt: Roshni asks: "When I do start, what if I get something wrong?"

options.text: "You won't. It's easy, so don't worry about it."
options.then: She smiles faintly. "If you say so." Her worry stays.

options.text: "Then maybe it's not for you. No harm in saying so."
options.then: Her face falls. "Oh. Okay."

options.text: "Don't worry. Someone will fix it if you slip up."
options.then: She frowns. "So I'd be a mistake someone cleans up."

options.text: "I'll show you once, and we'll check in after."
options.then: She relaxes. "Okay. That helps."

steps.why: Support and a check-in help new people feel safe to try.

steps.prompt: Roshni says: "My exams are coming up. Could I still help somehow?"

options.text: "Then it's best to wait until exams are over."
options.then: She nods. "Okay." The offer waits for months.

options.text: "Exams are no excuse. Plenty of others manage both."
options.then: She goes quiet. "I'll think about it."

options.text: "Do it whenever you feel like it. No schedule needed."
options.then: She smiles. "Okay." You don't know when she'll come.

options.text: "Yes. We'll keep it small, and you can skip a week."
options.then: She grins. "Then I'm in."

steps.why: A small role that bends around exams keeps her involved.

scenarios.relearn: A small, specific ask makes it easy for someone to join with you.

scenarios.hook: A teammate's mistake has cost your campaign a deadline.
scenarios.setup: Later, Arman finds you alone, looking worried.

steps.prompt: Arman says: "I'm really sorry. I sent the form to the wrong office."

options.text: "You always mess things up."
options.then: He winces. "I thought you'd understand."

options.text: "It's fine. Forget it ever happened."
options.then: He nods but looks unsure. The wrong office still has the form.

options.text: "I'll tell the others it was your mistake."
options.then: He goes pale. "Please don't. I'll fix it."

options.text: "Thanks for owning it. Let's fix it together."
options.then: He exhales. "Okay. I'll call the right office today."

steps.why: Thanking him and fixing it together keeps trust and gets the work back on track.

steps.prompt: Arman asks: "The deadline is gone. Should I step down from this task?"

options.text: "Yes. Maybe someone else should handle it."
options.then: He swallows. "Okay. I understand."

options.text: "Only if it happens again. Then we'll reconsider."
options.then: He frowns. "So I'm on a final warning."

options.text: "Do whatever you think is right. I'll back you."
options.then: He looks lost. "I wish I knew what's right."

options.text: "No. Let's set a new date and add a check step."
options.then: He nods. "A checklist would help me."

steps.why: A new date and a check step fix the system, not just the person.

steps.prompt: Arman asks: "Should I tell the rest of the team what happened?"

options.text: "No. Let's keep it between us."
options.then: He hesitates. "People might notice and wonder."

options.text: "Yes, with a long apology so they forgive you."
options.then: He winces. "That sounds like a lot."

options.text: "Let them find out themselves."
options.then: He looks away. "That could look worse."

options.text: "Yes. A short, honest update on what happened and what's next."
options.then: He relaxes. "I'd rather they hear it from me."

steps.why: A brief, honest update keeps trust and shows how the team handles mistakes.

steps.prompt: Arman asks: "What do I do if I'm not sure about something next time?"

options.text: "Use your judgement. Don't ask unless you must."
options.then: He looks unsure. "What if I'm wrong again?"

options.text: "Check everything with me. I'll approve it all."
options.then: He frowns. "That will slow us both down."

options.text: "Just don't make mistakes again."
options.then: He swallows. "I'll try. But I might."

options.text: "Ask the team chat. Quick questions are welcome."
options.then: He nods. "Okay. I'll message the chat first."

steps.why: Welcoming quick questions in the open prevents repeat mistakes without a bottleneck.

scenarios.relearn: Owning mistakes together keeps the team; blame drives allies away.

scenarios.hook: You're asking a school club to co-host your safe-walking event.
scenarios.setup: You meet the club's captain, Kavya, after practice.

steps.prompt: Kavya says: "You want us to join your event? What's in it for us?"

options.text: "Can you just lend us your room and a few members?"
options.then: Kavya's smile fades. "Lend? For what, exactly?"

options.text: "It's for a very good cause. Surely you want to help us."
options.then: Kavya shrugs. "Lots of things are good causes."

options.text: "Honestly, we could do it alone. It would just be slower."
options.then: Kavya raises an eyebrow. "Then why ask?"

options.text: "Co-host with us. You get a platform and we get your reach."
options.then: Kavya smiles. "Now that's a fair deal. Tell me more."

steps.why: Offering something in return shows the partnership is mutual.

steps.prompt: Kavya says: "Our members are busy. What would you need from us?"

options.text: "As many members as you can spare for the whole day."
options.then: Kavya frowns. "That's not a plan."

options.text: "We'll tell you what to do when you get there on the day."
options.then: Kavya looks unimpressed. "I'd like to know beforehand."

options.text: "Whatever you decide is fine with us. Just let us know."
options.then: Kavya smiles politely. "Then I'm not sure what you want."

options.text: "Two members for a game stall, and your name on posters."
options.then: Kavya nods. "Two is doable. We can handle that."

steps.why: A specific, modest ask makes it easy for the club to say yes.

steps.prompt: Kavya says: "My coach wants to know who decides what on the day."

options.text: "We'll decide, since it's our event and our idea."
options.then: Kavya's face cools. "Then we're just helpers."

options.text: "You decide, since you have more experience than us."
options.then: Kavya looks surprised. "That's a lot to hand over."

options.text: "We'll decide it on the day, as things come up."
options.then: Kavya frowns. "My coach won't like that."

options.text: "We'll plan together, with one lead from each side."
options.then: Kavya nods. "I'll tell the coach. That sounds fair."

steps.why: Shared decisions with named leads give both sides a real stake.

scenarios.relearn: Offer partners mutual benefit, not a one-way favour, to win real buy-in.

scenarios.hook: A new volunteer has joined your team but looks unsure she belongs.
scenarios.setup: She hovers near the door at her first meeting.

steps.prompt: Sana says softly: "I'm not sure I fit in here."

options.text: "Just sit and watch quietly until you get the hang of it."
options.then: She sits at the back. By the end she hasn't said a word.

options.text: "Everyone feels like that at first. You'll be fine."
options.then: She smiles weakly. "Okay." She still has no task.

options.text: "We're short on people, so you'll do for the time being."
options.then: She looks down. "Oh." It doesn't feel like being wanted.

options.text: "You're in. Here's a real job that's yours, and I'll back you."
options.then: Her shoulders drop. "Really? Okay. What is it?"

steps.why: A real role and support say you belong, not just that you're welcome.

steps.prompt: Sana asks: "What do I do if I get something wrong?"

options.text: "Try not to. We can't afford mistakes."
options.then: She tenses. "Then maybe I shouldn't touch anything."

options.text: "Just fix it quietly and don't tell anybody."
options.then: She nods. Nobody learns from it, and it happens again.

options.text: "Don't worry. You won't get anything wrong."
options.then: She smiles. "Really? I'm not so sure."

options.text: "Ask me or anyone on the team. Mistakes are how we learn."
options.then: She breathes out. "Okay. I'll ask."

steps.why: Making mistakes safe to share helps a newcomer settle in.

steps.prompt: Sana says: "Some members know each other well. I feel like an outsider."

options.text: "They'll warm up to you soon. Just give it time."
options.then: She nods, unsure. Nobody has asked her anything yet.

options.text: "Just join their chat and you'll be one of us."
options.then: She says she'll try. She never sends a message.

options.text: "Maybe you'd fit better in another group."
options.then: Her smile fades. "Oh. Maybe."

options.text: "Let's pair you with Neha for a month. I'll check in."
options.then: Sana smiles. "I'd like that. Neha seems nice."

steps.why: A buddy and a check-in turn welcome into belonging.

scenarios.relearn: Real inclusion gives a newcomer a genuine role and support, not the sidelines.

scenarios.hook: After a rough week, a teammate says she wants to leave your campaign.
scenarios.setup: She finds you after school, holding her bag tightly.

steps.prompt: Priti says: "I think I should quit. It's been such a hard week."

options.text: "Fine, leave if you want to. We'll manage without you."
options.then: Her eyes fill. "I thought you'd understand."

options.text: "You can't quit now. We're almost at the big moment."
options.then: She flinches. "Almost? Nothing feels close to me."

options.text: "Everything's going brilliantly. This week was nothing."
options.then: She stares. "It didn't feel like nothing to me."

options.text: "This week was hard, but we moved real things. Rest up."
options.then: She exhales. "Rest. Yes, I think I need that."

steps.why: Honesty about the hard week, plus rest, keeps her without false hype.

steps.prompt: Priti says: "I just feel like my work doesn't matter."

options.text: "Of course it matters. Everyone's work matters here."
options.then: She nods. The doubt doesn't move.

options.text: "Then maybe change roles, if you're getting bored of it."
options.then: She frowns. "I'm not bored. I'm tired."

options.text: "Don't think like that. It isn't helping anybody."
options.then: She falls quiet and doesn't say what else she feels.

options.text: "Your list brought in new names this week. That's real."
options.then: She blinks. "I hadn't counted. That's more than I thought."

steps.why: Pointing to something specific she did shows real value better than praise in general.

steps.prompt: Priti asks: "If I take a week off, will there still be a place for me?"

options.text: "Probably, but things may well have moved on by then."
options.then: She nods slowly. "That doesn't sound like much of a place."

options.text: "Only if you tell the others you're coming back."
options.then: She tenses. "I can't promise that yet."

options.text: "We'll see, depending on how the week goes."
options.then: She looks unsure. "Okay. I guess I'll see."

options.text: "Yes. Take a week. I'll keep your spot and check in once."
options.then: She smiles. "Then I'll be back next Monday."

steps.why: A clearly held spot lets her rest without losing her place.

steps.prompt: A week later, Priti says: "I'm back. Can I start with something small?"

options.text: "Great. We missed you. Take everything you had before."
options.then: She looks nervous. "All of it at once?"

options.text: "Sure, but we've moved on without you."
options.then: She winces. "I see. Okay."

options.text: "We'll see how you do for a few days first."
options.then: Her smile fades. "Like a trial?"

options.text: "Welcome back. Take the sign-up list, and say if it's too much."
options.then: She smiles. "That's perfect."

steps.why: A small restart with an open door helps her come back without pressure.

scenarios.relearn: Honest encouragement and a held-open spot keep a wavering teammate.

scenarios.hook: A friend wants to help your campaign but says she isn't a leader.
scenarios.setup: She says it while packing up her bag after school.

steps.prompt: Rhea says: "I'd love to help, but I'm not the leader type."

options.text: "Everyone has to lead something, or it doesn't count."
options.then: Rhea groans. "Then it's definitely not for me."

options.text: "Then maybe you can just watch for now."
options.then: Rhea nods, a bit relieved. She isn't needed either.

options.text: "Leaders aren't born. You'll learn it quickly."
options.then: Rhea shakes her head. "I don't want to learn that."

options.text: "You don't need to lead. Own the design posts. That's key."
options.then: Rhea laughs. "Really? I can do posters."

steps.why: Naming a real role that isn't leading shows she can matter without leading.

steps.prompt: Rhea asks: "I'm good at drawing. Would a posters job be real work, or just something small?"

options.text: "It's small, but it's something."
options.then: Rhea shrugs. "Something small. Okay."

options.text: "If you want a bigger job, you can take the lead."
options.then: Rhea steps back. "No, no. That's not what I meant."

options.text: "Don't overthink it. Just start and see."
options.then: Rhea sighs. "I need to know it counts."

options.text: "Real work. Posters are how people hear about our events."
options.then: Rhea nods. "Okay. I see why it matters."

steps.why: Saying exactly why the role matters makes it feel real.

steps.prompt: Rhea says: "A few people want me to speak at the meeting too."

options.text: "Yes, say yes. Speaking will make you braver."
options.then: Rhea frowns. "I'd rather decide for myself."

options.text: "Say no. It's safer to stay in your own lane."
options.then: Rhea hesitates. "Is that all I'm good for?"

options.text: "I'll answer for you. You don't need to worry about it."
options.then: Rhea nods, relieved, then feels left out of her own choice.

options.text: "You choose. Just posters is fine, or add an update."
options.then: Rhea thinks. "Maybe just the update on posters."

steps.why: Letting her choose how far to stretch keeps the role hers.

scenarios.relearn: Movements need many non-leader roles; right-size the ask to the person.

scenarios.hook: A teacher is unsure about backing your student campaign for fairer canteen queues.
scenarios.setup: Ms. Fernandes meets you in the staffroom with her tea.

steps.prompt: Ms. Fernandes says: "Why should I back a student-run campaign?"

options.text: "We just want you to make it all happen for us."
options.then: She sets her tea down. "That's handing it over."

options.text: "Because the principal would probably like it."
options.then: She smiles. "Don't guess. What do you want?"

options.text: "Because it will fix everything in this school."
options.then: She raises an eyebrow. "That's a big claim for a canteen queue."

options.text: "Fair queues by term-end. We need your advice."
options.then: She nods. "A specific goal. Tell me about the plan."

steps.why: A specific goal and a small ask earn a teacher's backing.

steps.prompt: Ms. Fernandes asks: "Whatever the goal, how will you know it worked?"

options.text: "People will say they like it, and we'll see online."
options.then: She smiles. "Likes aren't results."

options.text: "We'll just feel it. It'll be obvious."
options.then: She tilts her head. "Obvious to whom?"

options.text: "We'll know when other teachers praise it."
options.then: She laughs. "Don't aim for praise. Aim for change."

options.text: "Queue complaints drop. We'll count them each week."
options.then: She nods. "Measurable. I like that."

steps.why: A clear, countable sign of progress shows you're serious about results.

steps.prompt: Ms. Fernandes says: "Okay. What exactly do you need from me?"

options.text: "Whatever time you can spare. We'll adjust."
options.then: She sighs. "I'll need a clearer ask than that."

options.text: "Please come to every meeting and run them."
options.then: She raises her hands. "I have classes to teach."

options.text: "Nothing right now. We'll tell you if there's a problem."
options.then: She looks doubtful. "Come to me before there's a problem."

options.text: "Twenty minutes of advice and your signature on the request."
options.then: She opens her diary. "Thursday, after lunch."

steps.why: A small, clear ask makes it easy for a busy teacher to say yes.

steps.prompt: Ms. Fernandes asks: "And what happens when your exams start?"

options.text: "We'll just keep doing it ourselves."
options.then: She raises an eyebrow. "Through exams?"

options.text: "It will sort itself out if it works."
options.then: She shakes her head. "Things rarely do."

options.text: "We'll ask you to run it when we can't."
options.then: She laughs. "I'm busy enough already."

options.text: "We'll train two juniors to take over the counting."
options.then: She smiles. "Good. Handing over is how things last."

steps.why: Training others to take over helps a change last beyond your own time.

scenarios.relearn: A specific goal plus a small, clear ask earns a teacher's backing.

scenarios.hook: Midway through a meeting, a teammate proposes a far better tactic than yours.
scenarios.setup: The room turns to see what you will say.

steps.prompt: Zayn says: "What if we hold a lunch-hour stall instead of a rally?"

options.text: "Let's stick with my plan. I thought of it first, remember."
options.then: Zayn shrugs. "Fine." The room feels flat.

options.text: "Interesting. Let's keep both ideas and decide later."
options.then: Zayn nods. "Okay." Weeks pass without a decision.

options.text: "A stall seems small. Are you sure it works?"
options.then: Zayn bristles. "I wouldn't suggest it otherwise."

options.text: "That's stronger than my plan. Let's go with yours."
options.then: Zayn blinks, then smiles. "Really? Okay. Let's plan it."

steps.why: Saying yes to the stronger plan out loud puts the goal ahead of who thought of it.

steps.prompt: Later, Zayn asks: "If the stall goes ahead, should I lead it, or should we do it together?"

options.text: "I'll lead it, since I know the school better."
options.then: Zayn's face falls. "Sure. Your call."

options.text: "We'll both lead it, and I'll make the final calls."
options.then: Zayn frowns. "So it's still your plan."

options.text: "You do it, but check everything with me first."
options.then: Zayn nods stiffly. "Everything?"

options.text: "You lead it. I'll back you with the sign-ups."
options.then: Zayn grins. "Deal. I'll send a plan tonight."

steps.why: Backing the person with the idea lets them lead while you support.

steps.prompt: A teammate whispers: "Zayn gets a lot of attention in this team. Doesn't that make you look weak?"

options.text: "Maybe. Next time I'll hold my ground more."
options.then: She nods. Zayn, listening, looks uneasy.

options.text: "Honestly, I'm just keeping the peace with him."
options.then: She smiles. Zayn overhears and goes quiet.

options.text: "I'm not weak. I just want to look generous."
options.then: She laughs. It sounds like a performance.

options.text: "No. Backing the best idea, whoever's idea it is, is how a team gets results."
options.then: She considers it. "I hadn't thought of it that way."

steps.why: Choosing the strongest plan is a strength, not a weakness.

scenarios.relearn: Saying yes to the best idea, not your own, strengthens the team.

scenarios.hook: In a group meeting, Dev keeps cutting off Meera, the only other girl present.
scenarios.setup: Meera has just started a point about the survey.

steps.prompt: Dev cuts in: "Yeah, yeah, we get it. Moving on to the budget."

options.text: "Let's move on. We're short on time and the budget matters."
options.then: Dev smiles. Meera's point is never heard.

options.text: "Dev, stop being so rude to everyone."
options.then: Dev bristles. "Everyone? I'm not rude."

options.text: "Meera, you could speak up more, you know."
options.then: Meera looks down. "I was speaking."

options.text: "Hold on. Meera was mid-point. Let's hear her out first."
options.then: Dev blinks. "Oh. Sorry. Go ahead, Meera."

steps.why: Naming the interruption and protecting her turn includes everyone.

steps.prompt: Meera says quietly: "He does this a lot, you know."

options.text: "Just ignore him. He doesn't mean anything by it."
options.then: Meera frowns. "It feels like he does."

options.text: "Let's go to the teacher about Dev right now."
options.then: Meera hesitates. "I'd rather try the team first."

options.text: "You should tell him yourself, then."
options.then: Meera shifts. "That's hard to do alone."

options.text: "I'll suggest a turn-taking rule at the next meeting."
options.then: Meera nods. "That would help. Thank you."

steps.why: A shared rule fixes the pattern without making it Meera's job alone.

steps.prompt: Later, Dev says: "I didn't realise I was doing it. Was I that bad?"

options.text: "Yes, you were awful and everybody noticed."
options.then: Dev goes red. "Wow. Okay."

options.text: "It's fine. Forget it. Let's get back to the agenda now."
options.then: Dev shrugs. It happens again at the next meeting.

options.text: "Ask Meera. It was her turn you took."
options.then: Dev looks uncomfortable. "I'd rather hear it from you."

options.text: "You cut in a few times. Let's agree on turns for everyone."
options.then: Dev nods. "Fair. I'll try. Keep me honest."

steps.why: Honest, specific feedback with a shared rule helps him change.

scenarios.relearn: Naming an interruption and protecting the turn keeps a team inclusive.

scenarios.hook: A volunteer tells you she can't make Saturday's clean-up.
scenarios.setup: You meet her in the corridor on Thursday.

steps.prompt: Alisha says: "I'm really sorry. I can't make it on Saturday."

options.text: "If you skip Saturday, don't bother coming back at all."
options.then: Her face drops. "That's harsh. I said sorry."

options.text: "Okay, but you owe us two Saturdays now."
options.then: She winces. "That's not really fair."

options.text: "It's fine. Do whatever you want."
options.then: She shrugs. "Okay." She isn't sure she's still on the team.

options.text: "No worries. Want to take the online sign-ups instead?"
options.then: She relaxes. "Yes. I can do that from home."

steps.why: A flexible alternative keeps her involved and shows her time is valued.

steps.prompt: Alisha asks: "Could we do the clean-up on another day instead?"

options.text: "It has to be Saturday. There can't be any exceptions."
options.then: She sighs. "Okay. Then I really can't."

options.text: "We'll move it just for you."
options.then: She hesitates. "I don't want to change it for everyone."

options.text: "Don't make this about you."
options.then: She stiffens. "I'm only asking a question."

options.text: "The hall is booked then, but we could add a second one."
options.then: She brightens. "That would help me. Let me check a date."

steps.why: Explaining the limits and offering a second option keeps things fair and flexible.

steps.prompt: Alisha asks: "Can I help in some other way this weekend?"

options.text: "No, we've got it. Just come next time."
options.then: She nods, feeling unneeded.

options.text: "Only if you make up all the hours you owe."
options.then: She groans. "I don't owe hours. I volunteered."

options.text: "If you really care, you'll find a way to come."
options.then: She goes quiet. "I do care. Not everything is up to me."

options.text: "Yes. Write the thank-you notes for the helpers."
options.then: She smiles. "Easy. I'll bring them Monday."

steps.why: Offering a task that fits her situation keeps a willing volunteer.

steps.prompt: On Monday, Alisha asks: "How did Saturday go?"

options.text: "Fine. We managed without you."
options.then: She nods, the words stinging a little.

options.text: "Rough. We could have used you."
options.then: She winces. "I wish I'd been there."

options.text: "Not great. Next time please don't miss it."
options.then: She frowns. "I said it was important."

options.text: "Well. Thanks for telling us early. It helped us plan."
options.then: She smiles. "I'm glad. I'll make the next one."

steps.why: Thanking her for the early notice keeps a willing volunteer.

scenarios.relearn: Offering a flexible alternative keeps allies; ultimatums drive them off.

scenarios.hook: You're closing a meeting where progress was slow but real.
scenarios.setup: People are packing up, looking tired.

steps.prompt: Farhan says: "That took forever. Did we even get anywhere today?"

options.text: "Honestly, this is hopeless. We're getting nowhere."
options.then: Farhan's face falls. "Then why do we bother?"

options.text: "We got loads done today! We're nearly there."
options.then: Farhan snorts. "Nearly? Come on."

options.text: "Don't ask me. I'm tired too."
options.then: Farhan nods slowly. "Everyone's tired. I just wonder about next week."

options.text: "We took two real steps today. Same time next week?"
options.then: Farhan nods. "Two steps. Okay. I'll be here."

steps.why: Naming real, modest progress keeps people coming back.

steps.prompt: Farhan asks: "What if next week is the same?"

options.text: "It won't be. I promise we'll do much better."
options.then: Farhan raises an eyebrow. "Promise? Okay."

options.text: "Then maybe we should stop meeting."
options.then: Farhan looks shocked. "That was quick."

options.text: "Then we'll just have to work harder."
options.then: Farhan sighs. "We're already tired."

options.text: "Then we look at what slowed us and fix one thing."
options.then: Farhan nods. "One thing. I can handle that."

steps.why: Looking at what slowed the team turns slow weeks into learning.

steps.prompt: A teammate at the door says: "People are talking about quitting. Should we call it off?"

options.text: "No one's quitting. Don't spread that around."
options.then: She goes quiet. The worry doesn't go away.

options.text: "Maybe we should pause for a month."
options.then: She frowns. "A month with no plan for coming back? People may drift."

options.text: "Let them go. We'll find new people."
options.then: She looks troubled. "They're our friends."

options.text: "Let's share what we did and ask what's draining people."
options.then: She nods. "Okay. Let's put it on the agenda."

steps.why: Sharing real progress and asking what drains people addresses the worry honestly.

scenarios.relearn: Naming real, modest progress keeps a volunteer team coming back.

scenarios.hook: A senior offers help with your campaign, then starts giving your team orders.
scenarios.setup: At the end of the meeting, he turns to you.

steps.prompt: Rahul bhaiya says: "Your plan is messy. Do it my way and it'll work."

options.text: "Sure, you take over. You clearly know better than us."
options.then: He grins. "Great." By next week, your team's ideas are gone.

options.text: "Our plan is fine. We don't need your advice."
options.then: His smile tightens. "Okay. Good luck."

options.text: "We'll try your way for a week, then see."
options.then: He smiles. "Sure." The team grumbles about it later.

options.text: "Thanks, your advice is gold. The team decides direction."
options.then: He pauses, then laughs. "Fair. Tell me which parts help."

steps.why: Thanking him while keeping decisions with the team uses his advice without losing the cause.

steps.prompt: Rahul bhaiya says: "I told the principal your plan. You're welcome."

options.text: "Great, that saves us a lot of time. Thanks so much."
options.then: He smiles. Next time he speaks for you again.

options.text: "You had no right to do that, and you know it."
options.then: He bristles. "I was only helping."

options.text: "Thanks. Please ask us before speaking for the team."
options.then: He nods, a bit surprised. "Fair. I'll ask first."

options.text: "Fine. Just don't do it again, okay?"
options.then: He shrugs. "Okay." The tension sits between you.

steps.why: A grateful, clear boundary keeps help useful and the team in charge.

steps.prompt: Rahul bhaiya says: "The team should vote on my idea for the next event."

options.text: "No. Only our own ideas get a vote."
options.then: He folds his arms. "Then why did I offer to help?"

options.text: "Fine. Whatever you suggest, we do it."
options.then: He nods happily. The team looks at you in surprise.

options.text: "Let me ask them privately and tell you what they say."
options.then: He frowns. "Why not ask them with me there?"

options.text: "Sure. We'll put it to the team with the others."
options.then: The team votes. His idea gets a fair hearing.

steps.why: A fair hearing alongside other ideas keeps decisions with the team.

scenarios.relearn: Welcome a mentor's advice while keeping decisions with your team.

scenarios.hook: A teammate is anxious that your cause is too big to matter.
scenarios.setup: She says it quietly, after everyone else has left.

steps.prompt: Divya says: "I think this is too big for us. What's the point?"

options.text: "Yeah, it probably is too big for us."
options.then: Divya looks stricken. "I hoped you'd say something else."

options.text: "Don't think like that. Just be positive about it, please."
options.then: Divya nods. She doesn't feel any lighter.

options.text: "Maybe you should take a break from the team."
options.then: Divya blinks. "Is that what you want? I'd rather stay and see."

options.text: "We're not doing it alone. A small team, one goal, one step."
options.then: Divya breathes out. "One step. I can keep that in my head."

steps.why: Reminding her the team is a group with one small goal steadies the worry.

steps.prompt: Divya asks: "What if we try and nothing changes?"

options.text: "It will definitely change. Trust me."
options.then: Divya frowns. "You can't promise that."

options.text: "Then at least we tried, and that's enough."
options.then: Divya nods slowly. "Enough for who?"

options.text: "If nothing changes, we'll stop and find another cause."
options.then: Divya looks uneasy. "That's what I'm scared of."

options.text: "Then we learn what to try next. Small change counts."
options.then: Divya half-smiles. "Learning counts. Okay."

steps.why: Small, real progress and learning count even when change is slow.

steps.prompt: Divya says: "I don't even know which part is mine."

options.text: "Whatever you feel like doing is fine."
options.then: Divya sighs. "That's the problem. I don't know."

options.text: "Take the biggest task. You'll feel useful."
options.then: Divya's eyes widen. "The biggest? Now I'm more scared."

options.text: "Wait until you feel ready to choose."
options.then: Divya looks down. "I might never feel ready."

options.text: "Let's pick one small task for you this week."
options.then: Divya relaxes. "The notice board. I can do that."

steps.why: One small, chosen task makes a big cause feel doable.

scenarios.relearn: Reminding the team it's collective and small-stepped steadies anxiety.
