scenarios.hook: "A real movement has one strong leader at the top."

myth.un: A real movement has one strong leader at the top.
myth.re: Lasting movements share roles and credit; many people own pieces, not one person at the top.
myth.why: Shared ownership keeps a movement going when any one person steps back.

scenarios.relearn: Movements last on shared roles and credit, not a single leader at the top.

scenarios.hook: "To grow fast, pressure your friends until they join."

myth.un: To grow fast, pressure your friends until they join.
myth.re: Warm, specific, no-pressure invites recruit allies who actually stay; pressure makes people resent it.
myth.why: People who are invited, not pushed, stay committed far longer.

scenarios.relearn: Recruit with warm, specific invites; pressure wins bodies, not committed allies.

scenarios.hook: "Asking for help means you're a weak leader."

myth.un: Asking for help means you're a weak leader.
myth.re: Delegating and asking for help is a strength; it shares the load and keeps the team from burning out.
myth.why: No one sustains a movement alone. Sharing the load is what makes it last.

scenarios.relearn: Asking for help and delegating is leadership strength, not weakness.

scenarios.hook: "If you partner up, you'll lose all the credit."

myth.un: If you partner up, you'll lose all the credit.
myth.re: Partnering with known clubs and NGOs multiplies your reach; shared credit grows a cause, it doesn't shrink it.
myth.why: A bigger, shared win helps far more people than a small solo one.

scenarios.relearn: Partnering multiplies impact; sharing credit grows a cause, not shrinks it.

scenarios.hook: "Everyone on the team has to agree on everything."

myth.un: Everyone on the team has to agree on everything.
myth.re: You only need a shared goal; people can differ on tactics and still build together, no purity tests.
myth.why: Coalitions hold on common ground, not on total agreement.

scenarios.relearn: A shared goal, not full agreement, is what holds a team together.

scenarios.hook: "One bad week means the movement has failed."

myth.un: One bad week means the movement has failed.
myth.re: A setback is iteration. You learn, adjust and keep going; a single dip is feedback, not a verdict.
myth.why: Every lasting effort has rough weeks; adjusting is how it survives them.

scenarios.relearn: A bad week is feedback to adjust to, not proof the movement failed.

scenarios.hook: "The founder's idea should always win."

myth.un: The founder's idea should always win.
myth.re: The best idea should win, whoever it comes from; backing a teammate's stronger idea makes the team trust you.
myth.why: Teams commit to leaders who serve the goal over their own ego.

scenarios.relearn: Back the strongest idea, not the founder's; that earns a team's trust.

scenarios.hook: "A famous online stranger is the best partner you can get."

myth.un: A famous online stranger is the best partner you can get.
myth.re: Known, local, verifiable partners, like teachers, clubs, or registered NGOs, are safest and add real weight; fame-promisers are risky.
myth.why: A partner you can verify protects your team and your cause.

scenarios.relearn: Trust known, local, verifiable partners; fame-promising strangers are risky.

scenarios.hook: "My cause has to be brand-new. Someone's surely done it already."

myth.un: If others already work on it, there's no room for me.
myth.re: Joining or building on existing work is real changemaking; you add reach, not a copy.
myth.why: Movements grow by more hands, not by everyone starting from zero.

scenarios.relearn: Joining existing work on a cause is changemaking too. You add reach.

scenarios.hook: "A cause only counts if it's about something dramatic."

myth.un: Everyday problems are too small to be a real cause.
myth.re: An everyday problem you can name and reach, like a dark lane or unequal chores, is a strong cause.
myth.why: Concrete, close-to-home causes are the ones you can actually move.

scenarios.relearn: Everyday, close-to-home problems make strong, actionable causes.

scenarios.hook: "I should wait until I'm sure it's the 'right' cause."

myth.un: You must find the one perfect cause before you start.
myth.re: Start with one you genuinely care about now; clarity comes from doing, not waiting.
myth.why: You learn what fits by acting, not by deliberating forever.

scenarios.relearn: Start with a cause you care about now; clarity grows by doing.

scenarios.hook: "If I pick a cause, I'm stuck with it for life."

myth.un: Choosing a cause is a permanent, all-or-nothing commitment.
myth.re: Picking one now just gives you a place to start; you can refocus as you learn.
myth.why: A first cause is a starting point, not a life sentence.

scenarios.relearn: Picking one cause now is a starting point, not a forever vow.

scenarios.hook: "My cause isn't 'serious' enough next to GBV or poverty."

myth.un: Only the biggest issues are worth caring about.
myth.re: A cause you genuinely care about is worth starting; ranking causes just stalls you.
myth.why: Real energy comes from what actually pulls at you.

scenarios.relearn: A cause you care about is valid; don't rank yourself out of starting.

scenarios.hook: "To act on gender-based violence I'd have to confront people directly."

myth.un: Acting on GBV means personally taking on the people doing harm.
myth.re: A safe angle, like awareness or sharing helplines, with adult backing is real, effective action.
myth.why: Safe, backed angles help people without putting you at risk.

scenarios.relearn: On GBV, a safe awareness angle with adult backing is real action.

scenarios.hook: "A cause needs a huge audience or it doesn't matter."

myth.un: If only a few people are affected, the cause isn't worth it.
myth.re: Helping even a few people locally is real change and a solid place to begin.
myth.why: Durable change starts small and specific, not big and broad.

scenarios.relearn: Helping even a few people locally is real change worth starting.

scenarios.hook: "I need an official title before my cause is legitimate."

myth.un: You need a position or permission to make your cause count.
myth.re: You can start a cause you care about without a title; ordinary people drive change.
myth.why: Change comes from willing people, not from being in charge.

scenarios.relearn: You don't need a title or permission to start a cause you care about.

scenarios.hook: "Caring loudly online is the same as having a cause."

myth.un: Posting about an issue means I've taken up the cause.
myth.re: A cause becomes real when you name a concrete, local thing to act on.
myth.why: Substance (a specific, doable aim) is what moves things, not noise.

scenarios.relearn: A cause gets real when you name a concrete, local thing to act on.

scenarios.hook: "If the cause isn't fixed soon, I clearly chose wrong."

myth.un: A cause that takes a long time was the wrong one to pick.
myth.re: Real change is often slow; a slow cause isn't a failed choice, just a steady one.
myth.why: Steadiness, not speed, is what gets a cause there.

scenarios.relearn: A slow cause isn't a wrong choice; steady change takes time.

scenarios.hook: "My cause has to fix the root cause or it's pointless."

myth.un: If I can't reach the deep root, there's no point acting.
myth.re: Aim at the root where you can, but real partial progress on a symptom still counts and builds.
myth.why: You don't need to finish it alone; partial progress compounds.

scenarios.relearn: Aim at the root, but partial progress still counts and builds.

scenarios.hook: "A real changemaker just knows their cause instantly."

myth.un: You should already feel certain about your one cause.
myth.re: It's normal to care about several things; you sharpen one by acting, not by certainty.
myth.why: Clarity is built through doing, not waited for.

scenarios.relearn: It's normal to be unsure; you sharpen one cause by acting on it.

scenarios.hook: "Picking a local cause means I've given up on the big issue."

myth.un: Going local is settling for less than the real problem.
myth.re: A concrete local version of a big issue is how you actually move the big issue.
myth.why: Big causes are reached through small, local, doable steps.

scenarios.relearn: A local version of a big issue is how you start moving it.

scenarios.hook: "I can't pick a cause until I've researched every single one."

myth.un: You must study all possible causes before choosing.
myth.re: Notice what genuinely bothers you near you, and start there; that's enough to begin.
myth.why: What pulls at you locally is a solid, honest starting point.

scenarios.relearn: Notice what bothers you nearby and start there. That's enough.

scenarios.hook: "If a cause makes my family uncomfortable, I should pick a 'safer' topic."

myth.un: Drop any cause your family finds awkward.
myth.re: Choose a cause you care about and frame it respectfully; you can bring people along.
myth.why: Shared goals and respect win more support than avoiding the topic.

scenarios.relearn: Pick the cause you care about; frame it respectfully to bring people along.

options.then: She waits for more. It's still a feeling, not a plan.

options.text: Equal turns on the science-lab roster
options.then: "Oh, I can picture that," she says. "I'll help count turns."

options.text: Whatever the college can do for us
options.then: She shrugs. Nobody can tell what success would look like.

steps.why: A named, concrete change is one people can see and help with.

steps.prompt: A classmate says what you are taking on will not change anything. How do you answer?

options.text: Agree and switch to a bigger issue
options.then: The new issue is too large to touch. You lose your footing.

options.text: Say it's part of something bigger and widen your aim
options.then: The aim blurs. You're back to making everything fair.

options.text: Ask her to choose a better cause for you
options.then: She picks something she likes. It isn't yours.

options.text: Say a small fix is where it starts, and you can count it
options.then: She thinks. "Fine. If it works, others will ask for more."

steps.why: A small, measurable fix is real progress and can grow.

scenarios.debrief: The narrowed version is the part you can actually move.
scenarios.relearn: Narrow a broad cause to one concrete, local version.

scenarios.hook: You want to act on the harassment girls face on the walk to campus.

steps.prompt: Friends are angry and want to act. What is your first move?

options.text: Photograph the men and post them online
options.then: The post spreads. Threats appear in the comments, and some turn on you.

options.text: Plan an awareness drive with a teacher backing
options.then: A teacher agrees to meet you. Your friends feel relieved to have a plan.

options.text: Walk the girls to campus yourselves every day
options.then: A few girls feel safer. It's tiring, and it changes nothing for the others.

options.text: Tell the girls to avoid that route
options.then: Some stop going that way. The street stays exactly the same.

steps.why: A safe, lawful angle with adult backing works without putting anyone at risk.

steps.prompt: A week later, a teacher who has heard about it offers to help with an awareness drive. She asks what it will say. What do you tell her?

options.text: We'll warn people about specific men
options.then: She frowns. Naming people could put you and others at risk.

options.text: A powerful speech about how bad it is
options.then: She says it will move people, but asks what they should do afterwards.

options.text: What to do and where to get help
options.then: She smiles and offers to check the helpline details with you.

options.text: We'll decide closer to the day
options.then: She says you need something to show the school first.

steps.why: Accurate information and a next step let people act, not just nod.

steps.prompt: A girl in your group quietly says she was followed yesterday. What do you do?

options.text: Add her story to the drive's poster so people see
options.then: She sees it and is upset. She hadn't agreed to this.

options.text: Promise to keep it just between the two of you
options.then: She feels heard, but she is still carrying it alone.

options.text: Believe her and find a trusted adult together
options.then: She breathes out. "Okay. Could we go to the counsellor together?"

options.text: Go and look for the person who followed her
options.then: You get nowhere, and you could have put yourself at risk.

steps.why: Believe her, stay with her and bring in a trusted adult. It is never her fault.

steps.prompt: More volunteers join, and some want to chase the men down. What do you say?

options.text: Let them go ahead if they're careful about it
options.then: They try it. Someone gets threatened, and the drive is blamed.

options.text: Say what they do outside the group is up to them
options.then: They shrug. The group's name is still on whatever they do.

options.text: Tell them the drive is only about posters
options.then: They feel shut out. Two leave.

options.text: Keep it lawful and give them another job
options.then: One takes the helpline handouts. He's good at it.

steps.why: A group stays safe when it stays lawful, with a role for everyone.

scenarios.debrief: Harassment is never the victim's fault. Choose a safe, lawful angle with adult backing.
scenarios.relearn: For harassment, choose a safe, adult-backed angle, not shaming.

scenarios.hook: A classmate says your cause won't change anything anyway.

steps.prompt: He says it again in front of the class. What do you do?

options.text: Drop the cause so you don't look foolish
options.then: He looks satisfied. The idea starts slipping away, though a friend notices you went quiet.

options.text: Challenge him to prove it will work
options.then: He smirks. "Prove it won't." The class watches.

options.text: Say you're starting a small version anyway
options.then: He rolls his eyes. Two others look curious.

options.text: Keep going, but tell nobody
options.then: Nobody teases you. Nobody can join you either.

steps.why: You don't need everyone to believe in your cause before you start.

steps.prompt: Later, a friend privately asks if you are still doing anything about your cause. What do you show her?

options.text: A big plan with a name, a logo and a launch event
options.then: She likes the logo. She asks what happens on Monday.

options.text: A promise that things will change by next term
options.then: She raises an eyebrow. It sounds like a lot to promise.

options.text: Nothing yet. You'll wait until more people believe in it
options.then: She nods. Nothing is there to join yet, so you quickly put up a small notice.

options.text: One thing you can do this week, like a short notice
options.then: She nods. "I can help put it up." It's already real.

steps.why: A small thing you can do this week gives others something to join.

steps.prompt: Soon after, you put one small thing out, like a notice, and it gets a lukewarm response. What do you do?

options.text: Take it as proof the classmate was right
options.then: You stop for a few weeks. A friend nudges you to restart, and you do, smaller.

options.text: Notice what happened, change one thing, try again
options.then: You move the notice to the canteen. More people stop to read it.

options.text: Run a much bigger version to prove him wrong
options.then: It takes a lot of effort. The extra size doesn't fix the problem.

options.text: Wait for a better time before trying again
options.then: The better time does not come. A friend's nudge finally gets you going again.

steps.why: A weak first try is something to learn from, not a verdict.

steps.prompt: A month on, the same classmate asks if he can help with your cause. What do you do?

options.text: Say you told him so, and mean it
options.then: He winces. The offer to help disappears.

options.text: Say no, because he doubted you at first
options.then: He leaves. You lose a willing pair of hands.

options.text: Hand over the project to him
options.then: He's keen, but it isn't his plan.

options.text: Welcome him and give him a small job
options.then: He takes the posters. "Okay. I was wrong," he says.

steps.why: Bring doubters along with respect. Shared goals matter more than past doubts.

scenarios.debrief: You don't need everyone to rate your cause before you begin.
scenarios.relearn: Start a cause you care about with or without others' belief.

scenarios.hook: A national issue pulls at you, but you're one student with a phone.

steps.prompt: You want to do something about it this month. What do you do?

options.text: Announce a nationwide campaign online today
options.then: A few likes come in. You have no idea what to do next.

options.text: Share news posts about it every single day
options.then: You feel busy. Nobody around you has changed anything.

options.text: Wait until you have more followers
options.then: The number barely moves. Nothing starts.

options.text: Pick a local slice, like your block or campus
options.then: You think of the lanes near home. You know who lives there and what happens.

steps.why: A big issue becomes workable when you take the slice you can reach.

steps.prompt: A week later, you sit down to settle where you will actually act. Where do you aim?

options.text: A city-wide scheme you've only ever read about
options.then: It sounds important. You can't see where to start.

options.text: Whatever the news is covering this particular week
options.then: The topic changes in a few days, and so does your plan.

options.text: Something you can reach on foot, like your campus
options.then: You can see it, ask about it and check back next week.

options.text: Whatever friends say will get attention
options.then: It gets attention. It isn't what you care about.

steps.why: Something you can see and reach lets you follow through.

steps.prompt: You need people to help. Who do you ask first?

options.text: Everyone in your contacts at once
options.then: Replies trickle in. Few people know what you're asking.

options.text: A well-known person who might share it
options.then: No reply. You didn't have a clear ask for them anyway.

options.text: A teacher or club lead who knows the area
options.then: She says yes and suggests two classmates who care about it.

options.text: Strangers online who offer to help
options.then: One offers to take over. You don't know who they are.

steps.why: People who know you and the place are the safest, steadiest allies.

steps.prompt: A friend says a local win is too small for such a big issue. What do you say?

options.text: Maybe you're right. You'll go national later
options.then: You drift. Months pass without a local result.

options.text: Small wins add up, and others can copy them
options.then: He thinks about it. "Our hostel could try that too."

options.text: It isn't about the size. It's about being seen
options.then: He nods. You've started chasing attention.

options.text: Stop talking about it until it's big
options.then: He moves on. Nothing about your cause is visible.

steps.why: A real local win gives a big issue a foothold others can copy.

scenarios.debrief: The local slice of a big issue is the realistic place to start.
scenarios.relearn: Reach a big issue through the local slice you can act on.

scenarios.hook: Your cause idea is that people are rude, and you can't see a first step.

steps.prompt: You want to get started this week. What do you do?

options.text: Put up posters saying "be kinder"
options.then: The posters go up. People smile, and nothing changes.

options.text: Find the one place where rudeness shows up most
options.then: The canteen queue is where it hurts every day. You can see it.

options.text: Message everyone to ask them to be kinder
options.then: A few thumbs up appear. Nothing about how people behave changes.

options.text: Wait until it feels worse
options.then: Nothing happens, and nothing starts.

steps.why: A specific place gives a feeling something you can act on.

steps.prompt: A friend says the canteen queue is where it's worst. What aim do you write?

options.text: End rudeness everywhere in the whole college
options.then: It's a fine hope. You don't know what to do on Monday.

options.text: More kindness, in every corner of campus
options.then: She asks how you'd know it worked. You can't say.

options.text: Fix the queue problem once and for all
options.then: Forever is hard to plan around, or to measure.

options.text: A kinder canteen queue this term
options.then: She nods. "I can count the pushing at lunch. Let's track it."

steps.why: A clear, time-bound aim shows you what a first step should be.

steps.prompt: Your aim is set. What is the first thing you do?

options.text: Plan a big kindness drive for every hostel
options.then: The plan grows. It no longer fits a term.

options.text: Name the pushers on the notice board
options.then: People get angry. The queue gets worse.

options.text: Ask canteen staff what would help
options.then: The staff suggest a second counter at peak time. It's a real idea.

options.text: Wait for people to change on their own time
options.then: The pushing continues, and you've got nothing to show.

steps.why: Asking the people who see the problem daily gives you a real first step.

scenarios.debrief: A concrete, time-bound frame turns a feeling into a doable cause.
scenarios.relearn: Reframe a vague feeling into a concrete, time-bound cause.

scenarios.hook: Two causes tug at you: a cleaner campus and safer late-bus rides for girls.

steps.prompt: You can only start one this term. What guides your choice?

options.text: Whichever looks more impressive to others
options.then: You picture the applause. A week later, you're already bored of the idea.

options.text: Which one genuinely pulls at me most
options.then: You keep thinking about the late-bus rides. That tells you something.

options.text: Whichever already has more supporters
options.then: The cleaner campus has more fans. You doubt you'd stay with it when it gets dull.

options.text: Toss a coin and don't think about it
options.then: The coin says cleaner campus, and you feel a small pang.

steps.why: Real care gives you the fuel to keep going when it gets hard.

steps.prompt: A friend says a different cause would get far more help than yours. What do you say?

options.text: Switch, since popular causes get more help
options.then: You switch. Within weeks, you're going through the motions.

options.text: Do both so nobody is let down
options.then: Your time splits in two, and both go slowly.

options.text: Stay with yours, and cheer on the other cause
options.then: She grins. "Okay, I'll help with yours on Saturday."

options.text: Ask her to decide for you
options.then: She picks the popular one. It isn't what you care about.

steps.why: Starting from care lets you stay with it, and others can pick up the rest.

steps.prompt: A few weeks in, the work feels routine. What keeps you going?

options.text: Look for a more exciting cause
options.then: The new idea is fun for a week. Then it feels routine too.

options.text: Push through alone and say nothing
options.then: You keep going, but you're tired and quiet about it.

options.text: Stop until you feel inspired again
options.then: The break stretches. Inspiration doesn't arrive.

options.text: Set a small milestone and share it with a friend
options.then: You both tick it off. The dull stretch feels shorter.

steps.why: Small milestones and shared effort keep you steady.

scenarios.debrief: The cause that genuinely pulls at you is the one to begin with.
scenarios.relearn: Start from the cause that pulls at you, not the impressive one.

scenarios.hook: A friend wants to co-own a cause with you, but cares about a different angle.

steps.prompt: You each describe your angle. What do you do?

options.text: Ask them to adopt your angle first
options.then: They hesitate. "So it's your project, then?"

options.text: Say you'll each do your own thing
options.then: You each start. Soon you're asking the same teacher for the same hall, and have to sort it out.

options.text: Look for the goal you both want
options.then: Underneath, you want the same outcome. Only the route differs.

options.text: Drop both angles to keep it simple
options.then: What's left is something neither of you cares about.

steps.why: A shared goal is enough to start, even with different angles.

steps.prompt: Soon after, the two of you need to settle how to share the work. How do you set it up?

options.text: Give them small jobs and keep the decisions
options.then: They go along for now. They start to feel like helpers, not partners.

options.text: Decide everything together, every time
options.then: You agree on a lot, and spend hours agreeing.

options.text: Split roles by strength and agree one aim
options.then: They take the posters and you take the teachers. Both of you know the aim.

options.text: Write rules everyone must follow word for word
options.then: The rules are neat. The enthusiasm drops.

steps.why: Roles that fit each person's strengths keep a team moving together.

steps.prompt: They suggest a method you wouldn't have picked. What do you do?

options.text: Insist on your own method
options.then: They go quiet. The next idea comes less easily.

options.text: Agree to keep the peace, even though you doubt it
options.then: You do it their way and grumble in your head.

options.text: Check it against the shared goal and try it if it fits
options.then: It fits. The results are better than you expected.

options.text: Try both methods at once
options.then: You're both stretched thin. Neither method gets a fair try.

steps.why: The best idea for the shared goal wins, whoever it came from.

steps.prompt: A classmate wants to join but disagrees with you on some points. What do you do?

options.text: Ask them to agree with everything first
options.then: They leave. You've lost a helper over details.

options.text: Say the group is full
options.then: They shrug. You've closed a door for no reason.

options.text: Let them in, but with no say in decisions
options.then: They join and stay quiet. Their ideas never reach the table.

options.text: Welcome them if they share the goal
options.then: They bring a friend and a new idea to the next meeting.

steps.why: Shared goals beat total agreement, so you don't need purity tests.

scenarios.debrief: Shared goals, not identical views, are enough to start together.
scenarios.relearn: Start from a shared goal; you don't need total agreement.

scenarios.hook: You notice dowry being treated as normal in conversations around you.

steps.prompt: At a family function, a relative jokes about a going rate for grooms. What do you do?

options.text: Call him out loudly in front of everyone
options.then: He's embarrassed and angry. The room goes tense and nobody listens.

options.text: Laugh along so the moment passes
options.then: The joke moves on. You feel uneasy for the rest of the evening.

options.text: Post about the family online that night
options.then: Relatives find out. Trust takes a hit, and the post draws angry replies.

options.text: Stay calm now, and plan a safe awareness angle
options.then: You decide to talk to a trusted adult about what an awareness cause could look like.

steps.why: You can care about it without a public fight. A safe angle comes first.

steps.prompt: A school counsellor asks what you have in mind. What do you say?

options.text: Posters naming the local families who took dowry
options.then: She frowns. Naming families isn't safe or lawful.

options.text: A skit mocking local families and their customs
options.then: She says it would hurt people you want to bring along.

options.text: An adult-checked awareness session
options.then: She nods. "Let's check the facts together."

options.text: Collect stories from girls about their own families
options.then: She stops you. Private stories aren't campaign material.

steps.why: A checked, adult-backed awareness session informs people without exposing anyone.

steps.prompt: A classmate asks whether dowry is even allowed, since her family follows tradition. What do you say?

options.text: Tell her exactly what she and her family should do about it
options.then: She looks worried. That isn't your call to make.

options.text: Say tradition is tradition and leave it
options.then: She nods quietly. She still has her question.

options.text: Share what you read online, without checking if it's right
options.then: She repeats it, and a friend says it's wrong.

options.text: Say dowry is against the law, then ask an adult together
options.then: She relaxes. "I didn't know that. I'd like to ask someone with you."

steps.why: Dowry is against the law. A trusted adult can answer the legal details.

scenarios.debrief: Sensitive causes start with a safe, adult-backed awareness angle.
scenarios.relearn: On dowry, pick a safe awareness angle checked with a trusted adult.

scenarios.hook: You feel you must solve school dropout entirely, or not bother at all.

steps.prompt: A friend asks what you'll do about it. What do you say?

options.text: Nothing at all, if I can't end dropout
options.then: She says that sounds heavy. You close the notebook.

options.text: Plan a state-wide scheme for every school
options.then: It looks impressive on paper. You have no idea who'd run it.

options.text: Aim at one slice: five girls enrolled
options.then: She nods. "Five girls I could actually name. Okay."

options.text: Wait for the government to fix all of it
options.then: The months pass. You're no closer to anything.

steps.why: A reachable slice makes real progress possible.

steps.prompt: A week later, you settle on one slice: keeping five girls in school. A friend says that is nothing next to the whole problem. What do you say?

options.text: Admit it's too small to really matter
options.then: You nod and drop the big talk, but you keep tracking five girls on the quiet.

options.text: Switch to aiming for the whole district
options.then: The goal gets bigger. You still don't know where to begin, so you keep tracking five girls.

options.text: Say five girls in school is real change
options.then: He pauses. "Yeah. If it's your own class, that's real."

options.text: Say you'll feel bad about everyone you will miss
options.then: He sighs. The guilt makes starting harder.

steps.why: Real progress for a few people counts, and it can grow.

steps.prompt: Months on, two of the five girls have stayed enrolled, not all five. What do you do?

options.text: Feel you've failed and stop for good
options.then: You've done something real. You no longer count it.

options.text: Post that you reached five, to look successful
options.then: A friend asks who they are. You don't have names.

options.text: Hold off until you can reach all five girls
options.then: The two get no support while you wait.

options.text: Count the two and learn what helped
options.then: You note what helped them. It will help the next three.

steps.why: Honest progress, even if partial, builds into more.

scenarios.debrief: A reachable slice is real progress; you don't have to solve it all.
scenarios.relearn: Aim at a reachable slice; partial progress counts and builds.

scenarios.hook: Your cause matters to you, but no friend seems interested yet.

steps.prompt: You've shared the idea with three friends and nobody replies. What do you do?

options.text: Wait until a crowd joins before starting
options.then: A month passes with no crowd. You decide to try a tiny piece anyway.

options.text: Keep messaging them until someone agrees
options.then: One says okay, mostly to stop the messages. You decide to try a tiny piece anyway.

options.text: Start the smallest version yourself
options.then: You write a one-page plan and try the first piece.

options.text: Decide the cause isn't worth it
options.then: You feel flat for a few days, then sketch a tiny first piece anyway.

steps.why: A started thing draws people in better than an idea does.

steps.prompt: A classmate asks what you've been up to. What do you say?

options.text: Say you have a big plan and need volunteers
options.then: She asks what the plan is. You can't explain it in a line.

options.text: Say it's nothing, just an idea
options.then: She nods and the topic drops.

options.text: Ask her to join without saying what for
options.then: She hesitates. "Join what, exactly?"

options.text: Describe your small first piece and ask for one small help
options.then: She nods. "I can do that on Thursday." You have your first ally.

steps.why: People join something real when the ask is small and clear.

steps.prompt: One friend joins, then says she may drift away if it gets boring. What do you do?

options.text: Ask her to commit for the whole year
options.then: She winces. "That's too much."

options.text: Let her go so you don't have to beg
options.then: She leaves. You're alone with it again.

options.text: Give her a small job she'd enjoy
options.then: She picks the poster design and looks relieved.

options.text: Promise it will be exciting every week
options.then: She smiles. It won't be, and she'll notice.

steps.why: A small job that fits someone keeps them involved without pressure.

scenarios.debrief: Begin the small version; allies come to something real.
scenarios.relearn: Start the small version; allies join something already real.

scenarios.hook: You keep redesigning the name and logo instead of choosing the cause.

steps.prompt: It's late, and you've just made your fourth logo. What do you do?

options.text: Make a fifth one with a better font
options.then: It looks sharp. What it's for hasn't moved.

options.text: Ask friends to vote on the best name
options.then: The votes split. Nobody asks what the group does.

options.text: Stop and write the cause in one sentence
options.then: You write: a safer ride home for girls on the late bus. It's rough, but real.

options.text: Pay a designer to do it properly
options.then: A designer costs money. You still have no cause to give them.

steps.why: Choose the cause first. Branding follows once there's something to name.

steps.prompt: A friend asks if the group is ready to start. What do you say?

options.text: Not until the name and logo are final
options.then: She waits. Weeks pass with nothing done.

options.text: Not until more people have seen it
options.then: She nods. Nobody has anything to look at yet.

options.text: Yes, a rough cause is enough and the name can improve later
options.then: She grins. "Great. What's the first thing we do?"

options.text: Almost. I just want to compare a few other groups first
options.then: She waits. The comparing turns into another week of looking.

steps.why: A set cause lets you start. Presentation improves as you work.

steps.prompt: A week later, someone suggests a better name. What do you do?

options.text: Reopen the whole logo from scratch
options.then: The week is spent on colours. The work stalls.

options.text: Say the name is final and ignore it
options.then: She looks hurt. Next time, she keeps ideas to herself.

options.text: Hold the first step until the new name is printed
options.then: Printing takes two weeks. The step waits.

options.text: Thank her, use it if it fits and keep working
options.then: The name is better, and nobody stopped working for it.

steps.why: Use good ideas as they come, and keep the real work moving.

steps.prompt: A friend says to print T-shirts before the first session. What do you do?

options.text: Order shirts first so people take you seriously
options.then: The shirts cost money, and the session waits.

options.text: Spend the budget on a banner and a logo reveal
options.then: The banner is great. The session is still unplanned.

options.text: Ask the group to vote on the shirt colour first
options.then: The vote takes a week. The session slips.

options.text: Hold off on shirts and run the session
options.then: You run it in plain clothes. People remember what you said.

steps.why: Do the real step first. The look can follow.

scenarios.debrief: Lock the cause first; presentation can be refined by doing.
scenarios.relearn: Choose the concrete cause now; the name can come later.

scenarios.hook: A senior says to pick whatever cause gets the most likes online.

steps.prompt: She shows you a post with thousands of likes. What do you do?

options.text: Pick that topic since it clearly works
options.then: You copy the topic. In days, you're repeating what everyone else says.

options.text: Ask her which topics get the most likes
options.then: She lists three. None feels like yours.

options.text: Pick the funniest topic, for shares
options.then: The jokes get shares. People forget the topic by evening.

options.text: Ask which cause you care about and can reach
options.then: You think of the hostel mess hall. You can reach it, and you care.

steps.why: A cause you care about and can reach lasts longer than a trending one.

steps.prompt: A friend says likes bring more allies. What do you say?

options.text: You're right. Likes are the best measure
options.then: You start tracking likes each evening. They go up and down.

options.text: Then I'll ask a famous account to share it
options.then: Nobody famous replies. You've spent days waiting instead of asking anyone near you.

options.text: Ignore likes and post only once in a while
options.then: Few people hear about it. You miss a few possible helpers.

options.text: Allies come from real asks, so I'll count real outcomes
options.then: She nods. "So, count real changes, not likes?" "Exactly."

steps.why: Likes show attention. Real outcomes show change.

steps.prompt: A week later, your post gets few likes. What do you do?

options.text: Delete it and pick a trendier topic
options.then: The new topic is trendy for a day. Your care for it is thin.

options.text: Post something more dramatic
options.then: It gets clicks. It also gets arguments you didn't want.

options.text: Check who you've helped so far and go on
options.then: You write down each person you have helped so far. The list is short, but it is real.

options.text: Ask friends to like it so it looks popular
options.then: The number rises. Nothing else does.

steps.why: Impact is the people helped, not the numbers on a post.

steps.prompt: A friend suggests trending a hashtag for your cause. What do you do?

options.text: Make the hashtag the whole campaign
options.then: The tag spreads. On the ground, nothing changes.

options.text: Pay for ads to push it up
options.then: It costs you, and the views fade in a few days.

options.text: Skip posting about it at all
options.then: Fewer people hear about the work.

options.text: Use it only to point to a real action
options.then: You add a sign-up link. Six people join the next real action.

steps.why: Posts are useful when they lead people to something real.

scenarios.debrief: Genuine and actionable beats most-likeable when choosing a cause.
scenarios.relearn: Choose a cause for genuine care and local reach, not likes.

scenarios.hook: You want your club to be somewhere everyone belongs.

steps.prompt: You're choosing how to frame the cause. What do you pick?

options.text: A special side project for one group
options.then: It's well meant. Others in the club start to see it as someone else's thing.

options.text: A club where everyone belongs
options.then: Members nod. Everyone can see themselves in it.

options.text: Make the club more modern
options.then: Nobody can say what that means. The meeting drifts.

options.text: Wait until someone asks for it
options.then: Nobody asks. The club stays as it was.

steps.why: Inclusion works best as the default, so everyone can rally behind it.

steps.prompt: When the idea of a more welcoming club comes up at a meeting, a member says some people might feel uncomfortable. What do you do?

options.text: Drop the idea to avoid an awkward meeting
options.then: The meeting is easy. Nothing changes for anyone.

options.text: Tell them to accept it or leave the club
options.then: The room goes silent. Two members don't return.

options.text: Keep it vague so nobody objects to anything
options.then: Everyone nods. Nobody knows what they agreed to.

options.text: Say the club is for all and invite concerns
options.then: They say what worries them. You note it down.

steps.why: Listening respectfully brings people along without dropping the aim.

steps.prompt: A new member tells you privately, after the meeting, that they are gay. What do you do?

options.text: Mention it at the next meeting to show your support
options.then: They're stunned. It wasn't yours to share.

options.text: Tell the club president, just in case
options.then: They find out and feel exposed.

options.text: Ask them to lead a campaign about it
options.then: They feel put on the spot and step back.

options.text: Keep it private and let them choose who knows
options.then: They relax. "Thank you. I'll tell people when I'm ready."

steps.why: Who knows about their identity is theirs to decide. If they are unsafe, a trusted adult helps.

steps.prompt: Weeks later, a few members drift away. What do you do?

options.text: Assume they didn't care
options.then: You miss what drove them off.

options.text: Add strict rules everyone must follow
options.then: The rules feel heavy. More people leave.

options.text: Make the next meeting mandatory for all
options.then: Attendance goes up for a day, and feeling goes down.

options.text: Ask what would help everyone feel welcome
options.then: Two share useful ideas. One returns the next week.

steps.why: A club that listens keeps everyone included.

scenarios.debrief: Inclusion-by-default makes a cause everyone can join.
scenarios.relearn: Frame inclusion as the default: a cause where everyone belongs.

scenarios.hook: You're choosing between a cause near home and a trendy one far away.

steps.prompt: You only have time for one. What do you weigh first?

options.text: How trendy each one is right now
options.then: The far one is all over your feed. It feels exciting.

options.text: Whether I can really act on it
options.then: The near one is ten minutes away. You could go this Saturday.

options.text: What my friends will think
options.then: Half say the far one, half the near one. You feel more confused.

options.text: Which one has better photos
options.then: The far one has stunning photos. You can't do anything about them.

steps.why: A cause you can act on is one you can follow through.

steps.prompt: A friend says you can help the far one with a post. What do you do?

options.text: Switch to the far one, since everyone is talking about it
options.then: Everyone is talking about it. You can't see what you would actually do there.

options.text: Do both equally
options.then: Your time splits. Neither moves much.

options.text: Only post about it, and call that your cause
options.then: You feel involved. You haven't done anything yet.

options.text: Post once, and give your time to the near one
options.then: You post once, then go to the near cause on Saturday.

steps.why: Share what you like, but put your effort where you can make a difference.

steps.prompt: Two months in, your cause feels slow. What do you do?

options.text: Move to a trendier cause
options.then: The new cause is lively for a week. Then it's slow too.

options.text: Announce results that haven't happened yet
options.then: People cheer. Then someone asks to see them.

options.text: Quit until it feels exciting
options.then: The excitement doesn't return on its own.

options.text: Keep showing up and note small changes
options.then: You list three small changes. Slow doesn't mean failing.

steps.why: Steady effort on something local is what gets results.

scenarios.affirm: A cause you care about is worth beginning, with or without applause.

scenarios.hook: You want to start a cause at college, and your friend is unconvinced.
scenarios.setup: You are on the bench outside class.

steps.prompt: Your friend asks: "Why bother with a cause? We're just students."

options.text: "Students have done it before. Let's try one small thing."
options.then: She shrugs. "Like what?"

options.text: "Yeah, you're probably right. It's all pointless anyway."
options.then: She nods. "Told you." The idea dies on the bench.

options.text: "Maybe when we're older and a bit more important."
options.then: She laughs. "Sure, in twenty years."

options.text: "Forget it. I was only joking, and I'm not sure myself."
options.then: She smiles. "I knew it."

steps.why: Students have driven change before, and small local things count.

steps.prompt: A few days later, your friend asks: "If we did try something, what would we actually do?"

options.text: "Pick one thing on campus and fix it."
options.then: She tilts her head. "That I could do."

options.text: "Something big that will get us properly famous."
options.then: She frowns. "How, exactly?"

options.text: "I don't know. We'll figure it out someday, I think."
options.then: She rolls her eyes. "Okay, but that's not a plan."

options.text: "Whatever you think is best."
options.then: She shrugs. "Then I think nothing."

steps.why: One specific local thing is easy to start and easy to explain.

steps.prompt: Your friend asks: "What if nobody else cares?"

options.text: "Then we'll stop."
options.then: She nods, a little relieved. Then she looks at you. "Unless you still want to try?"

options.text: "We start with two, then invite others."
options.then: She smiles. "Okay. Two is a start."

options.text: "Then I'll do it alone and tell nobody about it."
options.then: She looks uneasy. "That sounds lonely."

options.text: "Then we'll be louder until they finally care."
options.then: She winces. "People hate that."

steps.why: A small start with a friend draws others to something real.

steps.prompt: A few days on, your friend asks: "If we did try this, when would we start?"

options.text: "Once we've got a perfect plan and a logo."
options.then: She nods. A month on, the logo isn't done.

options.text: "After exams, then we'll see what we feel."
options.then: She shrugs. After exams, something else comes up.

options.text: "This week. Let's book the notice board today."
options.then: She grins. "Okay. I'll bring the markers."

options.text: "Once more people say they're interested."
options.then: She sighs. "Then nobody starts."

steps.why: A real step this week beats a perfect start that never comes.

scenarios.relearn: Young people do drive change; start with one small, local thing.

scenarios.hook: Your cause is to fix gender inequality, and your teacher wants details.
scenarios.setup: She finds you after class.

steps.prompt: Your teacher asks: "That's a big goal. What will you actually do?"

options.text: "Equal lab turns for girls in our section, this term."
options.then: She nods. "That I can check."

options.text: "I'll try to fix all of inequality somehow."
options.then: She smiles gently. "How, though?"

options.text: "I haven't narrowed it down yet. It's just everything."
options.then: She waits. "Then it's hard to start."

options.text: "I'll start a big campaign and see what happens next."
options.then: She raises an eyebrow. "See what happens?"

steps.why: A named, local aim is something a teacher can back and you can check.

steps.prompt: Your teacher asks: "Who else needs to be on board?"

options.text: "Nobody. I can do this alone."
options.then: She frowns. "That's a lot to carry."

options.text: "Everyone in the college, if I can manage it."
options.then: She smiles. "That's a long list."

options.text: "The teacher in charge, a few classmates and a club."
options.then: She jots it down. "Start with those three."

options.text: "Only people who already agree with me on everything."
options.then: She nods slowly. "That might leave out useful allies."

steps.why: Mapping a few real allies makes a plan possible and keeps you from going alone.

steps.prompt: Your teacher asks: "How will you know it worked?"

options.text: "People will feel more fairly treated overall."
options.then: She nods. "Hard to measure, though."

options.text: "It'll get lots of likes."
options.then: She frowns. "Likes aren't the same as change."

options.text: "I'll know it when I see it."
options.then: She smiles. "Let's write something down."

options.text: "I'll count one clear thing by December, like lab turns."
options.then: She writes it on a sticky note. "That I can check. See me in a month."

steps.why: A measurable aim shows whether the plan is working.

scenarios.relearn: Narrow a big cause to one concrete, local aim you can name.

scenarios.hook: A classmate is angry about the harassment girls face near college.
scenarios.setup: He suggests a plan on the way back from class.

steps.prompt: Your classmate says: "Let's go and confront them ourselves."

options.text: "Okay, let's go and find them right now."
options.then: He grins. Then he says, "Wait, what if they get angry?"

options.text: "Let's run a drive with a teacher backing us."
options.then: He takes a breath. "Fine. Which teacher?"

options.text: "Let's post their photos online to shame them."
options.then: He hesitates. "Isn't that risky?"

options.text: "Let's tell the girls to avoid that road."
options.then: He frowns. "That puts it on them."

steps.why: A safe, adult-backed angle protects you and the people you want to help.

steps.prompt: On the walk home he asks: "Whatever we plan, will it actually stop them?"

options.text: "Not unless we confront them ourselves."
options.then: He looks unsure. "That feels dangerous."

options.text: "Probably not. So why bother at all?"
options.then: He sighs. The anger has nowhere to go.

options.text: "Not overnight. It shows girls where help is."
options.then: He nods slowly. "And others will know what to do."

options.text: "Only if we make the whole thing a lot louder and angrier."
options.then: He shrugs. "People might just shut us out."

steps.why: A drive gives people real information and a place to turn.

steps.prompt: The next day he says: "A girl told me she's scared on that road. Can we put her story on a poster?"

options.text: "Yes, her story is powerful. People need to hear it."
options.then: He pauses. "She didn't say we could."

options.text: "Tell her to keep quiet so it doesn't get worse."
options.then: He winces. "That doesn't sound right."

options.text: "Yes, but change her name."
options.then: He thinks. "People might still know who it is."

options.text: "No. It's hers. Let's help her reach the counsellor."
options.then: He nods. "Okay. I'll tell her we'll go with her to the counsellor today."

steps.why: Her story is not campaign material. She needs a trusted adult, and it's never her fault.

steps.prompt: He says: "I asked Ms. Iyer, and she'll back a helpline poster drive. Some call that too soft. What do we tell them?"

options.text: "Agree it's too soft and plan something harsher."
options.then: He frowns. "I don't want it to turn nasty."

options.text: "Tell them to run their own confrontation then."
options.then: He winces. "That could get someone hurt."

options.text: "It's safe, lawful and gives girls real help."
options.then: He nods. "Yeah. That's worth more than a fight."

options.text: "Ignore them and hope they get tired of asking."
options.then: He sighs. "They'll keep asking, though."

steps.why: A safe, lawful plan that points to real help is not soft. It works.

scenarios.relearn: On GBV, choose a safe, adult-backed angle over confrontation or shaming.

scenarios.hook: You have just put up the first notice for your cause.
scenarios.setup: A senior stops to read it.

steps.prompt: A senior says: "That's too small to bother with."

options.text: "You're right. I'll wait for a bigger one."
options.then: She shrugs. "Smart." Your hand hovers over the notice, but it stays up.

options.text: "Fine, forget it then."
options.then: She raises her hands. "I only said it."

options.text: "Then why don't you do something bigger?"
options.then: She stiffens. "I'm just saying."

options.text: "It's small on purpose. That's how it starts."
options.then: She tilts her head. "Hmm. Go on."

steps.why: Small and specific is where durable change starts.

steps.prompt: The senior asks: "But what will a notice even do?"

options.text: "It will end the problem completely, I hope."
options.then: She laughs. "Come on."

options.text: "It's a first step. We learn and go on."
options.then: She nods. "Fair. At least that's honest."

options.text: "Nothing, probably."
options.then: She shrugs. "Then why put it up?"

options.text: "It'll get us noticed."
options.then: She smiles. "That's not the same as helping."

steps.why: A first step is a test. You learn and take the next one.

steps.prompt: The senior says: "I'm not convinced. But if I helped, what would you ask me to do?"

options.text: "Take over the whole thing."
options.then: She backs off. "That's too much for me."

options.text: "Could you share it with your class?"
options.then: She nods. "Sure. I can do that on Monday."

options.text: "Join for the full year."
options.then: She hesitates. "I'm not sure about a year."

options.text: "No thanks. I'll do it alone."
options.then: She shrugs. "Alright." You're back to doing it all yourself.

steps.why: A small, clear ask is easy for someone to say yes to.

scenarios.relearn: Small and specific is where durable change starts, worth defending.

scenarios.hook: A friend is full of big ideas for your club.
scenarios.setup: He bounces over to you at the club table.

steps.prompt: Your friend says: "Let's launch five causes at once. It'll look amazing."

options.text: "Let's pick the one we care about most."
options.then: He pulls a face. "Just one? Okay, which one?"

options.text: "Sure, let's do all five and see what sticks."
options.then: He high-fives you. A week later, nobody can say what you do.

options.text: "Let's let the whole club vote on all five."
options.then: He likes the idea. The vote splits five ways and nobody feels any cause is theirs.

options.text: "Let's start all five and drop the weakest later."
options.then: He nods. You spend a month juggling and finishing nothing.

steps.why: One cause you can actually move beats five you can't.

steps.prompt: Later he says: "Whatever we pick, I worry it will look small. Nobody will notice."

options.text: "True. Let's add more causes so it looks even bigger."
options.then: He cheers. Your to-do list doubles.

options.text: "People notice results. Let's finish one first."
options.then: He considers. "Okay. One that's done is better than five started."

options.text: "Then let's make it sound bigger than it really is."
options.then: He hesitates. "Isn't that a bit dishonest?"

options.text: "Good point. I'll go along with whatever you think."
options.then: He shrugs. "Okay." He seems unsure, and you've handed over the plan.

steps.why: Real results are what people notice, and one finished cause shows them.

steps.prompt: A few days on he asks: "We have to begin somewhere. Which cause do we start with?"

options.text: "The one that will get the most likes online."
options.then: He grins. The liked topic isn't one you can reach.

options.text: "The biggest one, so it looks impressive."
options.then: He nods. It's too big to start this term.

options.text: "The one we both care about and can reach."
options.then: He pauses. "The hostel canteen. We can do that."

options.text: "Let's toss a coin and not overthink it."
options.then: He flips it. You both feel a bit lost with the result.

steps.why: Start with what you care about and can reach.

scenarios.relearn: Pick one cause you can move, not five you can't.

scenarios.hook: A peer is losing heart about starting anything at all.
scenarios.setup: You two are leaving the library.

steps.prompt: Your peer says: "There's no point. Change is way too slow."

options.text: "True. If it's slow, it's a waste of time."
options.then: She nods. "Exactly." The talk ends there.

options.text: "Real change is slow. Let's take one step."
options.then: She sighs. "One step. What kind of step?"

options.text: "Then let's wait until things speed up."
options.then: She nods, relieved. Things don't speed up, and nothing gets started.

options.text: "Then we make it faster, whatever it takes."
options.then: She frowns. "That sounds risky."

steps.why: Change is slow, and steady steps are what get there.

steps.prompt: A few days later, she asks: "If we did try a step and nothing happened, what then?"

options.text: "Then we learn and adjust. It isn't failing."
options.then: She nods. "So a try is a test, not a verdict."

options.text: "Then we quit and try something easier."
options.then: She looks unsure. "Easier at what?"

options.text: "Then we try something dramatic to get results."
options.then: She looks worried. "That could backfire."

options.text: "Then we blame the college for not caring."
options.then: She sighs. "That feels like an excuse."

steps.why: A step with no result is a test to learn from.

steps.prompt: She asks: "How do we keep going if it takes months?"

options.text: "By pushing ourselves harder every single day."
options.then: She laughs weakly. "I'd be flat by March."

options.text: "Small milestones and shared jobs."
options.then: She smiles. "And celebrate each one?" "Yes."

options.text: "By not telling anyone how slow it really is."
options.then: She frowns. "That's hiding it."

options.text: "By switching to something that's much quicker."
options.then: She grins. "Another new project?"

steps.why: A steady pace and shared load keep a team going.

scenarios.relearn: Change is slow but steadiness counts; take one step anyway.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Arjun has something to raise about your club's first cause.
scenarios.setup: He asks as you two plan it.

steps.prompt: Arjun asks: "Can our cause include queer students too?"

options.text: "Yes. A club where everyone belongs."
options.then: He smiles. "Everyone, by default. I like that."

options.text: "Let's keep that as a separate little side thing."
options.then: He nods slowly. "Okay." It feels like an afterthought.

options.text: "Better not mention it. People might get awkward."
options.then: He looks down. "Right. Okay."

options.text: "Sure, if you run that part on your own."
options.then: He raises his eyebrows. "On my own?"

steps.why: Inclusion works best as the default, so everyone is part of the cause.

steps.prompt: Arjun says: "Some members might push back. What do we say?"

options.text: "That they need to deal with it or leave."
options.then: He winces. "That'll just push people away."

options.text: "Nothing. We avoid the topic and hope it's fine."
options.then: He sighs. "Hoping isn't a plan."

options.text: "That the club is for everyone, and we'll listen."
options.then: He relaxes. "Okay. We can hear their worries."

options.text: "We drop it right away if anyone objects."
options.then: He goes quiet. "Then it always depends on who objects."

steps.why: Shared respect brings people along without dropping the aim.

steps.prompt: Arjun says: "A new member trusted me with something private. Should we use it as an example?"

options.text: "Yes. Real stories help everyone understand a lot."
options.then: He frowns. "It's not mine to share."

options.text: "Yes, as long as we leave out their name."
options.then: He hesitates. "Someone would still know."

options.text: "No. It's theirs to share. Use general examples."
options.then: He nods. "Right. I'll keep it to myself."

options.text: "Tell the group so everyone can be supportive."
options.then: He shakes his head. "That could really hurt them."

steps.why: Someone's private matters are theirs to share, and nobody should be outed.

scenarios.relearn: Frame inclusion as the default: a cause where everyone belongs.

scenarios.hook: You have told your family you want to start a cause.
scenarios.setup: Your aunt brings it up over tea at a family function.

steps.prompt: Your aunt says: "Pick a safe topic. Your cause might upset the family."

options.text: "I'll frame it respectfully. Can we talk it through?"
options.then: She softens. "Alright. Tell me what you have in mind."

options.text: "Okay. I'll drop anything uncomfortable from now on."
options.then: She smiles, pleased. You feel a small knot in your stomach.

options.text: "Fine. I won't have any cause at all, then."
options.then: She looks startled. "I didn't mean that."

options.text: "The family needs to learn to accept it."
options.then: She stiffens. "That's not how to talk to your elders."

steps.why: You can keep your cause and bring family along with respect.

steps.prompt: Your aunt asks: "If you ever speak up, what will you say to people who disagree?"

options.text: "I'll argue with them until they finally give in."
options.then: She winces. "People dig in when pushed."

options.text: "I'll post about them online instead."
options.then: She gasps. "That would shame everyone."

options.text: "I'll listen, share facts and find common ground."
options.then: She nods slowly. "That I can respect."

options.text: "I'll just avoid them altogether."
options.then: She sighs. "That won't help much."

steps.why: Listening and finding common ground bring people along.

steps.prompt: Your aunt says: "If your uncle objects, will you stop?"

options.text: "If an elder disagrees, the cause should end for good."
options.then: She hesitates. "Before even talking to him? Hmm."

options.text: "I'll carry on and ignore whatever he says."
options.then: She frowns. "That will make things worse."

options.text: "I'll hear him out and ask a teacher to help."
options.then: She smiles. "A teacher might help him see it."

options.text: "I'll do it quietly, without telling him."
options.then: She shakes her head. "Secrets get found out."

steps.why: A respectful talk with a teacher's backing can help him understand, and keeps the door open.

steps.prompt: Later your aunt asks: "However it goes, how will you keep the family informed?"

options.text: "I'll only tell you once it's all finished."
options.then: She frowns. "That's not very respectful."

options.text: "I'll keep it secret so nobody worries."
options.then: She shakes her head. "Secrets worry people more."

options.text: "I'll share updates and invite questions."
options.then: She smiles. "Then I'll tell the others to ask you."

options.text: "I'll tell everyone when it's in the news."
options.then: She laughs. "And if it never is?"

steps.why: Sharing updates with respect keeps family on side.
