scenarios.hook: Your project is ready, but you keep waiting for the right moment.

steps.prompt: A friend says you could start next week. What do you do?

options.text: Pick a date and put it in the calendar
options.then: You set Thursday at 4. It's on everyone's phone.

options.text: Wait until everything feels perfect
options.then: A week later you're still waiting. A teacher nudges you, and you settle on Thursday.

options.text: Start after the next festival break
options.then: The break goes by, and starting feels harder. You finally set Thursday.

options.text: Ask everyone for their ideal date first
options.then: Everyone has a different ideal day. In the end, you pick Thursday for them.

steps.why: A booked date is what makes a first step actually happen.

steps.prompt: Days before Thursday, you notice one thing is unfinished. What do you do?

options.text: Move the date back a week
options.then: The date slips. So does the energy.

options.text: Cut it down and keep the date
options.then: You drop the extras and keep what matters. You're ready.

options.text: Add three more things to make up for it
options.then: The list gets longer, and the date feels closer.

options.text: Cancel until everything is done
options.then: Everything is never done. A friend talks you into launching anyway, and you set a new date.

steps.why: A smaller launch on the planned date beats a perfect one that never comes.

steps.prompt: Your launch day goes well, but not perfectly. What do you do afterwards?

options.text: Decide it wasn't good enough, and stop
options.then: The small things that went wrong swallow what went right.

options.text: Wait for the next perfect moment
options.then: The wait stretches out again.

options.text: Note what worked and pick the next date
options.then: You write two lines of notes and set the next Thursday.

options.text: Try to fix everything before going again
options.then: The fixes take a month.

steps.why: Each small launch teaches you something and sets up the next one.

scenarios.debrief: A booked date is what makes the first step actually happen.
scenarios.relearn: Fix a date this week instead of waiting for the perfect moment.

scenarios.hook: You could start a hostel chore-fairness drive now or after exams.

steps.prompt: Exams are three weeks away. What do you do?

options.text: Pause everything until exams end
options.then: You close the folder. Chore rotas stay as unfair as before.

options.text: Launch the whole drive right now
options.then: You're up late planning. Your study notes pile up.

options.text: Do one tiny visible thing now
options.then: You put up one chore chart and ask two friends to try it for a week.

options.text: Ask the warden to decide the timing
options.then: She says it's up to you. You've lost two days.

steps.why: One tiny step now keeps the cause alive without hurting your studies.

steps.prompt: A friend from another floor asks about your idea. What do you say?

options.text: It's too busy to talk about right now
options.then: She shrugs. The idea stays unknown to her.

options.text: Ask her to run it for her whole floor by herself
options.then: She hesitates. "I don't have the time either."

options.text: Share your idea and invite one small try
options.then: She nods. "Okay, I'll try something small this week."

options.text: It will be done after exams, and she can join then
options.then: She nods. She doesn't think about it again.

steps.why: A small invitation brings allies in even when everyone is busy.

steps.prompt: Exams end. Friends are eager to scale up. What do you do?

options.text: Launch it across every hostel this week
options.then: It's too much too fast. Half the floors drop out.

options.text: Take a month off first
options.then: The energy drains away while you rest.

options.text: Hand it all over to them
options.then: They're keen, but they don't know your plan.

options.text: Add one more step at a steady pace
options.then: You add chore swaps for two floors. It works.

steps.why: A steady pace lets a small start grow without burning anyone out.

scenarios.debrief: A small step now plus a bigger push later beats all-or-nothing.
scenarios.relearn: Start small now even when life is busy; scale when you can.

scenarios.hook: You wrote a great plan, but nobody else has seen it yet.

steps.prompt: It's finished, and you could share it today. What do you do?

options.text: Keep refining it privately for weeks
options.then: The plan gets better in small ways. Weeks later, you finally show one friend.

options.text: Post it to the whole college group
options.then: Lots of views, few replies. One friend writes privately with a comment.

options.text: Send it to one teacher and one friend today
options.then: The friend replies in an hour. The teacher says she'll read it tonight.

options.text: Share it only after you've launched
options.then: Nobody can help before then. At the last minute, a friend asks to read it.

steps.why: A plan becomes real once someone else is in it with you.

steps.prompt: A friend sends back one tough comment on the plan. What do you do?

options.text: Defend every line
options.then: She backs off. Next time, she says less.

options.text: Rewrite the whole plan from scratch
options.then: The rewrite takes a month. The comment was about one part.

options.text: Thank her and fix what's clearly useful
options.then: She smiles. The plan is sharper, and she wants to help more.

options.text: Ignore it and carry on
options.then: You miss a gap that causes trouble later.

steps.why: Honest feedback makes the plan stronger and builds allies.

steps.prompt: A teacher says she'd back it if you ask clearly. What do you ask for?

options.text: Her full-time help to run it
options.then: She smiles tiredly. "I can't do that."

options.text: Money for the whole year
options.then: She winces. "That's beyond what I can arrange."

options.text: The room for one session
options.then: She nods. "Friday, third period. Done."

options.text: For her to speak for you in meetings
options.then: She hesitates. She doesn't know the plan well enough yet.

steps.why: A clear, small ask makes it easy for an adult to say yes.

scenarios.debrief: A plan only becomes real once someone else is in it with you.
scenarios.relearn: Show your plan to one trusted person this week to make it real.

scenarios.hook: Your first step needs a teacher's permission, and you don't have it yet.

steps.prompt: It's Monday and your step is planned for Friday. What do you do?

options.text: Skip asking and just do it quietly
options.then: You set up before school. A caretaker asks who allowed it, and you end up at the teacher's door.

options.text: Ask a friend to go and ask her on your behalf
options.then: The friend forgets. By Wednesday you finally go to the teacher yourself.

options.text: Wait quietly to see whether anyone objects
options.then: Thursday arrives with no answer. You aren't sure it's allowed, so you go and ask.

options.text: Ask the teacher with a short, clear request
options.then: She listens. "Show me what you're planning for Friday."

steps.why: A clear ask this week is safer than going around the teacher.

steps.prompt: The teacher says she'll approve it if you change one thing. What do you do?

options.text: Argue that the plan is perfect as it is
options.then: She sighs. The answer takes longer.

options.text: Say yes, then do it your way
options.then: She finds out. Next time, she trusts you less.

options.text: Drop the plan altogether
options.then: The idea cools. Weeks later, a friend nudges you, and you run a smaller version.

options.text: Listen, agree and adjust the plan
options.then: You change the timing. She signs off the same day.

steps.why: Adjusting to a teacher's backing keeps the step safe and real.

steps.prompt: After the first step, she asks how she can help next time. What do you say?

options.text: Say nothing. You'll handle it all yourself
options.then: She nods. You carry the load again.

options.text: Tell her to do whatever she thinks is best
options.then: She pauses. There's nothing for her to do yet.

options.text: Ask for the room again next Friday
options.then: She smiles. "Done. Let me block it."

options.text: Ask her to help with absolutely everything
options.then: She laughs kindly. "I can't do that. Pick one thing."

steps.why: A small, clear request is easy for a supporter to meet.

steps.prompt: Weeks later, a classmate wants to act without asking anyone. What do you say?

options.text: Let them go ahead, since it's their choice
options.then: They go ahead. A teacher stops them, and it's awkward for everyone.

options.text: Report them to the teacher without talking first
options.then: They feel you skipped talking to them, and stop sharing plans.

options.text: Say rules are for adults, not us
options.then: They shrug. You don't solve the problem.

options.text: Say asking first keeps it safe
options.then: They nod. "Fine. Can you come with me?"

steps.why: Getting backing is part of a safe launch, not a delay.

scenarios.debrief: A clear, backed ask is part of a safe launch, not a delay.
scenarios.relearn: Get the backing you need with a clear ask. Don't skip it.

scenarios.hook: Two friends say they'll help "sometime".

steps.prompt: They say it again at lunch. What do you say?

options.text: Thank them and wait for them to volunteer
options.then: Another week passes. "Sometime" hasn't come, so you finally pick Saturday.

options.text: Ask them to join the whole project properly
options.then: They exchange a look. "That's a big commitment." You offer one job on Saturday.

options.text: Tell them you'll do it alone
options.then: They look relieved. You do everything, until one offers a small job on Saturday.

options.text: Ask each to do one small job on Saturday
options.then: They look at each other. "Okay, what's the job?"

steps.why: A small, specific, dated task is easy to say yes to.

steps.prompt: A day before Saturday, one friend says she may not make it. What do you do?

options.text: Tell her she must come
options.then: She sighs. She comes, but she's annoyed.

options.text: Cancel the whole thing
options.then: The other friend is let down. Saturday goes ahead anyway, but smaller, with no plan.

options.text: Say it's fine and do her job yourself
options.then: You're back to carrying too much.

options.text: Ask what part she can manage, and adjust
options.then: She says she can do an hour. You move one task.

steps.why: A flexible, honest ask keeps people involved without pressure.

steps.prompt: After Saturday, they ask what else they can help with. What do you say?

options.text: Say nothing more is needed from them
options.then: They shrug. The chance passes.

options.text: Ask them to take over the whole project
options.then: They hesitate. It's more than they wanted.

options.text: Offer another small, dated job for next week
options.then: They nod. "Okay. Thursday, then."

options.text: Tell them to figure it out themselves
options.then: They look puzzled. Nothing gets done.

steps.why: Turn willingness into a steady rhythm of small tasks.

scenarios.debrief: People start when the ask is small, specific and soon.
scenarios.relearn: Turn vague help into a small, specific, dated task.

scenarios.hook: Your launch flopped, and only three people came.

steps.prompt: You're packing up afterwards. What do you do?

options.text: Decide the whole idea has failed
options.then: You go home feeling flat. The idea sits in a drawer.

options.text: Blame the people who didn't come
options.then: You send a cross message. A few people mute you.

options.text: Quietly drop it and avoid talking about it
options.then: Friends ask how it went. You change the subject.

options.text: Ask the three what worked and what didn't
options.then: One says it clashed with sports. Another liked the activity.

steps.why: A weak first try is data to learn from, not a verdict.

steps.prompt: A friend says to run it again with one change. What do you pick?

options.text: Change absolutely everything at once, to be safe
options.then: Nobody can tell which change helped.

options.text: Add a big prize to pull in a bigger crowd
options.then: The prize draws people who don't care about the cause.

options.text: Run it again exactly as it was before
options.then: Seven come, helped by word of mouth, but you learn nothing about what worked.

options.text: Move it to a time people are free
options.then: You move it to lunch. It's an easy change to try.

steps.why: Changing one thing lets you see what helped.

steps.prompt: The second run has seven people. How do you describe it?

options.text: Call it a huge success to everyone
options.then: A teacher asks for the numbers. Seven looks small next to "huge".

options.text: Call it still too small to really count
options.then: Your friends feel their effort is ignored.

options.text: Say it isn't worth mentioning to anyone
options.then: The chance to build on it passes.

options.text: Say seven came, up from three
options.then: People nod. The plan for the next run is on the board.

steps.why: Honest numbers build trust and show real progress.

steps.prompt: A few members say it's still too small. What do you do?

options.text: Agree and stop
options.then: The three-to-seven growth ends there.

options.text: Promise it'll triple next time
options.then: Then it doesn't, and your promise looks hollow.

options.text: Boost numbers by inviting people who won't engage
options.then: The room fills for one day, and then empties.

options.text: Keep running it and invite one new person each time
options.then: By month two, you have a dozen regulars.

steps.why: Steady, honest growth is what makes a project last.

scenarios.debrief: A small turnout is iteration, not failure. Keep going.
scenarios.relearn: Treat a weak first try as a test you learn from, not a failure.

scenarios.hook: You could launch a loud one-day stunt or a quiet weekly thing.

steps.prompt: Both look possible this month. Which do you choose?

options.text: A loud one-day stunt for attention
options.then: The stunt gets cheers on the day. By Monday, it's forgotten, so you start a quiet weekly thing.

options.text: Both at once to cover everything
options.then: You have double the planning and half the energy.

options.text: Whichever gets more likes
options.then: The stunt photographs better, but it fades faster, so you fall back to a weekly thing.

options.text: A small weekly thing you can keep up
options.then: You choose a ten-minute Friday chat. It fits your week.

steps.why: A repeatable weekly step shifts more than a one-day splash.

steps.prompt: A few weeks on, you are running a quiet weekly thing, and a friend says it's boring. What do you do?

options.text: Switch to a stunt to liven it up
options.then: The stunt is fun, and the weekly habit is gone.

options.text: Skip some weeks and see who notices
options.then: Attendance drops. Nobody says why.

options.text: Stop and look for something more exciting
options.then: The new thing is exciting for a month.

options.text: Keep the habit and add a little variety
options.then: You rotate the topic each week. Regulars stay.

steps.why: A steady habit, with a bit of variety, keeps people coming.

steps.prompt: A teacher asks what the weekly thing has achieved. What do you say?

options.text: It's changed everything
options.then: She asks for an example. You don't have a specific one.

options.text: It hasn't achieved anything yet
options.then: She frowns. You've missed what it did achieve.

options.text: It's too soon to tell
options.then: She nods, but she can't back what she can't see.

options.text: Here's how many came and what changed
options.then: She reads your tally. "This is working."

steps.why: Honest numbers show what a steady habit achieves.

scenarios.debrief: Durable change is a habit you can repeat, not a one-off splash.
scenarios.relearn: Choose a small repeatable step over a loud one-off.

scenarios.hook: You want to start an inclusion drive but fear doing too much at once.

steps.prompt: Your list has ten ideas. What do you do?

options.text: Launch all ten in the first week
options.then: Half the activities have no one running them. You feel swamped, so you cut back to the few that work.

options.text: Wait until all ten are planned properly
options.then: The list grows. The first week of the term passes, then you start with the easiest one.

options.text: Hand the list to the club and let them sort it
options.then: Everyone adds more ideas. The list is now twenty.

options.text: Begin with one easy, welcoming activity
options.then: You pick a welcome chai for new students. It's easy to run.

steps.why: One doable welcoming step gets the drive moving without burning anyone out.

steps.prompt: Some weeks on, members ask for more activities. What do you do?

options.text: Launch five new ones next week
options.then: The week is chaos. Two of them don't happen.

options.text: Say one is enough
options.then: They lose interest. The drive stalls.

options.text: Let each run their own without a plan
options.then: The activities clash, and some get no one.

options.text: Add one more, once the first is steady
options.then: You add a quiet corner at lunch. It fits.

steps.why: Add one step at a time so the whole team can keep up.

steps.prompt: A new member says what you have started feels like a one-off. What do you do?

options.text: Say it was never meant to last
options.then: She nods, a little disappointed.

options.text: Add ten more events to prove her wrong
options.then: You exhaust yourself and the team.

options.text: Let it fade and start something else
options.then: The welcome fades too.

options.text: Make it a regular day and ask her ideas
options.then: She says, "A sign-up sheet for new students." You add one.

steps.why: Make the welcome a habit, and ask people what would help.

scenarios.debrief: Start with one doable, inclusive step, not the whole programme.
scenarios.relearn: Make the first inclusion step small and genuinely doable.

scenarios.hook: On launch day, a key ally drops out at the last minute.

steps.prompt: It's an hour before the session. What do you do?

options.text: Cancel the whole launch
options.then: You send a cancel message, then see eight people arriving. You run a rough session anyway.

options.text: Run a smaller version with who's there
options.then: You cut the agenda to one activity. Five people stay and join in.

options.text: Wait an hour to see if she turns up
options.then: She doesn't. Half the group drifts away, and you run it with the rest.

options.text: Ask her to come, whatever her reason
options.then: She says she's sorry but can't. You both feel bad about it, and you run it anyway.

steps.why: A smaller launch with the people who are there keeps momentum going.

steps.prompt: Later, you hear she felt overloaded. What do you do?

options.text: Tell her she let the team down
options.then: She goes quiet. She doesn't offer to help again.

options.text: Say nothing and carry the extra work
options.then: You get through it, but you're worn out.

options.text: Take her name off the team
options.then: She finds out. Others start to wonder if they're next.

options.text: Ask how to share her load next time
options.then: She says she took too many jobs. You split them in two.

steps.why: Shared roles keep a team going and stop people from burning out.

steps.prompt: The launch went okay but not as planned. A friend wants to blame someone. What do you say?

options.text: Blame the ally who dropped out
options.then: The group's mood sours. Nobody shares ideas.

options.text: Blame the venue for being too small
options.then: It's not the venue's fault. The real lesson is missed.

options.text: Say it's fine and skip the review
options.then: The same gap shows up at the next event.

options.text: Say what you'll adjust next time, together
options.then: You make a short list. It feels fair.

steps.why: A calm review without blame helps you improve.

steps.prompt: You plan the next launch. How do you prepare for drop-outs?

options.text: Rely only on yourself
options.then: You can't be in three places at once.

options.text: Add extra people with no tasks
options.then: The list looks full, but nothing is covered.

options.text: Hope nobody drops out
options.then: Someone does, and you start again.

options.text: Name a backup for each key job
options.then: Two backups step in without any fuss next time.

steps.why: A backup for each job keeps the launch going when plans change.

scenarios.debrief: Adapt and launch smaller. Don't let one drop-out stop you.
scenarios.relearn: When someone drops out, shrink the step and still launch.

scenarios.hook: You're tempted to announce huge goals at your launch.

steps.prompt: You're writing your speech. What goal do you include?

options.text: End the problem completely by next month
options.then: It sounds big. Your friends ask how you'd ever do that.

options.text: Change the whole college within a year
options.then: People cheer. You can't say how.

options.text: Say nothing specific about what you want
options.then: The speech is warm. People can't tell what you want.

options.text: One honest goal you can reach this term
options.then: You write: "Ten girls signed up for the first session." It's clear.

steps.why: An honest, reachable goal builds trust and gets met.

steps.prompt: A teacher asks how you'll measure it. What do you say?

options.text: By how many likes we get
options.then: She frowns. "Likes aren't change."

options.text: We'll just know when it works
options.then: She smiles. "That won't work for a report."

options.text: Count sessions held and people reached
options.then: She nods. "Those you can show."

options.text: By how loud the cheering is
options.then: She laughs. "Let's count something real."

steps.why: Measure outcomes you can count, not noise.

steps.prompt: Halfway through, the goal is only half reached. What do you do?

options.text: Round it up so it looks like it's done
options.then: A friend checks. Now your numbers are in doubt.

options.text: Say the goal was too high and just quit
options.then: You stop with half of it achieved.

options.text: Hide the number until it improves
options.then: People wonder what's going on.

options.text: Share the honest number and next steps
options.then: People appreciate it. Two offer to help reach the rest.

steps.why: Honest numbers keep trust, even when the goal isn't met yet.

steps.prompt: A college newsletter asks about your results. What do you say?

options.text: Call it a record-breaking success for the college
options.then: The editor checks. The claim doesn't hold up.

options.text: Say it has already solved the whole problem here
options.then: People notice it hasn't. Your credit takes a hit.

options.text: Decline to say anything about the results
options.then: The story goes unwritten. Others don't hear about it.

options.text: Give the real numbers and what's next
options.then: The article is honest. Three new people join.

steps.why: Honest results and next steps build trust and bring people in.

scenarios.debrief: Launch on an honest goal you can actually meet.
scenarios.relearn: Open with a reachable goal, not an over-promise.

scenarios.hook: Your launch is a few weeks away, and you could use some help.

steps.prompt: A stranger online offers you money and fame for your launch. What do you do?

options.text: Hand the launch over to them for a bigger event
options.then: They post a flashy plan. You don't recognise it as yours.

options.text: Share your plan and address so they can start
options.then: They now know where to find you. You have no way to check them.

options.text: Politely decline and start small with people you know
options.then: You write a short, kind no. A teacher offers a room instead.

options.text: Reply to find out more, since they seem friendly
options.then: They answer fast and ask for your name, school and plan. You feel uneasy about sharing.

steps.why: People you know and can check are safer partners than a stranger.

steps.prompt: A friend says free help from anyone is worth taking. What do you say?

options.text: You're right. Say yes to anyone who offers
options.then: You open the door to people you can't check.

options.text: Let's take the money but not the fame
options.then: You still don't know who they are, or what they want.

options.text: Let's send them our account details so they can start
options.then: That hands them your private information.

options.text: Help is best from people we know and can check
options.then: She nods. "A teacher or a club, then."

steps.why: A small launch with trusted people keeps you in control.

steps.prompt: A teacher offers to connect you with a local group. What do you do?

options.text: Say you've got it covered
options.then: She nods. You miss a useful partner.

options.text: Ask for an introduction, and check them with her
options.then: She smiles. "I'll introduce you on Thursday."

options.text: Reply to the stranger instead
options.then: The stranger's offer is still unclear. You've used up two days.

options.text: Take the intro, and the stranger's money too
options.then: The two sources pull in different directions.

steps.why: Known, adult-backed partners multiply your impact.

steps.prompt: The stranger messages again, using your project's name. What do you do?

options.text: Reply to argue with them
options.then: They reply with more messages. It drags on.

options.text: Pay a fee to make them stop
options.then: It doesn't make them stop. It costs you money.

options.text: Post about them online
options.then: It escalates. You've started a public fight.

options.text: Tell a teacher and stop replying
options.then: She helps you report the account. It stops.

steps.why: Tell a trusted adult and stop engaging. It is never your fault, and you don't handle it alone.

scenarios.debrief: Good partners are people you know, not fame-promising strangers.
scenarios.relearn: Launch with trusted backers, not a stranger promising fame.

scenarios.hook: You want to launch a gender-based violence awareness step at college.

steps.prompt: You're planning your first step. What do you pick?

options.text: Stage a surprise confrontation of someone
options.then: A friend says that could get you into serious trouble. The counsellor suggests a session instead.

options.text: Hand out flyers without any adult knowing
options.then: A teacher takes the flyers down and asks who made them. She sends you to the counsellor to plan a session.

options.text: Post a long thread of strong opinions online
options.then: It draws angry replies and no help. A teacher steers you to the counsellor to plan a session.

options.text: Run an adult-backed awareness session
options.then: A teacher agrees to host it. The counsellor says she'll attend.

steps.why: A backed, accurate, lawful step helps people safely.

steps.prompt: The counsellor asks what contact details you'll share. What do you say?

options.text: Numbers we found online, since they look right
options.then: She asks you to check them first. Two are out of date.

options.text: Our own phone numbers so people can message us
options.then: She frowns. That puts you in a role you're not trained for.

options.text: Only verified helplines that she can check
options.then: She nods. "I'll confirm them with you."

options.text: None, to keep it simple
options.then: She says people need somewhere to turn.

steps.why: Verified helplines give people a safe next step.

steps.prompt: At the session, a student quietly says someone she knows is being hurt. What do you do?

options.text: Ask for every detail so you can really help
options.then: She goes quiet and looks scared.

options.text: Tell the whole group so they can help
options.then: She is upset. It was shared without her say.

options.text: Promise to keep it just between the two of you
options.then: She feels heard, but no one with training knows.

options.text: Believe her and go to the counsellor together
options.then: She nods. "Okay. Can you come with me?"

steps.why: Believe her, stay calm and bring in a trusted adult. It is never the fault of the person being hurt.

steps.prompt: After the session, a few friends want to do more. What do you say?

options.text: Stage a confrontation to go further
options.then: One of you gets hurt by the reaction.

options.text: Make the posters more shocking
options.then: People look away instead of reading.

options.text: Stop here since it went well
options.then: The momentum fades, and the next session never comes.

options.text: Plan the next adult-backed step together
options.then: You pick a date with the counsellor for the following month.

steps.why: Keep building with adults who back you, one safe step at a time.

steps.prompt: Months later, the counsellor offers to run the session each term. What do you do?

options.text: Say no. It should always be yours
options.then: You keep running it alone, and you get tired.

options.text: Say yes and walk away without a handover
options.then: The next one has the wrong numbers on the poster.

options.text: Say yes, then keep deciding everything yourself
options.then: She feels shut out of her own session. The project strains.

options.text: Say yes, and hand over with clear notes
options.then: The notes list the checked helplines. It lasts beyond you.

steps.why: Hand over roles and notes so a safe project outlives your part in it.

scenarios.debrief: For sensitive causes, launch safe, backed and accurate, never a confrontation.
scenarios.relearn: Launch sensitive causes safely with adult backing and real helplines.

scenarios.hook: Your first step worked, and you're unsure what comes next.

steps.prompt: People ask what's next. What do you say?

options.text: Nothing yet. Momentum will keep itself going
options.then: They nod. A few weeks later, it's quiet.

options.text: A big finale next month
options.then: They look excited, then ask who'll organise it.

options.text: The next small step, with a date
options.then: You say Friday week. Three people write it down.

options.text: I'll think about it and let you know
options.then: They wait. Most of them drift.

steps.why: Dating the next small step turns one win into momentum.

steps.prompt: A week later, you're tired. What do you do?

options.text: Skip it, since it worked once
options.then: The week passes, and part of the group moves on.

options.text: Ask a friend to take the first part
options.then: She says yes. The step starts on time.

options.text: Do it all in one night
options.then: You finish, but you're wiped out for days.

options.text: Delay it until you feel fresh
options.then: Fresh doesn't come, and it slides.

steps.why: Sharing the work keeps the pace sustainable.

steps.prompt: Later, you get the next step going again, and the turnout is smaller. How do you respond?

options.text: Call it a failure
options.then: The group deflates for now, though a few friends are still willing.

options.text: Blame the date and move on
options.then: You miss what really made the difference.

options.text: Ignore the turnout and carry on
options.then: Next time it drops further.

options.text: Check what changed and adjust
options.then: You see it clashed with a test. You pick a new day.

steps.why: A dip is information, not a verdict.

steps.prompt: A few weeks later, a friend says the group should celebrate how far it has come. What do you do?

options.text: Skip it. There's no time
options.then: The team feels unnoticed.

options.text: Throw a big party and pause everything else
options.then: The party is great. The project stalls for a month.

options.text: Post about it online to get more likes
options.then: Friends like it. The team still feels unnoticed.

options.text: Celebrate together, then set the next date
options.then: You share chai and pick the next date.

steps.why: Celebrating milestones keeps people going. Then you take the next step.

scenarios.debrief: After a win, immediately set the next small dated step.
scenarios.relearn: Keep momentum by choosing and dating your next small step.

scenarios.hook: You want to launch, but you worry you'll have to carry it all alone.

steps.prompt: You're ready to launch. Who's with you?

options.text: Nobody, and you hope help shows up later
options.then: You set up alone and feel stretched thin.

options.text: Ask everyone to commit to the whole thing
options.then: Most say no. Two say, "Maybe later."

options.text: Wait until ten people say yes
options.then: Nobody says yes. The date slips.

options.text: Ask two allies to share the first tasks
options.then: They agree. "Which tasks?" one asks.

steps.why: Sharing the first tasks means you don't carry it alone.

steps.prompt: Soon after, two people come forward to help, and they disagree about the first task. What do you do?

options.text: Decide alone to avoid arguments
options.then: They go along, but feel unheard.

options.text: Let them fight it out
options.then: They argue for an hour. Nothing is decided.

options.text: Let the louder one win
options.then: The quieter one feels sidelined.

options.text: Hear both, and choose by the goal
options.then: You pick the plan that fits the aim. Both agree.

steps.why: Pick the best idea for the goal, not the loudest voice.

steps.prompt: On launch day, you're doing most of the setup. What do you do?

options.text: Do all of it to save time
options.then: You finish tired, and the allies feel unneeded.

options.text: Tell them off for slacking
options.then: They go quiet. It was a misunderstanding about the jobs.

options.text: Say nothing and finish it yourself
options.then: You're annoyed, and they never learn the plan.

options.text: Name two clear jobs and ask each to take one
options.then: "Sure," they say, and one grabs the tables. It gets done.

steps.why: Clear shared jobs mean no one has to carry it alone.

scenarios.debrief: Change is collective. Build the first step with a couple of allies.
scenarios.relearn: Launch with allies sharing tasks, not as a lone hero.

scenarios.hook: You want a teacher's backing for your first step.
scenarios.setup: She has a free minute in the corridor.

steps.prompt: Your teacher says: "You wanted to ask me something?"

options.text: "Will you sponsor our whole year-long campaign for us?"
options.then: She laughs gently. "That's a big ask. What are you planning?"

options.text: "I need you to approve whatever we plan to do."
options.then: She raises an eyebrow. "Without knowing what it is?"

options.text: "Could we use the room Friday for one short session?"
options.then: She nods. "That I can probably do. What's it about?"

options.text: "Can you just tell the principal for us?"
options.then: She sighs. "I'd rather hear it from you first."

steps.why: A small, clear ask makes it easy for an adult to back you.

steps.prompt: She says: "Let's be concrete. What exactly will you do?"

options.text: "We'll figure it out once we get there, I think."
options.then: She frowns. "I'd want a plan first."

options.text: "Something big and exciting, I promise."
options.then: She smiles politely. "Exciting is not a plan."

options.text: "A full-day event with outside guests."
options.then: She shakes her head. "That's too much for a first step."

options.text: "A short talk about our goal and one next step."
options.then: She nods. "Short, with a next step. That I can back."

steps.why: A short, specific plan gives her something to back.

steps.prompt: She says: "I'd like to read your plan first. Can you send it?"

options.text: "It's still in my head. I'll send it later."
options.then: She waits. "Send it by Wednesday, then."

options.text: "Do you really need to read it? It's just a talk."
options.then: She raises an eyebrow. "I do. It's my room."

options.text: "Yes. I'll send a one-page plan today."
options.then: She smiles. "I'll reply tomorrow."

options.text: "I'll send it, but it's not finished yet."
options.then: She nods. "Fine. Finish it first."

steps.why: A clear, written plan helps her say yes quickly.

scenarios.relearn: A small, clear ask makes it easy for an adult to back your first step.

scenarios.hook: You're inviting a classmate to join your launch.
scenarios.setup: He is packing his bag after class.

steps.prompt: Your classmate asks: "You look excited. What's up?"

options.text: "Want to fully commit to running this with me forever?"
options.then: He laughs. "Forever? Slow down."

options.text: "You have to come. I've told everyone you will."
options.then: He frowns. "You told them before asking me?"

options.text: "It's complicated. I'll explain some other time."
options.then: He shrugs, still puzzled. "Okay. But is this something you want me in?"

options.text: "One hour Saturday: want to help set up?"
options.then: He thinks. "One hour? Sure. What are we setting up?"

steps.why: A small, specific invite is easy to accept.

steps.prompt: He asks: "So what would I actually have to do?"

options.text: "Just show up and look enthusiastic for me."
options.then: He grins. "That's not really a job."

options.text: "Run the registration table alone all day."
options.then: He winces. "Alone? All day?"

options.text: "Not sure yet. We'll see on the day."
options.then: He frowns. "Then I'm not sure either."

options.text: "Help carry chairs and put up two posters."
options.then: He nods. "Easy. I'll bring tape."

steps.why: A clear task makes it easy to say yes.

steps.prompt: He says: "I can only do the first half hour."

options.text: "Then it's not worth your coming at all."
options.then: He shrugs. "Okay, then." He leaves.

options.text: "Then I'll find someone who can stay longer."
options.then: He looks hurt. "Fine."

options.text: "Fine, but I'll remember you left early."
options.then: He narrows his eyes. "That's not fair."

options.text: "That works. Half an hour helps a lot."
options.then: He smiles. "Great. I'll be there at three."

steps.why: Taking what someone can give keeps allies willing and warm.

scenarios.relearn: A small, specific invite is easy to accept and gets people started.

scenarios.hook: You want the hostel warden to allow a notice on the board.
scenarios.setup: She sits at her desk with a cup of tea.

steps.prompt: Your warden asks: "What can I do for you?"

options.text: "You should really let us change all the hostel rules."
options.then: She stiffens. "All of them? Who is 'us'?"

options.text: "I need permission for a few things. I'll list them."
options.then: She waits. "Start with one."

options.text: "Everyone says the notice board is useless."
options.then: She frowns. "Do they? Why bring it up?"

options.text: "May we put one approved notice up this week?"
options.then: She nods. "Maybe. Tell me more."

steps.why: A small, respectful request earns a yes far more than a demand.

steps.prompt: She says: "Let's keep it simple. What would you actually put on the notice board?"

options.text: "Whatever the girls on our floor feel strongly about."
options.then: She raises an eyebrow. "That could be anything."

options.text: "A list naming the girls who skip their chores."
options.then: She shakes her head. "No. Not that."

options.text: "A short chore-fairness note, yours to approve."
options.then: She smiles. "Bring it tomorrow. I'll read it."

options.text: "I haven't written it yet."
options.then: She sighs. "Then give me the idea in one line, and bring the note tomorrow."

steps.why: A short note she can approve makes yes easy.

steps.prompt: She says: "Some girls may not like it. What then?"

options.text: "Then that's their problem and not really ours."
options.then: She frowns. "We live together. It's everyone's."

options.text: "We'll take it down and forget it."
options.then: She shrugs. "Then why put it up?"

options.text: "We'll put it up again, louder."
options.then: She sighs. "That will just make more noise."

options.text: "Then we'll listen and adjust the notice."
options.then: She nods. "Come and talk to me too."

steps.why: Listening to people keeps a hostel project fair and respectful.

steps.prompt: A week on, your warden asks: "Who's looking after the notice?"

options.text: "It should look after itself once it's up."
options.then: She raises an eyebrow. "Notices don't do that."

options.text: "Whoever has time can do it, I suppose."
options.then: She sighs. "That usually means nobody."

options.text: "Two of us will update it each week."
options.then: She nods. "Tell me when you change it."

options.text: "I'll update it when I remember to."
options.then: She smiles. "Let's make it more regular."

steps.why: Shared, regular care keeps a small step going.

scenarios.relearn: A small respectful request earns a yes far more than a demand.

scenarios.hook: You're organising a session and want verified helplines on your poster.
scenarios.setup: You phone a worker at a local organisation.

steps.prompt: The worker says: "Hello. How can I help?"

options.text: "Can you just plan and run our whole event for us?"
options.then: He laughs kindly. "I can't take it over. What do you need?"

options.text: "Could you tell me exactly what the law says?"
options.then: He pauses. "I can't give legal advice. I can point to those who can."

options.text: "I need a counsellor to come to our meeting tomorrow."
options.then: He pauses. "I can't arrange that so fast. What else do you need?"

options.text: "Could you share the right helpline numbers?"
options.then: He says, "Yes. I'll send the correct ones today."

steps.why: Asking for one concrete thing makes it easy for a partner to help.

steps.prompt: The worker asks: "Who is the session for, and who is backing it?"

options.text: "Just my friends. No adults know yet."
options.then: He hesitates. "Please bring an adult in first."

options.text: "Everyone in the city. It will be huge."
options.then: He raises an eyebrow. "That's a lot for a first session."

options.text: "Students, backed by our teacher and counsellor."
options.then: He relaxes. "That's a safe set-up."

options.text: "Anyone who shows up. We'll work it out later."
options.then: He frowns. "Better to decide who it's for first."

steps.why: Adult backing and a clear audience keep the session safe.

steps.prompt: He asks: "If someone shares something serious, what will you do?"

options.text: "Ask for all the details to help them better."
options.then: He shakes his head. "Please don't question them."

options.text: "Tell everyone so the community can help."
options.then: He shakes his head. "That would take away their privacy."

options.text: "Listen, believe them and bring in an adult."
options.then: He nods. "Yes. And remind them it isn't their fault."

options.text: "Promise them I'll keep it a secret forever."
options.then: He sighs. "You can't promise that if they're at risk."

steps.why: A serious disclosure needs privacy, belief and a trusted adult. It is never their fault.

scenarios.relearn: Asking for one concrete thing makes it easy for a partner to help.

scenarios.hook: You're recruiting your first ally for an inclusion drive.
scenarios.setup: She is chatting with a friend at the club stall.

steps.prompt: She says: "I saw your poster. What's it about?"

options.text: "You have to make everyone here feel included."
options.then: She hesitates. "That's a lot to ask of one person."

options.text: "Come to the meeting and you'll see what I mean."
options.then: She smiles uncertainly. "I don't know what I'm agreeing to."

options.text: "Want to help me welcome new students Friday?"
options.then: She brightens. "That sounds nice. What would I do?"

options.text: "It's mainly for students who feel left out."
options.then: She nods slowly. "Oh. I'm not sure it's for me."

steps.why: A warm, small invite gets an ally started without pressure.

steps.prompt: She says: "I'm shy. Is that okay?"

options.text: "You'll get over it. Just push yourself a bit."
options.then: She looks away. "I'd rather not."

options.text: "Then maybe this isn't the right job for you."
options.then: She shrugs. "Right. Okay." She hesitates. "I do still like welcoming people."

options.text: "That's fine. Come to the meeting and just watch."
options.then: She nods but looks unsure. "I'd still like to know what I would do."

options.text: "Of course. You could hand out chai at the door."
options.then: She laughs. "I can do that. Okay."

steps.why: A task that fits the person makes them feel welcome.

steps.prompt: She says: "What if I say something wrong to a new student?"

options.text: "Then you'll probably be taken off the welcome team."
options.then: She winces. "That sounds scary."

options.text: "Just don't talk to anyone new, to be safe."
options.then: She nods. The welcome job loses its point.

options.text: "Don't worry about it. Nobody will even notice."
options.then: She frowns. "I'd notice."

options.text: "Everyone slips. Say sorry and learn."
options.then: She smiles. "Okay. I can do that."

steps.why: Anyone can slip. A warm sorry keeps everyone included.

scenarios.relearn: A warm, small invite gets an ally started without pressure.

scenarios.hook: You want a school club to co-host your first event.
scenarios.setup: You catch the club captain after assembly.

steps.prompt: The captain asks: "Co-host? What exactly are you asking?"

options.text: "Could your club co-host one short event next week?"
options.then: He nods slowly. "One event, one week. That sounds doable. What's the topic?"

options.text: "Could your club just take over this whole campaign for us?"
options.then: He frowns. "Take over? That's a lot. I'd have to ask everyone."

options.text: "We have something big planned. Maybe join us sometime?"
options.then: He shrugs. "Sure, sometime. Message me when you know."

options.text: "Everyone else is joining, so your club should too."
options.then: He stiffens. "I don't like being rushed into things."

steps.why: A small, clear ask is easy to say yes to.

steps.prompt: Meera, a club member, asks: "What would our club actually do on the day?"

options.text: "Run one stall your own way. We'll sort out the room."
options.then: Meera lights up. "Our own way? We'd love to do a quiz stall."

options.text: "Whatever you like. We'll figure it out as we go."
options.then: Meera frowns. "That's not much to tell our members."

options.text: "I'll share the details closer to the day."
options.then: Meera sighs. "Okay, but people keep asking me now."

options.text: "It's easier if your club just follows our plan."
options.then: Meera folds her arms. "So we'd just be helpers?"

steps.why: Giving a clear role with some room makes people feel like partners.

steps.prompt: The captain asks: "Can we confirm by Friday? I'll need our teacher's okay."

options.text: "Yes. I'll book the room and send your teacher a note today."
options.then: He grins. "Great. Send it and I'll back you up."

options.text: "Let's wait and see if more clubs join first."
options.then: He shrugs. "Okay. My members may lose interest by then."

options.text: "Can your club handle the teacher part? We're busy."
options.then: He hesitates. "Alright, but it's your event."

options.text: "Let's confirm later, once our poster is perfect."
options.then: He nods slowly. "Fine. Friday was a good moment, though."

steps.why: Taking one concrete next step turns a yes into a real event.

scenarios.relearn: A clear, light ask to partner is easier to say yes to than a takeover.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Isha keeps going quiet whenever the campaign comes up.
scenarios.setup: You sit with her after school.

steps.prompt: Isha says: "I care a lot. I just don't know if I'm any good at this."

options.text: "Come along Saturday. You don't have to do anything yet."
options.then: Isha lets out a breath. "Okay. I can do that."

options.text: "You'll be fine. Anyone can do it, so stop worrying so much."
options.then: She smiles weakly. "Easy for you to say."

options.text: "If you really cared, you'd already be helping out by now."
options.then: Isha goes quiet. "Maybe I don't, then."

options.text: "Maybe wait until you feel ready. There's no rush at all."
options.then: She nods, relieved, and says she'll think about it.

steps.why: Lowering the bar lets a nervous friend take a real first step.

steps.prompt: A day later Isha asks: "If I did get involved, what would I even be doing?"

options.text: "Just watching, meeting people, maybe handing out a flyer."
options.then: She laughs. "That I can manage. Who's on the team?"

options.text: "Leading the table on day one. You're smart enough for it."
options.then: Her eyes widen. "Lead? On day one?"

options.text: "I'll explain later. Just show up and see how it goes."
options.then: She frowns. "Not knowing makes me more nervous."

options.text: "Whatever you like. Nobody will mind either way."
options.then: She shifts. "That doesn't help me decide."

steps.why: Naming one small job makes the first step feel doable.

steps.prompt: On Monday Isha says: "What happens next? I don't want to be left out."

options.text: "One small job of your choice, like the sign-up sheet."
options.then: She brightens. "The sheet? Yes, I'll do that."

options.text: "Next time, run the whole event. I think you're ready for it."
options.then: Isha pales. "All of it? I'm not sure."

options.text: "Nothing yet. Let's see if you feel braver first, okay."
options.then: She shrugs. "Okay." You don't hear from her for days.

options.text: "I'll pick your job and tell you exactly what to do."
options.then: She nods, but she seems smaller. "Fine, whatever you say."

steps.why: A small job she chooses keeps her in and builds her confidence.

scenarios.relearn: Lowering the bar lets a nervous friend take a real first step.

Waiting for a guarantee it'll work
