options.text: Say he was right and you should have waited
options.then: He shrugs. You feel less sure about everything you've already done.

steps.why: Showing real progress answers doubt with proof.

scenarios.debrief: A lightweight plan you begin beats a perfect one that never launches.
scenarios.relearn: A lightweight plan you start beats a perfect plan you never launch.

scenarios.hook: Your equality club has plenty of energy, but everyone is doing different things.

steps.prompt: At the next meeting, what do you suggest first?

options.text: Agree one shared goal for the term, together
options.then: People argue a little, then settle on one. The room feels lighter.

options.text: Let everyone carry on with their own project
options.then: Three posters and two petitions appear. None of them join up.

options.text: Pick the goal yourself to save time
options.then: It's done quickly. A few members say nobody asked them.

options.text: Add more activities so nobody feels left out
options.then: The calendar fills up. People are busier, but not more together.

steps.why: One shared goal points the whole club's energy the same way.

steps.prompt: Later, the club needs to pick its next focus. Two members push different goals and both feel theirs matters most. What do you do?

options.text: Test each goal against what's doable this term
options.then: Both ideas shrink a little. One clearly fits the term and both members see why.

options.text: Hold a quick vote and move on without discussing
options.then: The vote is split. The losing side comes to fewer meetings.

options.text: Back the one you personally like best
options.then: Some nod along. Others feel passed over and say less.

options.text: Run both goals at the same time
options.then: The club stretches thin and both goals slow down.

steps.why: Testing each goal against what is doable this term gives a fair reason to choose.

steps.prompt: Weeks later, a teacher asks what the club has achieved. What do you say?

options.text: Name the club's focus and one thing that has moved
options.then: She nods and asks how the school could help with the next part.

options.text: Say everyone has been super active
options.then: She smiles politely. She still can't tell what changed.

options.text: List every activity anyone has done
options.then: The list runs long. She gets lost and asks what it was all for.

options.text: Say it's too early to tell
options.then: She says fair enough. The club has nothing to point to yet.

steps.why: Naming one focus and one real result is honest and easy to follow.

scenarios.debrief: One shared, clear goal turns scattered energy into a real project.
scenarios.relearn: Agree one shared goal so the whole group's energy points the same way.

scenarios.hook: You're planning a drive against body-shaming for the first time.

steps.prompt: How big do you make the first project?

options.text: Your own class this term, with a pledge
options.then: The plan fits on one page. Classmates can see exactly what you ask.

options.text: Every school in the district within a month
options.then: The list grows past what your club can reach. People start to worry.

options.text: A big launch event, with guest speakers
options.then: Teachers like the energy but ask who will organise it. You have no answer.

options.text: No plan, just post about it online and see
options.then: A few likes arrive. Nobody in class knows what to do next.

steps.why: A right-sized scope can be finished, which gives you a real win to show.

steps.prompt: Your class teacher asks what success will look like. What do you tell her?

options.text: A count, like pledges signed by end of term
options.then: She writes it down and offers to help you track it.

options.text: That everyone in class will respect each other more
options.then: She smiles. Neither of you could say how you'd know.

options.text: That the posts go viral and people share them
options.then: She says that wouldn't show anything changed in your class.

options.text: That the principal says well done to the club
options.then: She says praise is nice, but it isn't the change you're after.

steps.why: Success you can count shows whether the project really changed something.

steps.prompt: The first week goes well and people ask for more. What do you do?

options.text: Grow one step at a time, once the first step is steady
options.then: The next step starts with a clear example to follow.

options.text: Take it to the whole district now while people are excited
options.then: The pace is too much. Even the first step stalls.

options.text: Stay put and say no to growing at all
options.then: Interested classmates wait for a while, then lose interest.

options.text: Hand the growing to the most excited person alone
options.then: She starts strong and runs out of steam within weeks.

steps.why: Growing a step at a time keeps the win steady while the project reaches further.

scenarios.debrief: A good plan is honest about what you can do now; right-sized beats grand.
scenarios.relearn: Right-size the scope: class or school scale is honest for a first project.

scenarios.hook: You're mapping allies for your project, and so far you've listed only two best friends.

steps.prompt: What do you do with the list?

options.text: Add a teacher, a club, a local NGO and classmates who care
options.then: The list grows, and you spot people who've been wanting to help.

options.text: Decide two friends are enough and stop there
options.then: You get started quickly. By week three, two people are doing the work of ten.

options.text: Add every student in school, whether or not they care
options.then: The list is long. You can't tell who would actually help.

options.text: Ask your friends to find allies for you
options.then: They say sure. A week passes and the list hasn't changed.

steps.why: Teachers, clubs and NGOs bring reach you can't get from two friends alone.

steps.prompt: A teacher hears about your project and asks why she should get involved. What do you say?

options.text: Share your goal and one small thing she could do
options.then: She thinks it over and says she can do that next week.

options.text: Say it matters a lot and she should care
options.then: She agrees it matters, then asks what you'd actually like from her.

options.text: Ask her to take the project over for you
options.then: She laughs kindly and says it isn't her project.

options.text: Say you'll ask later, when it's more ready
options.then: Weeks go by, and she hears about it from someone else.

steps.why: A clear goal and one small ask make it easy for an adult to say yes.

steps.prompt: Allies are joining, but they want different things from the project. What do you do?

options.text: Find the goal you all share and start from there
options.then: Everyone nods at the shared part. The rest becomes easier to sort out.

options.text: Keep only the allies who agree with you on everything
options.then: The group shrinks to four people who all think alike.

options.text: Say yes to every request to keep everyone happy
options.then: The plan swells with ideas, and none of them gets enough attention.

options.text: Let the loudest ally decide for the group
options.then: The loudest ally takes over. Quieter members stop coming.

steps.why: Shared goals bring people together even when they don't agree on everything.

scenarios.debrief: Map allies widely; you'll find more support than you expected.
scenarios.relearn: Map allies widely: teachers, clubs, NGOs and peers who share the goal.

scenarios.hook: Your goal is set, but you haven't named who can actually approve it.

steps.prompt: Your respect-week idea needs a yes from someone. What do you do?

options.text: Find out who can approve it and aim your ask at them
options.then: A teacher tells you it's the principal and how to ask for a meeting.

options.text: Pitch it only to other students and hope it spreads up
options.then: Many classmates like it. Nothing reaches anyone who can approve it.

options.text: Tell the first teacher you meet and hope he passes it on
options.then: He says it sounds nice. You can't tell if he'll mention it to anyone.

options.text: Wait for the school to announce something similar
options.then: Weeks pass. No announcement comes.

steps.why: Your ask only works if it reaches the person who can say yes.

steps.prompt: A week later, you finally get a chance to speak to the principal. How do you open?

options.text: State the goal, what you want approved, and by when
options.then: She nods and asks two practical questions.

options.text: Tell her about all the problems you see in school
options.then: She listens, then asks what exactly you want from her.

options.text: Say lots of students feel this way
options.then: She says she hears that, but not what you want approved.

options.text: Ask her what you should do
options.then: She says to bring a proposal. The meeting is nearly over.

steps.why: A clear goal, a specific ask and a date make it easy to decide.

steps.prompt: The principal says she needs to check with the school committee. What do you do?

options.text: Ask when it meets and offer a one-page summary
options.then: She gives you the date and says the summary will help.

options.text: Say it's urgent and press for an answer today
options.then: She turns stiff and says she'll let you know.

options.text: Thank her and wait to hear back
options.then: A month goes by. You haven't heard and the term is slipping.

options.text: Write to committee members yourself, to speed things up
options.then: A member is surprised and mentions it to the principal. The mood cools.

steps.why: Asking about the next step and offering a summary moves it forward politely.

steps.prompt: The committee asks for changes before saying yes. What do you do?

options.text: Ask which changes matter most and adjust the plan
options.then: They explain two concerns. You fix both and keep the goal.

options.text: Refuse, because your plan was already good
options.then: The committee says it will look at it again next term.

options.text: Agree to every change without asking why
options.then: The plan shifts shape. You're no longer sure it meets your goal.

options.text: Drop it and find a project that needs no approval
options.then: You feel relief for a day, then wonder what the work was for.

steps.why: Asking which changes matter most keeps the goal alive while meeting real concerns.

scenarios.debrief: Name the decision-maker so your ask reaches whoever can change things.
scenarios.relearn: Identify the decision-maker: the person who can actually approve your ask.

scenarios.hook: You feel the urge to design a logo and slogan before you've set a goal.

steps.prompt: It's day one of the project. Where does your time go first?

options.text: Set the goal and first tactic, then think about branding
options.then: By evening you have one clear line on what the project will do.

options.text: Perfect the logo for two weeks because it feels productive
options.then: The logo looks great. When people ask what it's for, you aren't sure.

options.text: Ask a designer friend for the logo and leave the goal for later
options.then: The logo arrives fast. The goal is still undecided.

options.text: Pick a catchy name first and let the goal follow
options.then: The name gets cheers. The goal gets vaguer the longer it waits.

steps.why: Goal and tactics are the plan's backbone, and branding can follow once they're real.

steps.prompt: Teammates ask what the project will actually do this term. What do you do?

options.text: Agree the goal and first tactic with them
options.then: The team finishes with one sentence everyone repeats.

options.text: Show them the logo and say the rest will follow
options.then: They like the look. They still don't know what they're doing.

options.text: Tell them to wait while you work it out alone
options.then: They wait. Two drift off to other things.

options.text: Say you'll explain once the branding is ready
options.then: The branding takes longer than planned. The team's questions pile up.

steps.why: Writing the goal and first tactic together gives everyone the same picture.

steps.prompt: A friend offers to print posters and T-shirts now. What do you say?

options.text: Ask them to wait until the team has agreed the message
options.then: They agree. A week later the posters say exactly what the team agreed.

options.text: Say yes and print everything now, ready for launch
options.then: The boxes arrive. Then the goal changes and the posters are out of date.

options.text: Say yes, and let them pick the message too
options.then: The posters look great but say something your team never agreed on.

options.text: Say no without explaining
options.then: They look hurt and offer the printing to another club.

steps.why: Printing waits until it can say something the team has agreed on.

scenarios.debrief: Goal and tactics are the plan's backbone; branding isn't the priority yet.
scenarios.relearn: Set the goal and tactics first; a logo isn't a plan.

scenarios.hook: A milestone slipped by a week and you feel like quitting the whole plan.

steps.prompt: The date has just passed with the task unfinished. What do you do?

options.text: Move the date and keep the goal
options.then: Writing a new date takes two minutes. The plan feels solid again.

options.text: Scrap the plan and start again from scratch
options.then: The team is stunned. A new plan starts, and the old work sits unused.

options.text: Pretend the date didn't pass and carry on
options.then: Nobody mentions it. The next date is quietly slipping too.

options.text: Blame a teammate for the delay
options.then: He gets defensive. Two others go quiet.

steps.why: One slipped date is a reschedule, not a verdict on the plan.

steps.prompt: Later, a teammate asks whether the dates ahead are realistic. What do you do?

options.text: Look at what caused the slip and build in some slack
options.then: The cause was exams. You leave a buffer around the next two dates.

options.text: Shorten the rest of the plan to catch up quickly
options.then: The dates get tight. The same crunch returns in two weeks.

options.text: Say it's realistic and change nothing
options.then: The team trusts you. The same problem turns up again.

options.text: Ask her to decide all dates from now on
options.then: She is surprised. You've handed over the plan without saying why.

steps.why: Finding the cause of the slip lets the new dates actually hold.

steps.prompt: Another milestone is coming up and some of the team are nervous. What do you do?

options.text: Check in on what each person can do, then adjust together
options.then: Two people say they need more time. The plan bends without breaking.

options.text: Tell them to stop worrying and work harder
options.then: They nod. A few quietly stop answering messages.

options.text: Cheer them on and avoid looking at the dates
options.then: Spirits lift for a day. The dates are still there.

options.text: Cancel that milestone to take the pressure off
options.then: Relief spreads. The goal slips further out of reach.

steps.why: Checking in and adjusting together keeps the pace humane and the plan alive.

scenarios.debrief: A slipped milestone is a reschedule, not a verdict; adjust and keep going.
scenarios.relearn: When a milestone slips, adjust the timeline and keep the goal; it's not failure.

scenarios.hook: Your plan is solid, but it assumes you will do every single task yourself.

steps.prompt: A friend reads the plan and says it's a lot for one person. What do you do?

options.text: Split the tasks into roles others can own
options.then: The plan turns into a list of roles with names to fill.

options.text: Keep all tasks in your name to stay in control
options.then: The plan stays tidy. You start skipping lunch to keep up.

options.text: Cut the plan down to what you can do alone
options.then: It's lighter, but now it can't reach the people you wanted.

options.text: Ask your friend to rework the plan for you
options.then: She rewrites it, but it no longer feels like yours.

steps.why: A plan with shareable roles is stronger and less likely to burn you out.

steps.prompt: The work needs more hands now, so you decide to ask classmates to take on roles. How do you ask?

options.text: Name a specific task and ask who'd like to own it
options.then: Two hands go up. One says she's good at posters.

options.text: Announce the roles and assign them without asking
options.then: Some accept. A few look unhappy and say little.

options.text: Ask who could help with anything at all
options.then: One person nods quietly and nobody else answers.

options.text: Say you'll do it yourself if nobody volunteers
options.then: A couple of people look relieved, and one says she'll see what she can do.

steps.why: A specific task and a real choice make it easy for people to say yes.

steps.prompt: Midway, a task is late and the person you were counting on has gone quiet. What do you do?

options.text: Check in kindly, ask what's in the way, and adjust
options.then: She says exams got in the way. A friend picks up half the task.

options.text: Take the task back and do it yourself
options.then: It gets done. You're back to doing everything.

options.text: Remind the whole group she's behind
options.then: She turns red and stops replying in the chat.

options.text: Wait and hope it gets done
options.then: The date passes. The next task depends on this one.

steps.why: A kind check-in finds the real problem, so the task can be shared again.

scenarios.debrief: A workable plan shares roles; change is collective, not a solo to-do list.
scenarios.relearn: Build the plan so roles can be shared, not all resting on one person.

scenarios.hook: You can't decide between three causes for your project.

steps.prompt: How do you choose just one?

options.text: Pick the one you care about most and can act on locally
options.then: You feel a small lift. The cause is still big, but now it's yours.

options.text: Try to run all three at once
options.then: Your time splits three ways. Each one moves slowly.

options.text: Choose whichever has the most followers online
options.then: It's popular, but your heart isn't really in it.

options.text: Ask your friends to pick for you
options.then: They split two to one. You still don't feel sure.

steps.why: A cause you care about and can reach keeps you going.

steps.prompt: A friend says you should choose the biggest cause so it matters more. What do you say?

options.text: Say a cause you can act on nearby will do more
options.then: She thinks about it. "Okay, but start with a small win," she says.

options.text: Agree and switch to the bigger cause
options.then: The new cause is huge. You aren't sure what to do on Monday.

options.text: Say you'll do both, one small and one big
options.then: Your week fills up with two plans and a half-done list.

options.text: Say nothing and quietly feel unsure
options.then: The doubt sits with you. You pick the one she suggested by default.

steps.why: Acting on something near you matters more than naming something bigger.

steps.prompt: Your cause still feels huge and fuzzy. How do you narrow it?

options.text: Pick one concrete local piece you could change this term
options.then: "Fair chores in my hostel" fits on a card, and you can start.

options.text: Keep it broad so nobody feels left out
options.then: It sounds big. People ask what exactly you're going to do.

options.text: Wait until the problem looks smaller on its own
options.then: A month passes. It looks just as big.

options.text: Narrow it to whatever is easiest, even if it doesn't matter to you
options.then: The task is simple. You lose interest within weeks.

steps.why: A concrete, local, time-bound piece is something you can really change.

steps.prompt: The other two causes still tug at you. What do you do?

options.text: Note them down and finish this one first
options.then: You feel calm knowing they're saved for later.

options.text: Start the second one next week
options.then: You split your attention. Both slow to a crawl.

options.text: Hand the others to friends without asking
options.then: Your friends are surprised. They didn't sign up for this.

options.text: Drop all three and take a long break
options.then: The break turns into months. The cause waits.

steps.why: Finishing one cause first keeps your effort from thinning out.

scenarios.debrief: Choose one cause you care about and can act on locally, then plan it.
scenarios.relearn: Pick one cause you care about and can act on locally; don't run three at once.

scenarios.hook: Your plan has a goal, allies and tactics, but no way to know if it worked.

steps.prompt: What do you add to the plan?

options.text: A simple count, like how many classmates joined the pledge
options.then: The count goes on the first page. You'll know where you stand each week.

options.text: A plan to count likes on your posts
options.then: Likes will be easy to count. They won't say whether anything changed.

options.text: A long survey for the whole school
options.then: Hardly anyone fills it in. You have a long form and few answers.

options.text: A plan to ask the principal if it felt like it worked
options.then: Her view is useful. It can't tell you what changed.

steps.why: One simple measure shows real progress, not just busy activity.

steps.prompt: Two weeks in, the numbers are small. What do you do?

options.text: Look at who joined and why, and try one change
options.then: You notice most people came through friends. You ask each member to bring one.

options.text: Stop counting so you don't feel bad
options.then: The plan feels calmer. You no longer know where you stand.

options.text: Round the numbers up when you report them
options.then: A teacher asks to see the list. The gap shows.

options.text: Switch to counting likes, which look bigger
options.then: The numbers climb. They don't show anyone joining.

steps.why: Small real numbers are a start, and learning from them is how plans grow.

steps.prompt: At the end of term you report to the school. What do you share?

options.text: The real counts, and what worked and what didn't
options.then: The principal asks how the school could support round two.

options.text: Only the biggest number, framed as a huge win
options.then: People clap. A teacher later asks how that number was counted.

options.text: The best photos from the events
options.then: The photos are lovely. Nobody learns what actually changed.

options.text: A promise that next term will be much bigger
options.then: They nod. The promise is bigger than the team you have.

steps.why: Honest counts and honest lessons earn trust and help the next step.

scenarios.relearn: Add one simple success measure, like how many classmates joined.

myth.un: A plan only counts if it covers every possible detail.
myth.re: A one-page plan with a clear goal, allies and first tactic is enough to begin.
myth.why: You add detail as you learn by doing; over-detailing just delays the start.

scenarios.relearn: A short plan with goal, allies and a first tactic is enough to begin.

scenarios.hook: "Real change means taking on the biggest version of the problem."

myth.un: Real change means taking on the biggest version of the problem.
myth.re: Durable change usually starts with one small, specific, local goal you can reach.
myth.why: A right-sized goal you finish builds momentum; an oversized one stalls.

scenarios.relearn: Start with one small, specific, local goal, not the biggest version of the problem.

scenarios.hook: "A goal like 'raise awareness' is specific enough to plan around."

myth.un: A goal like 'raise awareness' is specific enough to plan around.
myth.re: A strong goal names a number and a deadline, like '40 pledges by month-end'.
myth.why: Without a number and date you can't tell when you've actually reached it.

scenarios.relearn: Strong goals name a number and a deadline; 'raise awareness' is too vague.

scenarios.hook: "Mapping allies is a waste of time; just start and see who shows up."

myth.un: Mapping allies is a waste of time; just start and see who shows up.
myth.re: A quick ally map, teachers, clubs, NGOs, peers, reveals support before you start.
myth.why: You usually have more backing than you think, and naming it makes the plan stronger.

scenarios.relearn: A quick ally map reveals more support than waiting to see who shows up.

scenarios.hook: "Picking a tactic is just doing whatever feels most exciting."

myth.un: Picking a tactic is just doing whatever feels most exciting.
myth.re: You pick the tactic that fits the goal, advocacy for a rule, awareness for attitudes.
myth.why: A fitting tactic actually moves the goal; an exciting mismatch wastes effort.

scenarios.relearn: Pick the tactic that fits the goal, not just the most exciting one.

scenarios.hook: "A plan without dates is fine, you'll just work on it whenever."

myth.un: A plan without dates is fine, you'll just work on it whenever.
myth.re: A timeline with a few milestones keeps a plan moving instead of drifting.
myth.why: 'Whenever' tends to become never; gentle deadlines turn intent into action.

scenarios.relearn: Add a timeline with milestones; a plan without dates quietly drifts.

scenarios.hook: "Planning means deciding everything alone before you tell anyone."

myth.un: Planning means deciding everything alone before you tell anyone.
myth.re: A good plan is shaped with allies and shares roles from the start.
myth.why: Shared planning brings more ideas, more hands, and a plan that doesn't rest on you.

scenarios.relearn: Shape the plan with allies and share roles; it isn't a solo decision.

scenarios.hook: You're asking your class teacher to back your class pledge plan.
scenarios.setup: After school, she has ten minutes spare.

steps.prompt: Your teacher asks: "So, what did you want to talk about?"

options.text: "Could you back our class respect pledge this term?"
options.then: She sits down. "Tell me more. Who else is in?"

options.text: "Um, I had a vague idea about doing something nice, if that's okay?"
options.then: She smiles. "Something nice. What kind?" You say a class pledge.

options.text: "Everyone says we should do something, so... yeah?"
options.then: She frowns. "Who is everyone? Do what?" You mention the pledge.

options.text: "Can I just get your signature on this for now?"
options.then: She reads the pledge. "I'd like to know what I'm signing first."

steps.why: A clear ask with a goal gives her something specific to say yes to.

steps.prompt: Your teacher asks: "Who else is on board with the pledge?"

options.text: "Three classmates so far. I'll ask the debate club next."
options.then: She nods. "Good start. Keep adding to that list."

options.text: "Everyone in the class, basically."
options.then: She raises an eyebrow. "Everyone? Can you give me a few names?"

options.text: "Nobody yet, but they'll all join once you say yes."
options.then: She smiles. "I'd rather see a few people join first."

options.text: "Just me for now. I thought you could find others."
options.then: She shakes her head. "I'll help, but it should come from you."

steps.why: Naming real allies shows the plan has people behind it.

steps.prompt: Your teacher asks: "How will you know it worked?"

options.text: "By how many classmates sign the pledge."
options.then: She writes it down. "That I can help you track."

options.text: "We'll just see how it feels in class."
options.then: She says: "Feelings matter. But we couldn't show anyone."

options.text: "If the principal likes it."
options.then: She says: "That's one opinion. I'd want something we can count."

options.text: "If people post about it online."
options.then: She says: "Posts come and go. What would change in class?"

steps.why: A number you can count tells you what really changed.

steps.prompt: Your teacher checks the time and says: "Let's get practical. What do you need from me?"

options.text: "Ten minutes in class, and your name on the notice."
options.then: "That I can do," she says, and adds it to her diary.

options.text: "Anything you can do. Really, anything."
options.then: She laughs. "That's kind of you, but I don't know where to start."

options.text: "Could you run it for us?"
options.then: She smiles. "I'd rather you lead and I support."

options.text: "Nothing yet. I'll tell you if I think of something."
options.then: She nods. "All right. Don't wait too long."

steps.why: A specific, small request is easy for an adult to say yes to.

scenarios.relearn: A clear ask names your goal, allies and date; vagueness is easy to brush off.

scenarios.hook: You want a classmate who cares to join your project team.
scenarios.setup: You catch her at the canteen, mid-lunch.

steps.prompt: Your classmate looks up from her lunch and says: "Oh, hi. What's up?"

options.text: "We're starting a Friday listening corner. Co-host one with me?"
options.then: She puts down her spoon. "Hm. Tell me more."

options.text: "You should totally join my thing. It's going to be huge."
options.then: She smiles. "Your thing? What is it?"

options.text: "Nobody else will help, so you kind of have to, right?"
options.then: She frowns. "I don't have to do anything."

options.text: "I need someone. Anyone who cares at all will do. Are you in?"
options.then: She hesitates. "Anyone? I'm not sure that's me."

steps.why: A specific, friendly invite is easy to say yes or no to.

steps.prompt: Your classmate says after a pause: "I'm not sure. I've got exams coming up."

options.text: "That makes sense. Could you try just one Friday?"
options.then: She thinks. "One Friday I can maybe do."

options.text: "Everyone has exams. You can't use that as an excuse."
options.then: She goes quiet. "I wasn't making an excuse." She doesn't walk away.

options.text: "Okay, forget it, then. I'll find someone who has time."
options.then: She shrugs, then lingers. "Okay."

options.text: "You'll regret it if you miss this chance."
options.then: She narrows her eyes. "That sounds like pressure." She stays, though.

steps.why: Respecting her limits and offering a small try keeps the door open.

steps.prompt: Your classmate says: "If I did, what would I actually do?"

options.text: "Welcome people, listen, and point worried ones to a counsellor."
options.then: She nods. "I can do that. I'll tell my mum."

options.text: "Give them advice and fix their problems for them."
options.then: She looks worried. "I don't think I'm qualified for that."

options.text: "Whatever you like. I haven't really thought it through yet, sorry."
options.then: She laughs awkwardly. "Then how would I know what to do?"

options.text: "Take notes on what they say and share it with the group."
options.then: She pauses. "Wouldn't people mind that?"

steps.why: Listening, respecting privacy and pointing to adults keeps a peer corner safe.

scenarios.relearn: Invite allies warmly and specifically; don't hype or pressure them.

scenarios.hook: Your friend is keen to start posting about your cause.
scenarios.setup: In the group chat, she's already typing a first post.

steps.prompt: Your friend says: "Let's just post. Planning takes forever."

options.text: "First one goal and a date, so each post points somewhere."
options.then: She pauses. "Fine. But can it be quick?"

options.text: "Okay, post away. We'll sort out the plan later, maybe."
options.then: She posts. The comments are friendly and go nowhere.

options.text: "Fine, but I'll approve every post before it goes out."
options.then: She sighs. Each post now waits on you for days.

options.text: "Posting is pointless, so let's skip it altogether."
options.then: She goes quiet. "I thought you wanted people to know."

steps.why: One clear goal and a date make every post point somewhere.

steps.prompt: Your friend says: "So what is the goal, then? There's so much to fix."

options.text: "One thing we can reach this term. Which matters most?"
options.then: She thinks. "Probably the jokes in class. That one."

options.text: "All of it. We'll just keep posting about everything."
options.then: She laughs. "That's a lot of posts."

options.text: "Whatever you want. I don't mind, really."
options.then: She shrugs. "Okay. Then I'll pick something."

options.text: "Something huge, so people really notice us."
options.then: Her eyes widen. "Huge sounds scary. Where do we start?"

steps.why: One goal you can reach this term is better than many you can't.

steps.prompt: Your friend says: "Fine. How will we know the posts are working?"

options.text: "By real steps, like sign-ups for our first meeting."
options.then: "Okay. So each post needs a sign-up link," she says.

options.text: "By likes and shares, mostly. They add up fast."
options.then: She nods. The numbers rise and nobody comes to meetings.

options.text: "We'll just feel it. It'll be obvious when it works."
options.then: She laughs. "I guess we'll see."

options.text: "By whether the principal replies to any of our posts."
options.then: She frowns. "What if she doesn't see them?"

steps.why: Real steps like sign-ups show impact better than likes do.

scenarios.relearn: Set the goal and date first; then your posts actually point somewhere.

scenarios.hook: You have a short slot with the student council to present your plan.
scenarios.setup: You step to the front of the room.

steps.prompt: The council head says: "You have two minutes. Go ahead."

options.text: "Our goal is 50 respect pledges by Diwali. Here's our plan."
options.then: Pens move. A member asks to see the plan.

options.text: "We want to do good things about equality, somehow."
options.then: The members glance at each other. Nobody writes anything.

options.text: "Let me start with some background on gender inequality."
options.then: A member checks the clock. Half your time goes on background.

options.text: "Before I start, sorry, I'm not a great speaker."
options.then: She nods kindly. A minute of your time has gone.

steps.why: A specific goal and ask in the first line get the council listening.

steps.prompt: A council member asks: "Why does this matter to our school?"

options.text: "Jokes in class hurt. A pledge sets a shared rule."
options.then: A member nods. "I've seen that too."

options.text: "It just does. Everyone knows it."
options.then: The member waits. You have no example to give.

options.text: "Other schools are doing it, so I think we should too."
options.then: A member frowns. "We're not other schools."

options.text: "You'd feel it if it happened to you."
options.then: A member bristles. "That sounds like we're to blame."

steps.why: A real reason from school life helps the council see why it matters.

steps.prompt: Another member asks: "What do you need from us, exactly?"

options.text: "A slot in assembly, and two members to hand out pledges."
options.then: "That's doable," she says, and notes it down.

options.text: "Whatever help you can give. Honestly, anything at all."
options.then: She frowns. "We'd need something specific to vote on."

options.text: "Your support, and a large budget for printing and prizes."
options.then: She shakes her head. "We don't have a budget like that."

options.text: "Nothing yet. I just wanted you to know."
options.then: She shrugs. "Then let us know when you need us."

steps.why: A specific request lets the council say yes or no.

steps.prompt: The council head says: "Time's nearly up. Anything to add before you go?"

options.text: "Thanks. I'll send a one-page summary today for everyone."
options.then: "Please do," she says. A few members smile.

options.text: "Please vote yes. We've worked so hard on this, honestly."
options.then: She nods. "Hard work is good. We'll look at the plan."

options.text: "If it's a no, we'll just do it anyway, without any of you."
options.then: The room cools. A member whispers that it sounds like a threat.

options.text: "No, that's all. Sorry for taking your time."
options.then: She nods and moves on. The summary is never sent.

steps.why: A closing summary makes it easy for the council to decide well.

scenarios.relearn: Open a pitch with your specific goal and a clear ask, not a vague hope.

scenarios.hook: A local NGO offers to help your club with its project.
scenarios.setup: The video call connects, and she smiles at the camera.

steps.prompt: Their coordinator, Ms. Kapoor, says: "Happy to help. What would be useful?"

options.text: "Could you run a session for us and share poster templates?"
options.then: "We can do that," she says. "Which week suits you?"

options.text: "Anything, everything, whatever you have. We'll take it all."
options.then: She laughs. "That's kind, but I need something specific."

options.text: "I'm not sure. Can you just decide for us?"
options.then: She smiles. "I'd love to, but you know your club best."

options.text: "Could you fund the whole project and run it for us?"
options.then: She shakes her head. "That's bigger than we can do."

steps.why: A focused request is easy for a partner to say yes to.

steps.prompt: Ms. Kapoor says: "I'd like to know a little about your club first."

options.text: "We're a student club with a goal, and a teacher backs us."
options.then: "Lovely," she says. "That helps us work with you."

options.text: "We're going to be huge. You'll want your name on this."
options.then: She nods slowly. "We'll see how it goes."

options.text: "We're just kids, so we don't know much."
options.then: She smiles. "Everyone starts somewhere." She still needs details.

options.text: "We'll tell you more once you agree to help."
options.then: She pauses. "I'd need to know a bit before I can say."

steps.why: A plain, honest description builds trust with a partner.

steps.prompt: Ms. Kapoor says: "We usually agree a few ground rules with partners. Is that okay?"

options.text: "Yes. Please share them and I'll check with our teacher."
options.then: "Perfect. I'll email them to you both," she says.

options.text: "No rules. We want to do it our way."
options.then: She hesitates. "Then it may be hard for us to join."

options.text: "Sure, whatever you say."
options.then: She frowns. "Please read them first. They affect your club."

options.text: "I'll agree now. My teacher doesn't really need to know."
options.then: She pauses. "We always speak to a teacher first."

steps.why: Ground rules and your teacher's say-so keep the partnership safe.

scenarios.relearn: Ask a partner for something specific; a focused request is easy to say yes to.

scenarios.hook: A senior reads the first draft of your plan.
scenarios.setup: She has circled the words "whole district" on your page.

steps.prompt: The senior says: "This is too big for a first project."

options.text: "Fair. Let's right-size it to our class and grow it if it works."
options.then: She smiles. "That I can back."

options.text: "No. We'll cover the whole district this term. Go big or go home."
options.then: She sighs. "Big plans need a bigger team than yours."

options.text: "Maybe we should just cancel the whole thing then."
options.then: She shakes her head. "I said smaller, not cancel."

options.text: "Could you rewrite it to the right size for us?"
options.then: She smiles. "It'll work better if you do the cutting."

steps.why: Right-sizing keeps the goal and makes it reachable.

steps.prompt: The senior asks: "What's the smallest version that still matters?"

options.text: "One class pledge and a poster, with a count of who signs."
options.then: "That I could see finishing," she says.

options.text: "The same plan, but with fewer words in it."
options.then: She looks at the page. "The size is the same."

options.text: "I'd need to ask the whole club. They'll want it big."
options.then: She nods. "Ask them, but bring a smaller option."

options.text: "Maybe just one post. That's the smallest, right?"
options.then: She frowns. "A post isn't a plan. What else?"

steps.why: The smallest real version can be finished and then built on.

steps.prompt: A week later, with the plan cut down, the senior asks: "When would you grow it?"

options.text: "After the first class finishes, once we have a count."
options.then: She nods. "Then you'd have real proof."

options.text: "Right away, as soon as people say they like it a lot."
options.then: She shakes her head. "Liking it isn't finishing it."

options.text: "Never. Small is enough for us, I think."
options.then: She smiles. "It could be. But why close the door?"

options.text: "Whenever a more senior student tells us to."
options.then: She shrugs. "It should be your call, based on how the first part goes."

steps.why: Growing after a first win means you build on proof, not hope.

scenarios.relearn: When scope is too big, right-size it and grow later. Don't quit or over-reach.

scenarios.hook: Your small team meets for the first time to plan your project.
scenarios.setup: Everyone looks at you, since it was your idea.

steps.prompt: A teammate asks: "So, who's doing what?"

options.text: "You take posters and I'll book the room. Who wants sign-ups?"
options.then: Two hands go up. The room relaxes.

options.text: "I'll just do everything myself. It's easier that way, honestly."
options.then: Nobody argues. By next week, you're doing it all.

options.text: "We'll sort out roles later. Let's just get started right now."
options.then: People start on different things. Two of them overlap.

options.text: "I'll give everyone a role. Please don't argue about it."
options.then: The room goes quiet. Nobody feels like it's their plan.

steps.why: Naming who owns each task shares the load and shows the plan is real.

steps.prompt: A teammate says: "I'm not sure what I'd be good at."

options.text: "No problem. What are you good at? We'll find a fit."
options.then: "I'm okay with numbers," he says. "I could track sign-ups."

options.text: "You'll manage. It's not hard. You'll see."
options.then: He looks unsure. His first task comes out messy.

options.text: "Then I'll just do that part too. Don't worry about it."
options.then: He looks relieved. Your list is longer again.

options.text: "Everyone has to do what they're given. That's how it works."
options.then: He says nothing. He's less keen at the next meeting.

steps.why: Matching roles to strengths keeps everyone included and doing well.

steps.prompt: A quieter teammate asks: "Can I just help whenever?"

options.text: "Yes. Could you take one small job each week?"
options.then: She nods. "That I can do."

options.text: "Sure, help whenever. We'll manage somehow, no problem."
options.then: She smiles. Nobody knows when she'll turn up.

options.text: "No. Everyone needs a fixed role from day one, no exceptions."
options.then: She looks uneasy. "Then maybe I'll skip it."

options.text: "Okay, but I'll check whether you actually do it."
options.then: She flushes. "I would, you know."

steps.why: A small, clear job each week keeps her included and the team in sync.

scenarios.relearn: Share the load by naming who owns each role; don't carry it all yourself.

scenarios.hook: You are drafting a plan that includes everyone in your class.
scenarios.setup: It comes up in the planning chat.

steps.prompt: A peer says: "Why bother with all that inclusion stuff?"

options.text: "Because it should work for everyone in class. That's the point."
options.then: He shrugs. "Okay. I hadn't thought of it that way."

options.text: "Ugh, fine. It's extra work, but we're supposed to do it."
options.then: He smirks. "So you don't really want it either." The chat goes quiet.

options.text: "I don't know. You decide. I don't want to argue about it."
options.then: He says: "Okay, I will." The decision shifts to him.

options.text: "Because that's how it's supposed to be, all right?"
options.then: He rolls his eyes. "That's not really an answer."

steps.why: A plan that works for everyone is the point, not extra work.

steps.prompt: The peer says: "But planning for everyone will take longer."

options.text: "A bit, maybe. But nobody is left out, and more people join."
options.then: He thinks. "Fair. More people could help us."

options.text: "It won't take longer. Don't worry about it at all."
options.then: He frowns. "It will, though. Be honest."

options.text: "Then let's only plan for most people, to keep it simple."
options.then: He nods. A few classmates are quietly left out.

options.text: "If you don't like it, you can always just leave the team."
options.then: He goes silent. He stays, but he has little to say.

steps.why: A little more time now means more people can join in.

steps.prompt: A classmate says: "Can I help? I don't think I'd fit in."

options.text: "You'd fit fine. Let's find you a job and ask what you need."
options.then: She smiles. "I'd like to try the sign-up table."

options.text: "Sure. We'll try to fit you in somewhere, I suppose."
options.then: She nods. Nobody tells her where.

options.text: "Maybe. Let's see if it works out for everyone."
options.then: She shrinks a little. "Okay."

options.text: "Don't worry about it. Just watch for now, if you like."
options.then: She nods and stays on the edge of the group.

steps.why: Asking what a person needs and offering a real job makes room for them.

scenarios.relearn: Plan to work for everyone by default; inclusion is the point, not a hassle.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that would make this plan stall or over-reach.

scene.text: "Let's wait till the plan is flawless."
"I'll ask two teachers to back us."
"We'll fix the whole state this term."

scenarios.why: Waiting for a flawless plan stalls you, and a whole-state goal over-reaches; the rest are sound.
scenarios.relearn: A plan stalls when it waits for perfection or over-reaches; keep it light and right-sized.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two goals that are too vague to plan around.
scenarios.why: 'Make everyone care, somehow' and 'do something big' name no number or date, so you can't track them.
scenarios.relearn: Vague goals name no number or date; strong goals do, so you can tell when they're reached.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two 'priorities' that are really just distractions for a first project.
scenarios.why: A perfect logo and chasing virality are distractions; the goal, allies and timeline are the real priorities.
scenarios.relearn: Goal, allies and a timeline come first; logos and virality are distractions, not priorities.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two scopes that over-reach for a student's first project.

scene.text: A respect-pledge drive in your own class
A noticeboard series at your school
Ending dowry across the state by exams

scenarios.why: A national TV campaign and ending dowry statewide over-reach; class and school-scale moves are realistic.
scenarios.relearn: Over-reaching scopes stall a first project; right-size to class or school scale.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two moves that quietly derail a plan that started well.

scene.text: Adding a brand-new goal every week

scenarios.why: Constant new goals and no fixed dates derail a plan; progress checks, clear owners and milestones hold it.
scenarios.relearn: Scope-creep and no dates derail a plan; clear owners, milestones and progress checks keep it on track.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two planning habits that leave you carrying it all alone.

scene.text: Keeping the plan secret till it's perfect
Inviting a teacher to back it

scenarios.why: Doing every task solo and hiding the plan leave you alone; mapping allies and sharing roles spread the load.
scenarios.relearn: Doing it all yourself or hiding the plan isolates you; map allies and share roles instead.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that confuse noise with a real plan.

scene.text: "If it goes viral, the work does itself."
"Let's set a date for the first session."
"Ask the principal to review the rule."

scenarios.why: Counting on virality and treating likes as proof confuse noise with impact; the rest are real plan steps.
scenarios.relearn: Virality and likes aren't a plan or proof; measure real participation and aim at the decision-maker.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two assumptions that would weaken your stakeholder map.

scene.text: "A teacher and the club could back us."

scenarios.why: "I'm on my own" and "only the popular kid matters" miss real allies and those affected; map widely.
scenarios.relearn: Don't assume you're alone or that one popular name is the plan; map allies, deciders and those affected.

scenarios.hook: Sort each sign of progress: a real measure, or just a vanity number?

items.text: The lane got a new streetlight
A trending hashtag for a day

scenarios.relearn: Pledges signed, a light fixed and allies joined are real; views, likes and a trend are vanity numbers.

scenarios.hook: Sort each into the tactic family it belongs to.

items.text: A letter asking to change a rule
A short film to shift attitudes

scenarios.relearn: Noticeboards and films are awareness; rule-asks are advocacy; listening corners and buddy schemes are service.

scenarios.hook: Sort each line: a real milestone you can tick, or not one yet?
scenarios.relearn: A milestone is something you can tick: allies confirmed, a workshop run, a count; a feeling isn't.

scenarios.hook: Sort each ally by the main strength they'd add to your project.

items.text: A teacher who can offer a room
A peer who designs posters fast
An NGO with years of experience
A friend who speaks well in public
A classmate good with sign-up forms

scenarios.relearn: Allies bring different strengths: backing and venues, strong voices, or practical skills and tools.

scenarios.hook: Sort each step into the order a plan moves through.
scenarios.relearn: A plan moves goal-allies-tactic first, then act, then measure and hand over; order keeps it sane.
The POSH Act 2013 makes workplace sexual harassment a real, actionable matter.
scenarios.hook: "Harassment at work is just office politics; no law touches it."

myth.un: Harassment at work is just office politics; no law touches it.
myth.re: The POSH Act 2013 requires workplaces to act on sexual harassment.
myth.why: It's a real, enforceable law a campaign can point colleagues to.

scenarios.relearn: Demanding or giving dowry is illegal under the Dowry Prohibition Act.
scenarios.hook: "Dowry is a custom, so there's no law against asking for it."

myth.un: Dowry is a custom, so no law can stop someone asking for it.
myth.re: The Dowry Prohibition Act makes demanding or giving dowry a punishable offence.
myth.why: A campaign can cite this real law, not just argue about custom.

scenarios.relearn: Equality before the law is a constitutional right, not a favour.
scenarios.hook: "Equal treatment is a nice idea, not something the law guarantees."

myth.un: Equal treatment is a nice idea, not something the law guarantees.
myth.re: The Constitution guarantees equality before the law for everyone in India.
myth.why: A cause can stand on a real right, not just a hope.

scenarios.relearn: Serious crimes against women are covered by the BNS 2023.
scenarios.hook: "The criminal law is ancient and ignores crimes against women."

myth.un: The criminal law is ancient and ignores crimes against women.
myth.re: The BNS 2023 is India's current criminal code and covers serious crimes against women.
myth.why: A campaign can point to the law that's actually in force today.

scenarios.relearn: Protection from domestic violence covers more than physical harm.
scenarios.hook: "The domestic violence law only counts if someone is physically hit."

myth.un: The domestic violence law only counts if someone is physically hit.
myth.re: The Domestic Violence Act 2005 also covers emotional, economic and verbal abuse.
myth.why: Knowing its real scope lets a campaign inform people accurately.

scenarios.hook: A classmate is worried about a woman she knows.
scenarios.setup: She wants a number now, before the bell goes.

steps.prompt: Your classmate asks: "Where can a woman call if someone is hurting her?"

options.text: "The women's helpline is 181, and 112 in an emergency."
options.then: She takes a pen. "Thanks. Say them once more."

options.text: "Um, there's some number. Maybe search for it online later."
options.then: She nods. She searches and finds many numbers.

options.text: "I think there's a number. Ask around. Someone will know."
options.then: She asks two friends. Neither is sure, and she still has no number.

options.text: "She should try to sort it out herself first."
options.then: She frowns. "Sort it out how?"

steps.why: Giving the verified numbers at once gives her a real route, with no guesswork.

steps.prompt: Your classmate says: "Is there one number for everyone, or only for women?"

options.text: "181 is for women. Under 18s can call Childline 1098."
options.then: "Good to know," she says, and notes it.

options.text: "Only women. Nobody else can get help from any helpline."
options.then: She looks worried. "Nobody else?"

options.text: "I think anyone can call any number and they'll sort it out."
options.then: She shrugs. She isn't sure which to choose.

options.text: "Don't worry about the details. Just call whichever you like."
options.then: She nods. She's still not sure which one fits.

steps.why: Matching each person to the right service gets them help faster.

steps.prompt: Your classmate says: "What if she's too afraid to call?"

options.text: "A trusted adult can help her call. She can choose who."
options.then: She nods. "That helps. She isn't alone."

options.text: "Then she should just ignore it and hope it passes."
options.then: She frowns. "That leaves her with nothing to do."

options.text: "Then calling isn't for her. Some people just can't do it."
options.then: She looks unhappy. "That doesn't feel right."

options.text: "Then nobody can help until she calls by herself."
options.then: She frowns. "That can't be right. Someone should be able to help."

steps.why: A trusted adult can help her take the first step safely. It is never her fault.

steps.prompt: Your classmate asks: "Can I put the helpline numbers on our class board?"

options.text: "Yes. I'll check each number against a verified source first."
options.then: "Perfect," she says. "I'll make space on the board."

options.text: "Sure. Copy them from our chat. They should be right."
options.then: She copies them. A digit is wrong.

options.text: "Yes, and add a few others you remember too."
options.then: She adds three numbers. Two of them are wrong.

options.text: "No. They're private and shouldn't go on a board."
options.then: She looks surprised. The board stays empty.

steps.why: Checking each digit against a verified source keeps the board accurate.

scenarios.relearn: Point people to the real helpline instead of guessing a number.

scenarios.hook: A friend pulls you aside after a meeting, looking upset.
scenarios.setup: Part of you thinks her story could help the campaign.

steps.prompt: Your friend says quietly: "Something's wrong at home."

options.text: "Thank you for telling me. I believe you. It's not your fault."
options.then: Her eyes fill. "I thought you'd think I was making it up."

options.text: "This would make such a powerful story for our campaign page."
options.then: She stiffens. "No. I didn't tell you for that."

options.text: "Are you sure? Families fight. It might be nothing."
options.then: She shrinks. "Maybe. I don't know. Forget it."

options.text: "Tell me everything that happened, from the very start."
options.then: She goes quiet. "I can't. Not all at once."

steps.why: Believing her and saying it's not her fault makes it safe to say more.

steps.prompt: Your friend says: "Please don't tell anyone."

options.text: "I won't share it around. A trusted adult could help. Who?"
options.then: She nods slowly. "Maybe the counsellor."

options.text: "Okay, I promise. I'll keep it secret forever, whatever happens."
options.then: She relaxes. Nothing changes at home.

options.text: "I'll tell the principal right now. She'll fix it."
options.then: She backs away. "Not like that. Not yet."

options.text: "Okay. Let's forget it. It will probably get better."
options.then: She nods quietly, but the worry stays in her eyes.

steps.why: A trusted adult can help in ways a friend can't, and she chooses who.

steps.prompt: Later, your friend asks: "Is there somewhere I can call?"

options.text: "Childline 1098 is free for under 18s. 112 in danger."
options.then: She repeats both numbers. "I'll save them."

options.text: "Just call whoever. Maybe somebody will answer you."
options.then: She nods vaguely. She doesn't know who.

options.text: "No. Better to wait and see what happens first."
options.then: She looks down. "Okay."

options.text: "Post about it. Someone will reply with advice."
options.then: She goes pale. "Please don't post anything."

steps.why: Childline 1098 is for anyone under 18, and 112 is for danger right now.

steps.prompt: Your friend says: "Will you come with me when I tell someone?"

options.text: "Yes. Whenever you're ready, I'll be right beside you."
options.then: She squeezes your hand. "Tomorrow, maybe."

options.text: "I'll tell them for you, so you don't have to say it."
options.then: She hesitates. "I wanted to say it myself."

options.text: "Maybe later. I'm busy this week with the campaign."
options.then: She nods. She looks hurt.

options.text: "You can do it alone. You're stronger than you think."
options.then: She nods. She walks away alone.

steps.why: Staying beside her while she tells a trusted adult makes it feel safer.

scenarios.relearn: On a disclosure, protect privacy and route to a trusted adult. Never expose it.

options.text: Share lawful complaint routes and helplines with an adult
