options.text: Print posters naming and shaming him all over the market
options.then: The posters go up. He hears of it, and the risk now lands on your team.

options.text: Gather the team and confront him at the market
options.then: He shouts back. A crowd gathers and people feel less safe.

options.text: Say it's not your business and do nothing about it
options.then: The team deflates. The market stays the same.

steps.why: Lawful routes and helplines protect people without risking you or others.

steps.prompt: A teammate says naming him online would get the campaign far more attention. What do you say?

options.text: Say naming him is unlawful and risky, and offer routes
options.then: Her eyes narrow, then she nods. "Okay. That's true."

options.text: Say any attention is good attention, so go for it
options.then: The idea sticks. A few people start drafting captions.

options.text: Say yes, but only if we blur his face in the photo
options.then: It feels like a compromise. He's still easy to identify.

options.text: Say we can't decide, so let's drop the whole thing
options.then: The meeting ends flat. The anger has nowhere to go.

steps.why: Naming him is unlawful and risky, while accurate routes to help keep people safe.

steps.prompt: A shopkeeper tells you women avoid that lane. What do you do?

options.text: Thank him, tell a trusted adult, and share the routes
options.then: He nods. "Good. Someone should know."

options.text: Tell him to deal with it himself
options.then: He shrugs. The lane stays the same.

options.text: Ask women in the lane to give their names for a list
options.then: Women hesitate. Some worry about who will see the list.

options.text: Post what the shopkeeper said online
options.then: A post goes up. The comments turn into rumours.

steps.why: Passing it to a trusted adult and sharing routes helps without exposing anyone.

scenarios.debrief: Lawful, accurate action protects your cause and everyone in it.
scenarios.relearn: Choose the lawful, accurate route over a vigilante stunt.

scenarios.hook: A volunteer drafts a flyer claiming a brand-new law you've never heard of.

steps.prompt: The flyer is due at the printers today. What do you do?

options.text: Ask where it comes from and check a real source
options.then: The volunteer admits he saw it on a forwarded message.

options.text: Print it as drafted, since it sounds about right
options.then: The flyers go out. A teacher later asks where the claim came from.

options.text: Ask him if he's really sure, then print it if so
options.then: He says yes. He has no source either.

options.text: Add the word "reportedly" and then print it as is
options.then: The flyers look careful. The claim is still unchecked.

steps.why: Checking a legal claim before it's printed keeps your campaign reliable.

steps.prompt: A fresh print deadline is close. The volunteer says checking the claim will make you miss it. What do you say?

options.text: Say a late flyer is better than a wrong one
options.then: He sighs. "Okay. I'll help look it up."

options.text: Say okay, and fix it in the next print run
options.then: This print run goes out with the claim still in it.

options.text: Print half now and check the rest later
options.then: Half the flyers circulate with the claim. Some are already in bags.

options.text: Say it's his job to sort out
options.then: He gets defensive. He stops volunteering for the week.

steps.why: A late flyer is fine, but a wrong one can mislead people.

steps.prompt: You find the claim is only partly true. What do you do?

options.text: Correct the flyer, and kindly tell him why
options.then: He nods. "That makes sense. Thanks for checking."

options.text: Keep the claim in, with the word "maybe" added
options.then: The flyer is hedged. It still misleads.

options.text: Print it now and fix the facts online a bit later
options.then: The paper copies stay out there. The online fix reaches few.

options.text: Throw out the flyer and all of his other work too
options.then: He feels humiliated and leaves the team.

steps.why: Correcting the flyer and saying why helps the volunteer learn.

scenarios.debrief: Accuracy is the tool: verify every legal claim before it goes out.
scenarios.relearn: Verify a legal claim before you put it on a campaign.

scenarios.hook: Someone at your stall asks you to tell her exactly what to do in her legal case.

steps.prompt: She waits for your answer. What do you say?

options.text: Say you can't advise, and point her to legal aid and 181
options.then: She writes down the details and thanks you.

options.text: Give her a confident plan from what you've read online
options.then: She leaves with a plan. Part of it doesn't fit her situation.

options.text: Say you'll look it up and give her the answer tomorrow
options.then: She comes back. Your answer is still a guess.

options.text: Tell her to forget the case and move on
options.then: She looks stung and steps away from the stall.

steps.why: Pointing to legal aid and a helpline gives her accurate, qualified guidance.

steps.prompt: Later, she says she's afraid it will be too much hassle. What do you say?

options.text: Say it's worth a try, and offer to look together
options.then: She nods. "Okay, let's look."

options.text: Say you're sure it'll be quick and simple for her
options.then: She relaxes. Later it turns out to be slower than that.

options.text: Agree that it's probably not worth all the effort
options.then: She nods. She leaves without trying.

options.text: Say you'll call them yourself and handle all of it
options.then: She is relieved. You can't speak for her case.

steps.why: Offering to find the contact details with her makes the next step feel smaller.

steps.prompt: A teammate suggests keeping notes on visitors' cases. What do you say?

options.text: Say no, because people's cases are private
options.then: He shrugs. "Okay. I just thought it would help."

options.text: Say yes, because it will help the campaign
options.then: The notes pile up. Visitors don't know who may read them.

options.text: Say yes, and keep them in the group chat
options.then: Everyone in the group can now see them. Visitors would be upset to know.

options.text: Say yes, but only for the interesting cases
options.then: The notebook fills with stories of people who didn't agree.

steps.why: People's cases are private, so the stall keeps no personal notes.

steps.prompt: A visitor asks you to come to her hearing as her helper. What do you say?

options.text: Say you can't speak for her, and help find legal aid
options.then: She nods. "Okay. Could a teacher come with me too?"

options.text: Say yes and speak for her at the hearing
options.then: You go along. You aren't able to answer the questions asked.

options.text: Say yes and prepare her answers for the hearing
options.then: She learns your lines. They don't fit her real situation.

options.text: Say no politely and wish her the best of luck
options.then: She thanks you politely and heads home alone.

steps.why: You can help her find qualified support, not speak for her.

scenarios.debrief: Knowing your limits and pointing to qualified help is responsible.
scenarios.relearn: Point to qualified help instead of improvising legal advice.

scenarios.hook: Your colony talk on women's safety is going well, with two minutes left.

steps.prompt: How do you end the talk?

options.text: Write 181, 1098 and 112 where people can copy them
options.then: People copy the numbers into their phones before leaving.

options.text: End with a slogan and applause, and thank everyone
options.then: The room claps warmly. Few remember what to do next.

options.text: Ask everyone to share your page and like your posts
options.then: Some do. Your page grows and nobody has a number to call.

options.text: Say people can ask you privately if they're worried
options.then: A few look at the floor. Asking you feels harder than a number.

steps.why: A usable route to help stays with people after the applause fades.

steps.prompt: A neighbour stays behind and asks which helpline she should call, and for what. What do you say?

options.text: 181 is for women, 1098 for under 18s, 112 for emergencies
options.then: She writes it down in her phone with labels.

options.text: Say they're all basically the same, so any of them will do
options.then: She looks puzzled. She isn't sure which to try first.

options.text: Say you'll check later and get back to her next week
options.then: She waits a week. The question stays open.

options.text: Say to call whichever number comes to mind first, really
options.then: She nods. Later she can't remember which one she dialled.

steps.why: Giving each number's purpose clearly keeps people from calling the wrong one.

steps.prompt: An older man says the talk makes women afraid. What do you say?

options.text: Thank him and say knowing where to turn feels safer
options.then: He pauses. "Fair enough. I hadn't seen it like that."

options.text: Argue loudly with him until he finally backs down
options.then: The room goes tense. Others stop listening.

options.text: Agree and promise to tone down the talk next time
options.then: He nods. The next talk has no helplines.

options.text: Say he doesn't understand and walk away from him
options.then: He mutters. A few neighbours decide not to come next time.

steps.why: Bringing people along with respect, and explaining why, keeps the talk useful.

steps.prompt: A neighbour says she tried 181 and it was busy. What do you say?

options.text: Say sorry, ask her to retry, and call 112 if she's in danger now
options.then: She nods. "Okay. I'll keep 112 for an emergency."

options.text: Say the number must be wrong and stop sharing it
options.then: She stops trusting the helpline. Others in the colony do too.

options.text: Say she probably dialled it wrong
options.then: She looks embarrassed and doesn't try again.

options.text: Say helplines are always busy, so don't bother
options.then: She shrugs and puts her phone away.

steps.why: A busy line doesn't mean help isn't there, and 112 is for danger right now.

scenarios.debrief: Awareness plus a concrete route to help is what changes outcomes.
scenarios.relearn: Pair awareness with a concrete next step and helpline.

scenarios.hook: A heated teammate wants to take matters into your own hands after a local case.

steps.prompt: He's furious and wants action tonight. What do you say?

options.text: Say you'll push lawfully, with accurate info and an adult
options.then: He frowns. "That's slow." But he stays to listen.

options.text: Agree that sometimes you have to break rules to be heard
options.then: He grins. A few others nod along, uneasy.

options.text: Say it will blow over in a few days
options.then: He rolls his eyes. "That's what everyone says."

options.text: Tell him to calm down or leave the group
options.then: He glares, then stays, still angry and muttering.

steps.why: Lawful pressure with accurate info and adults keeps the campaign safe and credible.

steps.prompt: A day later, he says the group must show it really means to act, and asks what you will do. What do you say?

options.text: Say lawful steps feel slow, but they keep people safe
options.then: He sighs. "I just hate waiting." He says little for the rest of the meeting.

options.text: Say you'll try something bolder to show you mean it
options.then: The group starts planning a risky stunt.

options.text: Say nothing, because you don't want to argue
options.then: He takes your silence as agreement.

options.text: Agree to a small stunt, just once
options.then: The stunt goes ahead. A parent hears about it and the team is nervous.

steps.why: Slow routes still keep people safe and the cause credible.

steps.prompt: A few days on, the team is tense and he is still wound up. What do you do?

options.text: Check in with him, and offer him a clear role
options.then: He says he was angry for a good reason. He agrees to a trial role.

options.text: Remove him from the group chat for being so angry
options.then: He gets the message that his anger isn't welcome.

options.text: Let the group talk about him behind his back
options.then: The talk turns unkind. People pick sides.

options.text: Go along with his plan, just to keep him close
options.then: He feels like he won. The plan drifts toward risk.

steps.why: Checking in and offering a clear role keeps him in the cause.

steps.prompt: A week later, a teacher asks how the team is doing. What do you say?

options.text: Tell her honestly what happened and ask for backing
options.then: She listens, and offers to sit in on the next meeting.

options.text: Say everything is fine and the team is doing well
options.then: She smiles. The same tension returns next week.

options.text: Say nothing much and change the subject quickly
options.then: She senses something is off and asks someone else.

options.text: Say it was really just one person's fault
options.then: She frowns. The team feels blamed and defensive.

steps.why: Telling the teacher honestly gets backing and keeps everyone safe.

scenarios.debrief: Non-violent, lawful, adult-backed action keeps a cause alive.
scenarios.relearn: Keep activism non-violent, lawful and adult-backed.

scenarios.hook: At your stall, a younger student asks who a person can talk to about abuse.

steps.prompt: She waits for your answer. What do you tell her?

options.text: Childline 1098 is free, and a trusted adult can help
options.then: She repeats the number twice to remember it.

options.text: Say she can wait until she's 18 and then call them
options.then: She nods. The waiting feels very long.

options.text: Say you'll find out and bring the answer next week
options.then: She nods. A week is a long time to carry a worry.

options.text: Ask her to explain exactly what has happened to her
options.then: She goes quiet and steps back from the stall.

steps.why: Childline 1098 is for anyone under 18, and a trusted adult can help too.

steps.prompt: She says she doesn't want her teacher to know. What do you say?

options.text: Say she can pick the adult, like a counsellor
options.then: She thinks. "Maybe the counsellor, not my teacher."

options.text: Promise to keep it a secret from everyone at school
options.then: She smiles. Nothing changes and you can't help further.

options.text: Say you'll go and tell her teacher yourself today
options.then: She looks upset. She says she shouldn't have asked.

options.text: Say she's old enough to handle it all herself
options.then: She nods stiffly. She hesitates, looking unsure.

steps.why: A trusted adult she picks can help, so she isn't carrying it alone.

steps.prompt: She asks if calling will get her in trouble. What do you say?

options.text: Say it's not her fault and Childline is there to help
options.then: Her shoulders ease. "Okay. I think I'll call."

options.text: Say you're not sure, so she should be careful
options.then: She frowns. She puts the number away.

options.text: Say it might, so she should think twice about it
options.then: She goes quiet. The number stays in her pocket.

options.text: Say to try it once and just see what happens
options.then: She nods. She feels alone with the choice.

steps.why: Calling for help isn't something she'd be blamed for, and it's not her fault.

scenarios.debrief: Pointing people to the right service gets real help faster.
scenarios.relearn: Match the person to the correct service.

scenarios.hook: In your group chat, someone posts that reporting harassment never does anything.

steps.prompt: A few others start agreeing. What do you do?

options.text: Gently correct it and share the real routes to help
options.then: A couple of people say they didn't know about the routes.

options.text: Agree, to seem relatable and keep the chat friendly
options.then: More people pile on. The chat gets quieter about help.

options.text: Ignore it and hope the topic passes
options.then: The message stays at the top for days.

options.text: Reply angrily with a long lecture
options.then: He replies in capitals. Others leave the thread.

steps.why: A gentle correction with real routes keeps people trusting that help can be reached.

steps.prompt: He says his cousin reported once and nothing happened. What do you say?

options.text: Say sorry it went that way, and share 181 and other routes
options.then: He softens. "I didn't know about the others."

options.text: Say his cousin must have done it wrong
options.then: He bristles. "That's unfair to say."

options.text: Say he's right, so never mind
options.then: The thread dies. Nobody mentions help again.

options.text: Ask for his cousin's name to look into it
options.then: He hesitates. His cousin's privacy is now at risk.

steps.why: Acknowledging it and pointing to other routes keeps trust and hope.

steps.prompt: The chat goes quiet. How do you keep the information alive?

options.text: Pin a short note with the helplines and say help is real
options.then: People thank you. It stays at the top of the group.

options.text: Drop a long article into the chat
options.then: A few react. Nobody reads the whole thing.

options.text: Move on to another topic and say nothing more
options.then: The chat stays quiet. The myth stays unanswered.

options.text: Message each person privately asking if they've been harassed
options.then: Some feel put on the spot and go silent.

steps.why: A short, calm pinned message keeps the routes in view without pressure.

steps.prompt: Someone messages you privately that something happened to her. What do you say?

options.text: Say it's not her fault and find a trusted adult
options.then: She says it's the first time she's told anyone.

options.text: Ask for every detail so you know exactly what to do
options.then: She feels like she's being questioned and stops replying.

options.text: Promise to keep it secret and not tell anyone ever
options.then: She feels relieved. Nothing changes for her.

options.text: Share it in the group chat, anonymously, to make a point
options.then: She sees it and feels exposed. She leaves the chat.

steps.why: Believing her, saying it's not her fault, and helping her reach a trusted adult keeps her safe.

scenarios.debrief: 'Reporting is pointless' is a rumour worth correcting with real routes.
scenarios.relearn: Correct a discouraging rumour rather than let it spread.

scenarios.hook: A follower DMs your campaign a person's name as the guy to expose.

steps.prompt: What do you do with the message?

options.text: Skip the name and reply with lawful routes and helplines
options.then: She reads your reply. She says she hadn't known about the routes.

options.text: Post the name so others can stay alert
options.then: The post spreads fast, and so does a rumour about someone else with the same name. You take it down.

options.text: Ask for proof and post the name if it looks convincing
options.then: She sends a screenshot. You can't tell if it's real.

options.text: Delete the message and say nothing back to her
options.then: She waits for a reply that never comes.

steps.why: Sharing lawful routes helps without making your campaign an accusation account.

steps.prompt: The follower writes again, saying naming him is the only thing that works. What do you say?

options.text: Explain that naming can backfire, and offer routes
options.then: She goes quiet, then writes: "Okay. Where do I start?"

options.text: Give in and promise to post his name tonight, as asked
options.then: She thanks you. A friend of his messages you angrily.

options.text: Block her without a word, just to end the argument
options.then: She vanishes from your inbox. Whatever she needed goes unanswered.

options.text: Argue back at her until she finally backs down
options.then: She stops replying. She feels lectured, not helped.

steps.why: Explaining why naming can hurt people, and offering routes, keeps trust.

steps.prompt: A teammate wants to hint at the name with just an initial. What do you say?

options.text: Say no, because a hint still points at him
options.then: He sighs. "Fine. The routes it is."

options.text: Say yes, as long as the initial isn't obvious
options.then: People guess within an hour. The comments get ugly.

options.text: Say yes, as long as you don't tag him
options.then: The post hints at a person without proof. It spreads on its own.

options.text: Say let's put it to a group vote
options.then: The vote splits. Some members feel unheard either way.

steps.why: Hints still point at him, so your campaign sticks to info and routes.

steps.prompt: A week later, she reaches out again, saying the person keeps bothering her. What do you do?

options.text: Believe her, say it's not her fault, share helplines and a trusted adult
options.then: She says she'll talk to her aunt, a teacher. Hearing it isn't her fault helps.

options.text: Post the name this time, since she's still struggling
options.then: The post is shared widely and reaches him. Things get harder for her.

options.text: Ignore her, since you've already replied once
options.then: She feels brushed off and stops reaching out.

options.text: Tell her to confront him herself
options.then: She goes quiet. You can't know how it ended.

steps.why: Believing her, saying it's not her fault and offering a trusted adult helps more than public accusation.

scenarios.debrief: Your job is accurate routes to help, not public accusations.
scenarios.relearn: Keep accused people's privacy and share routes. You inform; you don't accuse publicly.

scenarios.hook: A teammate is shaking after a stranger threatened her near your meeting place.

steps.prompt: She is upset. What do you do first?

options.text: Make sure she's safe and stay with her
options.then: She leans on you. "Thank you. I didn't want to be alone."

options.text: Ask for every detail right away to write it down
options.then: She stops talking. Her breathing gets faster.

options.text: Tell her it's nothing and to shake it off
options.then: She nods. She is shaking harder.

options.text: Suggest she posts about it so the campaign looks brave
options.then: She looks horrified. She says it isn't a show.

steps.why: Staying with her and keeping her safe comes before anything else.

steps.prompt: She says he might still be nearby. What do you do?

options.text: Move to a place with adults and call 112
options.then: A shopkeeper lets you wait inside. An officer is on the way.

options.text: Go and confront him as a group
options.then: He raises his voice and the situation gets worse, until a shopkeeper steps in and he leaves.

options.text: Wait and see if he leaves by himself
options.then: He doesn't leave. The two of you stand tense until a shopkeeper asks if you are all right.

options.text: Take a photo of him to post later
options.then: He notices the phone and walks toward you. You hurry into a shop, shaken.

steps.why: Moving to adults and calling 112 is the safe response to a threat.

steps.prompt: Later, once she is somewhere safe, she asks if she should tell anyone. What do you say?

options.text: Say yes, and tell a trusted adult who can help
options.then: She nods slowly. "My mum, I think. And my teacher."

options.text: Say better not to, in case it makes things worse
options.then: She nods. She walks home alone, still frightened.

options.text: Say tell only your campaign group
options.then: The group hears. The adults who could help don't.

options.text: Say wait a week and see if it happens again
options.then: The week passes. No adult knows, so nobody can help her.

steps.why: A trusted adult can help report it and keep her safe.

steps.prompt: Some teammates' parents have heard and are worried. What do you do?

options.text: Share the plan with parents and agree safer arrangements
options.then: The parents ask questions. Several agree to keep letting their children come.

options.text: Keep meetings secret from parents so they don't worry
options.then: A parent finds out. The trust is damaged.

options.text: Stop the campaign for good, since it's not worth it
options.then: The team is deflated and the cause loses momentum. A few friends still want to meet up.

options.text: Move meetings to somewhere more hidden
options.then: Nobody can find the new place. Parents feel more anxious.

steps.why: Telling adults the plan and agreeing safer arrangements keeps the team together and safe.

steps.prompt: A week on, a teammate asks how to get to a meet-up safely. What do you say?

options.text: Walk in a group, tell an adult your route, and keep 112 handy
options.then: She feels calmer. The group works out a rota.

options.text: Say it's fine, since nothing will happen
options.then: She nods. She still feels uneasy on the way.

options.text: Say she should go alone, so she isn't seen with the group
options.then: She walks alone. The route feels longer.

options.text: Say she should carry something to defend herself
options.then: She worries more. The idea makes the meetings feel dangerous.

steps.why: Walking in groups and keeping an adult informed lowers the risks.

scenarios.debrief: Real safety threats go to a trusted adult and 112, fast. It is never her fault.
scenarios.relearn: Loop in a trusted adult for a serious safety threat.

scenarios.hook: Your audience speaks little English and finds the legal terms confusing.

steps.prompt: How do you explain the protection?

options.text: Say it in simple local language, with the helpline
options.then: Heads nod. Someone says: "So this is for me too."

options.text: Read out the legal sections word for word, slowly
options.then: Faces go blank. People start talking among themselves.

options.text: Hand out an English leaflet and let people read it
options.then: Most people fold it into a bag. Few read it.

options.text: Use a few big words so you sound sure of the facts
options.then: The words sound impressive. People leave unsure what they mean.

steps.why: Plain local language, with the helpline, makes rights usable.

steps.prompt: An elder says rights are for city people. What do you say?

options.text: Say rights are for everyone, and give a local example
options.then: He listens. "Hm. I didn't think that applied here."

options.text: Tell him flatly that he's wrong about all of this
options.then: He folds his arms. The talk gets tense.

options.text: Agree with him and quickly move to the next point
options.then: He nods. The people near him lose interest.

options.text: Say you'll bring a lawyer along next time instead
options.then: The elder shrugs. It's a promise you can't be sure to keep.

steps.why: Respectful examples show that rights belong to everyone.

steps.prompt: Afterwards, people ask you to write down the helpline numbers for them. What do you do?

options.text: Write them in local script and check with a teacher
options.then: They copy them carefully. A teacher confirms the digits.

options.text: Write them from memory, as clearly as you possibly can
options.then: You get most right. One digit is swapped.

options.text: Tell them to just take a photo of your slide instead
options.then: Many can't. A few photos are blurry.

options.text: Give only one number for everything, to keep it simple
options.then: People leave with a single number for every situation.

steps.why: Checked, clear numbers in local script are usable by everyone present.

scenarios.debrief: Rights are only a tool when people can understand and use them.
scenarios.relearn: Plain-language legal facts make rights usable for everyone.

scenarios.hook: You're deciding the tone of a poster on workplace harassment.

steps.prompt: Which version do you draft?

options.text: State the protection and the route calmly
options.then: Readers stop, read and note the route.

options.text: Use a terrifying image to shock people
options.then: People flinch and look away. Few read the small print.

options.text: Add a joke to make it less awkward
options.then: People laugh. Some think it can't be serious.

options.text: Only describe the problem, with no route
options.then: People understand the problem. Nobody learns what to do.

steps.why: Calm information and a clear route help people act without fear.

steps.prompt: A teammate says the poster still won't get noticed on a busy wall. What do you say?

options.text: Say clear and calm is easier to trust and act on
options.then: She thinks. "Okay. But make the headline big."

options.text: Agree and add scarier wording to stand out
options.then: The poster gets noticed. It also upsets younger readers.

options.text: Say let's use bold red capitals for everything
options.then: It shouts at every reader. People stop reading it.

options.text: Say let's put the poster on hold and make a video first
options.then: The poster waits. The video takes weeks to plan.

steps.why: Clear and calm is easier to trust, and people can act on it.

steps.prompt: A friend sees the poster draft and worries it will make people nervous about work. What do you do?

options.text: Keep it calm and add a line that help exists
options.then: She reads it again. "That does feel steadier."

options.text: Pull the poster to avoid worrying anyone
options.then: The wall is blank again. Readers lose a route to help.

options.text: Make the poster funnier to lighten the mood
options.then: The jokes grow. The route gets harder to spot.

options.text: Add a statistic to prove it's serious
options.then: The number sounds scary. People ask where it came from.

steps.why: Adding that help exists lets calm information reassure instead of scare.

scenarios.debrief: The law works best stated calmly with a clear route.
scenarios.relearn: Use the law as a calm backbone, not a scare tactic.

scenarios.hook: During a Q&A, someone asks a detailed legal question you don't know.

steps.prompt: The room waits for your answer. What do you say?

options.text: Say you'll check a source, and point to legal aid
options.then: She nods and writes down where to go.

options.text: Make up a confident-sounding answer on the spot
options.then: She thanks you. Part of what you said is not accurate.

options.text: Say everyone has this question, and move on quickly
options.then: She sits down, still without her answer.

options.text: Pass the question to a friend who read about it once
options.then: Your friend guesses, and the room can tell he isn't sure.

steps.why: Admitting what you don't know and pointing to qualified help is honest and useful.

steps.prompt: Later, she finds you again and asks about her question. What do you do?

options.text: Check a verified source and share what you find
options.then: You find a source and read it carefully. It isn't a simple yes or no.

options.text: Let it go, now that the Q&A has ended
options.then: She waits for an answer. Nothing comes.

options.text: Ask a friend who thinks she knows the answer
options.then: The friend sounds sure, but has no source either.

options.text: Post your best guess on the group page for now
options.then: Several people share it. A reader later points out an error.

steps.why: Following through with a verified source keeps your word and your campaign's trust.

steps.prompt: A week later she asks once more. By now you have read a verified source: the answer depends on the case. What do you tell her?

options.text: Say it depends, and legal aid can look at it
options.then: She says: "Okay. At least I know where to go."

options.text: Give your best guess anyway, so she has something
options.then: She leaves with an answer. It may not apply to her.

options.text: Say nothing, since you can't give a clear answer
options.then: She waits, then leaves without any direction.

options.text: Tell her not to worry because it will work out
options.then: She smiles. You've promised something you can't know.

steps.why: Saying plainly that it depends, and where to turn, is the honest answer.

scenarios.debrief: 'I'll check, and here's qualified help' beats a confident guess.
scenarios.relearn: When unsure of a legal fact, defer to a verified source or qualified help.

scenarios.hook: A classmate tells you a senior keeps harassing her at her internship.

steps.prompt: She is upset. What do you say first?

options.text: Tell her you believe her and it's not her fault
options.then: She wipes her eyes. "I thought it was just me," she says.

options.text: Tell her to quit the internship and forget about it
options.then: She looks stung. The internship was important to her.

options.text: Ask what she did that made him act that way
options.then: She goes red and stops. She starts to wonder if she's to blame.

options.text: Tell her to ignore him and stay polite
options.then: She nods. The behaviour doesn't change.

steps.why: Believing her and saying it's not her fault keeps her talking.

steps.prompt: She asks what she can do. What do you say?

options.text: Tell her about the complaint committee and offer to help
options.then: She sits up. "I didn't know there was one."

options.text: Say she should quit quietly and move on to another one
options.then: She looks away. She would lose the internship.

options.text: Say you'll go and complain on her behalf yourself
options.then: She panics. She wanted to decide for herself.

options.text: Say to wait until the whole internship ends first
options.then: She nods. The weeks feel long for her.

steps.why: Naming the committee as a lawful route gives her a real option.

steps.prompt: A week later, she's thinking about making a complaint and feels nervous. What do you do?

options.text: Offer to go with her, plus a trusted adult
options.then: She relaxes. "Mr. Rao would come," she says.

options.text: Say she'll be fine going in on her own
options.then: She goes in alone. She feels very small.

options.text: Say she should let it go instead
options.then: She nods. The senior sees her again next week.

options.text: Say you'll write the whole complaint for her
options.then: She feels relieved, then realises it isn't in her words.

steps.why: Going with her, with a trusted adult too, keeps her supported and in charge.

steps.prompt: She asks if you should tell the group, to get support. What do you say?

options.text: Say it's her story, so it stays private
options.then: She smiles. "Thank you. I might tell them myself later."

options.text: Say yes, because it will help the campaign
options.then: She looks hurt. She didn't want her story to be a poster.

options.text: Say yes, but only to your closest friends
options.then: The closest friends tell their closest friends. It spreads.

options.text: Say yes, as long as you leave out her name
options.then: People can still guess who. She feels exposed.

steps.why: It's her story, so it stays private unless she chooses otherwise.

scenarios.debrief: A built-in lawful route can support her, and her story stays hers.
scenarios.relearn: A workplace complaint committee is a lawful, built-in route worth naming.

scenarios.hook: A teammate isn't sure of the Childline number and wants to just guess.

steps.prompt: He's about to print the poster. What do you do?

options.text: Look up the verified Childline number, 1098, before printing
options.then: The poster is printed with 1098. It matches the source.

options.text: Let him print a guessed number, since it's close enough
options.then: The poster goes up. The number doesn't connect.

options.text: Print "Childline" with no number, so no one can get it wrong
options.then: The poster is correct, and nobody can call from it.

options.text: Ask another friend what number they remember
options.then: She remembers a different one. You now have two guesses.

steps.why: A verified number is the difference between help and a dead end.

steps.prompt: The next poster is due, and he says checking numbers every time is a waste. What do you say?

options.text: Say a wrong number sends someone nowhere
options.then: He rubs his neck. "Okay. I hadn't thought of it that way."

options.text: Say it is his call and leave it as it is
options.then: The poster goes ahead with the guess.

options.text: Say you'll check quietly after it's printed
options.then: The checked number arrives too late for the first batch.

options.text: Say print two numbers to cover the guess
options.then: The poster lists two numbers. One of them is wrong.

steps.why: A wrong number sends someone nowhere at the moment they need help.

steps.prompt: A neighbour asks for copies of the poster for her building. What do you do?

options.text: Check the number against the source, then share that version
options.then: She pins the poster up. The numbers match the source.

options.text: Let her retype it for the building's noticeboard
options.then: She retypes it. One digit is typed wrong.

options.text: Hand her a draft with a note to fix any errors
options.then: She doesn't know what to fix. The draft goes up as it is.

options.text: Say no, to avoid any mistakes
options.then: She looks disappointed. Her building gets no poster.

steps.why: Sharing a version checked against the source keeps every copy accurate.

scenarios.relearn: Share helplines exactly; a wrong number sends people nowhere.
